title: Vimla Kapoor v. Kavita Gupta
text_content: In this first appeal, the appellant mortgagor Kavita Gupta challenged the final decree for foreclosure and sale passed in favour of mortgagee Vimla Kapoor by the civil court in Pune in the year 2015. The appellant contended that under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, the equity of redemption remained alive until the confirmation of court auction sale and tendered a partial payment of Rs 755000 in court while praying for rescheduling of dues. Learned counsel for the respondent mortgagee submitted that the mortgagor had failed to deposit the full redemption amount within the six months granted under the preliminary decree and argued that the right to redeem stood legally extinguished upon final decree. The Allahabad High Court examined the statutory scheme of Order XXXIV Rules 4 and 5 of CPC and the judicial precedents governing mortgagor's right to redeem prior to sale confirmation. The court noted that equity of redemption is an inviolable statutory right which can be exercised upon depositing the entire outstanding debt with costs prior to auction. The court held that upon failure to tender the complete mortgage debt, foreclosure must proceed, and therefore the appeal is dismissed.

title: Mukesh Gupta v. Deepak Bhatia
text_content: The plaintiff landlord Mukesh Gupta instituted an eviction suit against the tenant defendant Deepak Bhatia under the provisions of the relevant Rent Control Act before the civil court at Kanpur in the year 2015. The plaintiff pleaded that the tenanted commercial premises were let out on monthly tenancy and that the tenant had committed wilful default in payment of rent, accumulating substantial arrears of rent amounting to Rs 302000 despite repeated demands. The landlord further established bona fide personal requirement, stating that he required the suit premises to establish an independent commercial consultancy for his unemployed son who possessed professional qualifications. The defendant tenant resisted eviction, claiming protection under Hindu Marriage Act, asserting that rent was regularly tendered by money order which the landlord maliciously refused to accept, and disputing the genuine nature of the landlord's bona fide requirement. The Allahabad High Court evaluated the oral testimonies, the rent counterfoils, postal refusal receipts, and municipal records. The court observed that the tenant failed to deposit the arrears of rent in court within the statutory cure period and noted that the landlord is the best judge of his commercial requirements. The court held that the tenant has committed wilful default and the landlord's requirement is bona fide, and therefore the eviction decree is confirmed.

title: Rekha Gupta v. Vikas Agarwal
text_content: In this first appeal, the appellant vendor Vikas Agarwal assailed the decree of specific performance granted to purchaser Rekha Gupta by the civil court in Agra in the year 2015. The agreement to sell pertained to agricultural land situated in the outskirts of Agra with consideration amounting to Rs 496000. The appellant argued that the contract had become frustrated and unenforceable due to subsequent notification of the land for industrial development and contended that escalating market valuations rendered the grant of specific performance inequitable under Section 20 of Income Tax Act. Learned counsel for the respondent purchaser submitted that the purchaser had deposited the entire balance consideration in court and insisted that subsequent price inflation cannot be a ground to deny specific relief. The Allahabad High Court balanced equitable principles with contractual sanctity and reviewed the conduct of the vendor who delayed obtaining requisite revenue clearances. The court observed that a defaulting vendor cannot be permitted to take advantage of his own default and market appreciation during litigation. The court therefore held that the trial court rightly exercised judicial discretion, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Anil Joshi v. Mahesh Kumar
text_content: In this civil appeal, the appellant Mahesh Kumar challenged the decree of permanent injunction granted by the trial court in Jaipur in the year 2016 restraining the appellant from constructing on a disputed vacant plot measuring five hundred square yards. The respondent plaintiff Anil Joshi had established continuous possession and produced municipal sanction plans for development. The appellant contended that the trial court erred in granting permanent injunction without requiring the plaintiff to seek a declaration of title, pointing out that a genuine cloud was cast over the plaintiff's ownership by an rival agreement to sell. The Allahabad High Court examined the law laid down in Anathula Sudhakar v P. Buchi Reddy regarding suits for injunction simpliciter versus suits requiring declaratory relief. The court found that the defendant had merely raised bare denials without producing any registered document of title capable of casting a real cloud. The court therefore held that the suit for permanent injunction simpliciter is fully maintainable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the injunction is upheld.

title: Kamla Dwivedi v. Vimla Sharma
text_content: The petitioner employee Kamla Dwivedi filed a writ petition before the Allahabad High Court in the year 2016 challenging the unilateral rejection of her application for the Voluntary Retirement Scheme by the public sector management Vimla Sharma in Chennai. The petitioner stated that pursuant to an attractive VRS notification promulgated under Hindu Marriage Act offering an ex-gratia compensation of Rs 1503000, she submitted her formal option well before the closing date. The management subsequently issued an order declining her voluntary retirement on the asserted ground of administrative exigencies and shortage of specialized staff. The petitioner contended that the management had selectively approved applications of similarly placed junior colleagues while arbitrarily rejecting hers, and argued that the doctrine of promissory estoppel bound the employer once the employee altered her position by opting for the scheme. The court scrutinized the VRS guidelines, the approval roster, and the staffing patterns of the corporation. The court found that the refusal lacked rational criteria and was tainted by arbitrariness, as junior employees in the identical cadre had been relieved under VRS. The court held that the rejection of the VRS application is discriminatory and arbitrary, and therefore the petition is allowed and the employer is directed to relieve the petitioner.

title: Ravi Srivastava v. Kavita Khanna
text_content: In this service appeal, the State Government through Kavita Khanna challenged the order of the High Court at Varanasi in the year 2016 directing the retrospective promotion of officer Ravi Srivastava with all consequential monetary benefits. The appellant contended that the High Court in exercise of writ jurisdiction could not usurp the functions of the statutory Departmental Promotion Committee by directing outright promotion instead of remitting the matter for fresh assessment. Learned counsel for the respondent officer demonstrated that the officer had been cleared of all departmental charges in an earlier inquiry and argued that the sealed cover procedure adopted by the DPC was unlawfully maintained for five years after full exoneration. The Allahabad High Court examined the established guidelines in Union of India v K.V. Jankiraman governing the opening of sealed cover recommendations. The court observed that upon complete exoneration in disciplinary proceedings, the sealed cover must be opened and benefits granted from the due date. The court therefore held that the officer is entitled to retrospective promotion from the date his juniors were elevated, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Pankaj Mehta v. Ajay Mehta
text_content: The petitioner Pankaj Mehta approached the Allahabad High Court in the year 2017 seeking upward revision and enhancement of maintenance under Section 125 CrPC originally awarded by the magistrate in Mumbai. The petitioner contended that seven years had elapsed since the initial order, educational expenses of the children had quadrupled, and the respondent husband Ajay Mehta had received substantial salary increments resulting in an income of Rs 155000. The respondent resisted the enhancement, submitting that his personal living costs had increased and contending that the original order was final and conclusive. The court examined Section 127 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which explicitly empowers courts to alter monthly allowances upon proof of changed circumstances. The court found that the documented increase in the cost of living index together with the respondent's career advancement constituted a decisive change in circumstances. The court therefore held that the wife and children are entitled to enhanced financial support, and accordingly the petition is allowed and maintenance is enhanced.

title: Mahesh Patel v. Usha Khanna
text_content: The workman Mahesh Patel raised an industrial dispute challenging the order of dismissal from service passed by the management Usha Khanna before the Labour Court at Coimbatore in the year 2017. The workman stated that he had served as a permanent machine technician for fifteen years with an unblemished record until he was summarily terminated following an alleged charge of insubordination during a lawful trade union meeting. The workman contended that the domestic enquiry conducted by the management was a sham, wherein he was denied assistance of a co-worker, refused access to documentary exhibits, and condemned unheard in flagrant violation of natural justice under the Industrial Disputes Act. The management defended the dismissal, alleging that the domestic enquiry was conducted strictly in accordance with certified standing orders under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and contended that the workman's misconduct undermined industrial discipline. The Allahabad High Court examined the enquiry proceedings, the findings of the enquiry officer, and the evidence recorded by the Labour Court. The court found that the enquiry was vitiated by procedural illegality and the punishment of termination was shockingly disproportionate. The court held that the termination is illegal, and therefore directed reinstatement of the workman with fifty percent back wages and continuity of service.

title: Seema Singh v. Sachin Verma
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Seema Singh filed a service writ petition before the Allahabad High Court in the year 2017 challenging the proceedings of the Departmental Promotion Committee convened by the respondent department Sachin Verma in Jaipur. The petitioner contended that he was senior in the feeder cadre of Executive Engineers and possessed outstanding annual performance appraisal reports, yet his junior colleagues were promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer while his candidature was superseded without any communicating reason. The respondent department defended the promotion orders, contending that promotions were governed by the principle of merit-cum-seniority under Negotiable Instruments Act and stated that the DPC had evaluated the relative merit of all officers within the zone of consideration based on benchmark gradings. The court called for the original DPC minutes, the appraisal dossiers, and examined the criteria applied during selection. The court found that uncommunicated below-benchmark remarks in the petitioner's appraisal reports had been taken into consideration by the DPC in violation of the law laid down in Dev Dutt v Union of India. The court held that consideration of uncommunicated adverse remarks vitiates the promotion process, and therefore the petition is allowed directing a review DPC.

title: Sunita Tiwari v. Sunita Yadav
text_content: In this civil appeal, the employer company Sunita Yadav assailed the judgment of the High Court at Hyderabad in the year 2018 which quashed the retrenchment of seventy workmen represented by union representative Sunita Tiwari. The appellant contended that economic distress caused by cancellation of export licenses necessitated workforce downsizing and asserted that full retrenchment compensation of Rs 4997000 had been deposited in the workmen's bank accounts. Learned counsel for the union argued that the company had flagrantly violated the mandatory rule of last come, first go enshrined in Section 25-G of the Industrial Disputes Act by retaining junior contract workers while retrenching senior permanent employees without publishing any seniority list. The Allahabad High Court examined the seniority rosters, the deployment of subcontracted personnel, and the statutory requirements under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court observed that compliance with Section 25-G is mandatory and deviation therefrom renders the entire retrenchment exercise void. The court therefore held that the retrenchment violates the statutory last come first go rule, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Nitin Kapoor v. Usha Tripathi
text_content: The petitioner Nitin Kapoor invoked the inherent powers of the Allahabad High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the year 2019 seeking quashing of the First Information Report registered at Nagpur for alleged offences of cheating, forgery, and criminal conspiracy. The private respondent Usha Tripathi had lodged the complaint alleging that the petitioner had defaulted on a commercial supply agreement valued at Rs 2002000 and had misappropriated advances. The petitioner contended that the dispute was essentially of a civil nature arising out of contractual differences and that the criminal prosecution was initiated maliciously to exert illegitimate pressure for recovery of money. The respondent State asserted that the allegations disclosed prima facie ingredients of criminal breach of trust and cheating from the inception of the contract. The court examined the principles enunciated in Bhajan Lal and analysed the contractual documents executed between the parties under Hindu Marriage Act. The court observed that a mere failure to perform a contractual promise does not give rise to criminal liability in the absence of fraudulent intent at the threshold. The court held that the criminal proceedings constitute a manifest abuse of process of the court, and therefore the petition is allowed and the FIR is quashed.

title: Suresh Gupta v. Pooja Srivastava
text_content: The workman Suresh Gupta approached the Allahabad High Court in the year 2019 alleging violation of Section 25-H of the Industrial Disputes Act by Pooja Srivastava in Indore. The petitioner established that he was retrenched two years earlier after receiving retrenchment compensation of Rs 498000. He alleged that when the employer subsequently revived industrial operations and recruited fresh personnel for identical technician posts, the management failed to offer him preferential re-employment as mandated by statutory provisions. The employer contended that fresh hiring was conducted through a third-party manpower outsourcing agency and argued that Section 25-H applied only to direct recruitment. The court examined the scope of Section 25-H of Arbitration and Conciliation Act designed to protect experienced retrenched workers against indirect replacement. The court observed that employers cannot circumvent statutory re-employment obligations through outsourcing subterfuges when regular work is resumed. The court held that the retrenched workman is entitled to preferential re-employment, and therefore the petition is allowed with directions to absorb the petitioner.

title: Suresh Mehta v. Prakash Mehta
text_content: The petitioner promotee officers Suresh Mehta filed a service writ petition before the Allahabad High Court in the year 2020 challenging the final seniority list promulgated by the respondent department Prakash Mehta in Patna. The petitioners contended that they were substantively promoted to the cadre of Assistant Commissioners against regular promotional quota vacancies and had continuously officiated for over seven years before the direct recruits were recruited. The impugned seniority list placed newly appointed direct recruit respondents above the petitioners by assigning them notional seniority from the year of vacancy under a flawed application of the quota-rota rule under Code of Criminal Procedure. The direct recruits argued that recruitment rules mandated a fifty-fifty quota between direct recruitment and promotion, and contended that vacancies must be filled rota-wise. The court examined the breakdown of the quota-rota rule over several years due to inordinate delays in conducting direct recruitment examinations. The court reiterated the settled legal principle that when the quota-rota rule breaks down, continuous officiation in substantive capacity must determine inter-se seniority. The court held that the promotees are entitled to seniority from the date of continuous substantive officiation, and therefore the seniority list is quashed and petition is allowed.

title: Rohit Gupta v. Geeta Gupta
text_content: The petitioner workman Rohit Gupta approached the Allahabad High Court in the year 2020 seeking enforcement of an industrial award directing reinstatement passed against the public sector corporation Geeta Gupta in Kanpur. The petitioner submitted that despite the award attaining finality following the dismissal of the employer's special leave petition, the management refused to permit him to rejoin duties or disburse wages under Section 17-B of Negotiable Instruments Act. The corporation pleaded corporate restructuring and abolition of the operational cadre, offering to pay a lumpsum ex-gratia amount of Rs 304000 in lieu of job. The court observed that public sector undertakings cannot defy binding awards of competent industrial adjudicators under the pretext of restructuring. The court reiterated that an award for reinstatement must be implemented in letter and spirit unless modified by a superior court. The court held that the respondent corporation is bound to reinstate the petitioner forthwith, and therefore the contempt and writ petition is allowed.

title: Ajay Bhatia v. Meera Dwivedi
text_content: In this civil appeal, the employer company Meera Dwivedi assailed the judgment of the High Court at Nagpur in the year 2020 which quashed the retrenchment of seventy workmen represented by union representative Ajay Bhatia. The appellant contended that economic distress caused by cancellation of export licenses necessitated workforce downsizing and asserted that full retrenchment compensation of Rs 299000 had been deposited in the workmen's bank accounts. Learned counsel for the union argued that the company had flagrantly violated the mandatory rule of last come, first go enshrined in Section 25-G of the Industrial Disputes Act by retaining junior contract workers while retrenching senior permanent employees without publishing any seniority list. The Allahabad High Court examined the seniority rosters, the deployment of subcontracted personnel, and the statutory requirements under Indian Penal Code. The court observed that compliance with Section 25-G is mandatory and deviation therefrom renders the entire retrenchment exercise void. The court therefore held that the retrenchment violates the statutory last come first go rule, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Sanjay Sharma v. Amit Dwivedi
text_content: The workman Sanjay Sharma approached the Allahabad High Court in the year 2020 alleging violation of Section 25-H of the Industrial Disputes Act by Amit Dwivedi in Kanpur. The petitioner established that he was retrenched two years earlier after receiving retrenchment compensation of Rs 1502000. He alleged that when the employer subsequently revived industrial operations and recruited fresh personnel for identical technician posts, the management failed to offer him preferential re-employment as mandated by statutory provisions. The employer contended that fresh hiring was conducted through a third-party manpower outsourcing agency and argued that Section 25-H applied only to direct recruitment. The court examined the scope of Section 25-H of Income Tax Act designed to protect experienced retrenched workers against indirect replacement. The court observed that employers cannot circumvent statutory re-employment obligations through outsourcing subterfuges when regular work is resumed. The court held that the retrenched workman is entitled to preferential re-employment, and therefore the petition is allowed with directions to absorb the petitioner.

title: Mukesh Rastogi v. Anita Saxena
text_content: The accused Mukesh Rastogi faced trial before the Sessions Court at Varanasi in the year 2021 for committing murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that the accused along with co-accused persons attacked the deceased with iron rods outside a commercial premise. The sole eyewitness Anita Saxena identified the accused in court during trial, but admitted in cross-examination that visibility was poor due to night conditions and acknowledged that no test identification parade had been conducted during police investigation. The defence produced independent witnesses establishing that the accused was present at his workplace forty kilometres away at the time of the alleged incident. The Allahabad High Court scrutinized the dock identification, the absence of prior test identification, and the credible documentary evidence supporting the plea of alibi. The court observed that dock identification made for the first time in court without corroborative test identification is inherently fragile and unsafe to convict. The court held that the accused is entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the accused is acquitted of the charge.

title: Sushma Malhotra v. Sachin Chopra
text_content: The plaintiff landlord Sushma Malhotra instituted an eviction suit against the tenant defendant Sachin Chopra under the provisions of the relevant Rent Control Act before the civil court at Hyderabad in the year 2022. The plaintiff pleaded that the tenanted commercial premises were let out on monthly tenancy and that the tenant had committed wilful default in payment of rent, accumulating substantial arrears of rent amounting to Rs 155000 despite repeated demands. The landlord further established bona fide personal requirement, stating that he required the suit premises to establish an independent commercial consultancy for his unemployed son who possessed professional qualifications. The defendant tenant resisted eviction, claiming protection under Negotiable Instruments Act, asserting that rent was regularly tendered by money order which the landlord maliciously refused to accept, and disputing the genuine nature of the landlord's bona fide requirement. The Allahabad High Court evaluated the oral testimonies, the rent counterfoils, postal refusal receipts, and municipal records. The court observed that the tenant failed to deposit the arrears of rent in court within the statutory cure period and noted that the landlord is the best judge of his commercial requirements. The court held that the tenant has committed wilful default and the landlord's requirement is bona fide, and therefore the eviction decree is confirmed.

title: Vijay Yadav v. Rekha Khanna
text_content: The plaintiff Vijay Yadav instituted a civil suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell against the defendant vendor Rekha Khanna before the civil court at Vadodara in the year 2022. The plaintiff stated that the parties had entered into a registered agreement to sell an immovable commercial property for a total sale consideration of Rs 5004000, whereof a substantial earnest money deposit was duly paid upon execution. The plaintiff averred that he was always ready and willing to perform his part of the contract by paying the balance consideration and obtaining the sale deed. The defendant resisted the suit, contending that time was of the essence of the contract and claiming that the plaintiff had defaulted in paying the balance amount within the agreed ninety days, thereby forfeiting the earnest money deposit under Indian Penal Code. The Allahabad High Court examined the correspondence between parties, the bank solvency certificates produced by the plaintiff, and the terms of the agreement. The court reiterated the settled legal principle that in agreements for sale of immovable property, time is ordinarily not the essence of the contract unless explicitly so stipulated. The court held that the plaintiff has established continuous readiness and willingness throughout, and therefore the suit for specific performance is decreed.

title: Anil Srivastava v. Sushma Bhatia
text_content: The State prosecuted the accused appellant Anil Srivastava for committing the offence of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code arising out of an incident that occurred at Nagpur in the year 2022. The prosecution alleged that due to longstanding animosity over partition of ancestral land, the accused assaulted the deceased with a lethal sharp-edged weapon, intentionally inflicting fatal injuries. The prosecution examined eyewitnesses including Sushma Bhatia, whose testimony was corroborated by the post-mortem report confirming that the cranial injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The defence contended that the incident occurred during a sudden fight without premeditation, argued that the witnesses were interested family members, and pleaded that the offence at most attracted Exception 4 of Section 300 punishable under Section 304 Part I of Transfer of Property Act. The Allahabad High Court meticulously analysed the medical evidence, the nature of weapon employed, and the multiplicity of brutal blows directed at vital body parts. The court noted that the repeated infliction of forceful blows on the head ruled out any plea of sudden fight or absence of intention to kill. The court held that the prosecution has established the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore the conviction is confirmed and the appeal is dismissed.

title: Ramesh Gupta v. Suresh Joshi
text_content: In this writ appeal, the management Suresh Joshi challenged the order of the appellate authority under the Payment of Gratuity Act at Coimbatore in the year 2022 which directed payment of enhanced gratuity to employee Ramesh Gupta. The appellant argued that under the company's internal gratuity scheme, the maximum gratuity was capped at Rs 147000 and contended that the employee was bound by the contractual limit agreed at the time of appointment. Learned counsel for the employee submitted that under Section 4(5) of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, an employee is entitled to receive better terms of gratuity under any award, agreement, or contract, but the statutory ceiling prescribed by Parliament acts as the minimum floor below which no employer can contract out. The Allahabad High Court analyzed the overriding effect of Section 14 of the Payment of Gratuity Act over all other contractual agreements or company rules. The court observed that beneficial social legislation must be interpreted to maximize the welfare of the superannuated workman. The court therefore held that the employee is entitled to the full statutory gratuity amount, and accordingly the management appeal is dismissed.

title: Nirmala Shah v. Mukesh Rastogi
text_content: The plaintiff Nirmala Shah filed a civil suit for partition against Mukesh Rastogi seeking metes and bounds division of an ancestral residential building in Surat in the year 2023. Following the preliminary decree determining one-half share each, disputes arose during final decree proceedings regarding the feasibility of physical division of the single compact residential structure. The court commissioner submitted a report stating that dividing the small structure into two separate residential units would render both portions uninhabitable and destroy their economic value. The plaintiff moved an application under the Partition Act seeking public auction of the property and division of sale proceeds, which the defendant opposed. The Allahabad High Court examined Sections 2 and 3 of Hindu Marriage Act governing sale in lieu of partition where physical division cannot reasonably be made. The court observed that where metes and bounds partition destroys utility, court-directed sale amongst co-owners or public auction is the sole practical remedy. The court held that the property shall be put to sale with first option to co-sharers, and therefore the final decree application is allowed with directions.

title: Rohit Tiwari v. Ajay Chopra
text_content: In this land acquisition appeal, the acquiring authority Ajay Chopra challenged the judgment of the Reference Court at Delhi in the year 2024 which enhanced the market valuation of acquired lands from Rs 4997000 to double the amount in favour of claimant Rohit Tiwari. The appellant contended that the Reference Court committed patent illegality by relying on post-notification sale exemplars and failed to make necessary deductions for developmental charges in a large-scale acquisition of over two hundred acres. Learned counsel for the landowners supported the enhancement, submitting that the acquired lands were surrounded by established educational institutions and commercial complexes possessing exceptional infrastructural advantages. The Allahabad High Court examined the topographical maps, the timeline of notifications under Negotiable Instruments Act, and the settled principles governing developmental deductions. The court found that the Reference Court had applied correct deduction percentages commensurate with the large tract of land acquired. The court therefore held that the enhanced compensation determined by the Reference Court is just and reasonable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Suresh Verma v. Naresh Kapoor
text_content: The resolution applicant Suresh Verma approached the Arbitration Tribunal in the year 2015 challenging an order passed by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal at Chennai which rejected its approved resolution plan for corporate debtor Naresh Kapoor involving a total financial outlay of Rs 501000. The NCLAT had set aside the plan on the ground that it offered differential settlement percentages between financial creditors and operational creditors. The petitioner contended that the resolution plan had received unanimous ninety-eight percent voting approval from the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom. The court examined Section 30 and Section 31 of Negotiable Instruments Act and reviewed the Constitution Bench rulings in Essar Steel and Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel. The court observed that the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is non-justiciable unless the plan violates specific statutory provisions. The court held that the resolution plan complies with all statutory requirements, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the resolution plan is reinstated.

title: Kavita Rastogi v. Ajay Khanna
text_content: In this company appeal under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the suspended director Ajay Khanna challenged the order of the NCLT at Chennai in the year 2017 which admitted a Section 9 application filed by operational creditor Kavita Rastogi. The appellant contended that the operational creditor's claim of Rs 1499000 was subject to a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods raised in email correspondence long prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice under Section 8 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act. Learned counsel for the operational creditor submitted that the alleged dispute was a spurious defense raised after demand notice to evade insolvency proceedings. The Arbitration Tribunal examined the email exchanges, the rejection notes, and the seminal ruling in Mobilox Innovations v Kirusa Software. The court found that contemporaneous communications revealed that the corporate debtor had rejected the consignments and raised debit notes prior to notice. The court therefore held that a genuine pre-existing dispute exists barring Section 9 insolvency, and accordingly the appeal is allowed and CIRP is quashed.

title: Dinesh Srivastava v. Renu Agarwal
text_content: In this commercial first appeal, the appellant principal manufacturing company Renu Agarwal challenged the decree of damages passed in favour of commercial agent Dinesh Srivastava by the Commercial Division at Vadodara in the year 2017. The appellant contended that it was entitled to terminate the sole selling agency agreement without notice because the agent had acted against company interests by promoting competing merchandise in alleged breach of Section 211 of Industrial Disputes Act. Learned counsel for the agent demonstrated that the agency agreement contained no exclusivity bar against non-competing allied products, and proved that the principal had abruptly terminated the five-year contract in its second year without compensating the agent for substantial market penetration investments of Rs 196000. The Arbitration Tribunal examined the law governing agency contracts under Chapter X of the Indian Contract Act. The court observed that where an agency is created for a fixed term, the principal must make compensation to the agent for premature revocation without reasonable cause. The court therefore held that the termination of agency was premature and unlawful, and accordingly the principal's commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Vikas Tripathi v. Vimla Chaturvedi
text_content: In this commercial appeal, the appellant contractor Vimla Chaturvedi challenged the decree of damages passed in favour of project owner Vikas Tripathi by the Commercial Division of the High Court at Ahmedabad in the year 2018. The appellant contended that the project owner had contributed to construction delays by failing to provide unencumbered site access, delayed architectural drawings, and argued that the liquidated damages clause of Rs 5002000 was a punitive penalty unenforceable under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act without proof of actual pecuniary loss. Learned counsel for the respondent project owner demonstrated that the contractual completion schedule was agreed as essential, that site access was timely provided, and pointed out that the liquidated damages represented a genuine pre-estimate of loss incurred due to delayed commercial operations. The Arbitration Tribunal reviewed the landmark principles laid down in Kailash Nath Associates v DDA regarding liquidated damages under Section 74. The court found that the pre-estimated liquidated damages were reasonable and commensurate with the commercial loss suffered by the owner. The court therefore held that the contractor is liable for contractual delay damages, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Pushpa Yadav v. Meera Rastogi
text_content: The petitioner del-credere agent Pushpa Yadav filed a commercial suit against the principal corporate enterprise Meera Rastogi in Patna in the year 2018 seeking recovery of commission dues of Rs 299000 and indemnification for customer default payments liquidated by the agent under Indian Penal Code. The plaintiff established that under the del-credere agency agreement, he had guaranteed customer payments and had remitted full invoice amounts to the principal, yet the principal unlawfully withheld accrued commission incentives on the pretext of general sales target deficits. The defendant enterprise contended that commission was contingent on achieving annual regional sales quotas which the agent failed to meet. The court examined the contract terms, the commission ledger accounts, and the legal obligations of a principal towards a del-credere agent. The court observed that an agent who discharges customer credit defaults is legally entitled to his contractual commission without arbitrary withholding. The court held that the principal is bound to release the commission dues, and therefore the suit is decreed with eighteen percent commercial interest.

title: Pooja Kapoor v. Sushma Khanna
text_content: The plaintiff non-banking finance company Pooja Kapoor filed a commercial recovery suit against Sushma Khanna in Vadodara in the year 2021 seeking recovery of unpaid equipment lease rentals of Rs 45000. The plaintiff established that the defendant had taken industrial machinery on hire-purchase, defaulted on instalments, and retained the equipment without paying hire charges. The defendant contended that the machinery was defective and alleged that the finance company was in breach of an oral warranty to provide maintenance under Hindu Marriage Act. The court examined the lease agreement which clearly stipulated that the finance company was merely a financer without liability for mechanical maintenance. The court found that the defendant had signed unconditional delivery acceptance certificates acknowledging satisfactory operational condition. The court held that the borrower cannot evade repayment obligations by asserting unverified defects, and therefore the suit for recovery is decreed with interest.

title: Ajay Khanna v. Priya Rastogi
text_content: The petitioner Ajay Khanna approached the Arbitration Tribunal in the year 2024 seeking to set aside a foreign arbitral award under Section 48 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act in enforcement proceedings initiated by foreign supplier Priya Rastogi in Surat. The award had granted commercial dues of Rs 145000. The petitioner contended that the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties because the arbitral institution had appointed a sole arbitrator in violation of the contractually mandated three-arbitrator clause. The respondent submitted that institutional rules to which the parties had agreed provided for sole arbitrator appointment in expedited commercial cases. The court examined the arbitration agreement, institutional rules, and the strict grounds for refusing enforcement of New York Convention awards under Industrial Disputes Act. The court observed that where parties agree to institutional arbitration, the institutional procedural rules govern the composition of the arbitral tribunal. The court held that the tribunal was validly constituted in accordance with agreed rules, and therefore the objections are rejected and enforcement is allowed.

title: Pankaj Tripathi v. Dinesh Saxena
text_content: In this commercial first appeal, the appellant principal manufacturing company Dinesh Saxena challenged the decree of damages passed in favour of commercial agent Pankaj Tripathi by the Commercial Division at Bhopal in the year 2024. The appellant contended that it was entitled to terminate the sole selling agency agreement without notice because the agent had acted against company interests by promoting competing merchandise in alleged breach of Section 211 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. Learned counsel for the agent demonstrated that the agency agreement contained no exclusivity bar against non-competing allied products, and proved that the principal had abruptly terminated the five-year contract in its second year without compensating the agent for substantial market penetration investments of Rs 75000. The Arbitration Tribunal examined the law governing agency contracts under Chapter X of the Indian Contract Act. The court observed that where an agency is created for a fixed term, the principal must make compensation to the agent for premature revocation without reasonable cause. The court therefore held that the termination of agency was premature and unlawful, and accordingly the principal's commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Vikas Tripathi v. Priya Srivastava
text_content: The plaintiff non-banking finance company Vikas Tripathi filed a commercial recovery suit against Priya Srivastava in Varanasi in the year 2024 seeking recovery of unpaid equipment lease rentals of Rs 754000. The plaintiff established that the defendant had taken industrial machinery on hire-purchase, defaulted on instalments, and retained the equipment without paying hire charges. The defendant contended that the machinery was defective and alleged that the finance company was in breach of an oral warranty to provide maintenance under Consumer Protection Act. The court examined the lease agreement which clearly stipulated that the finance company was merely a financer without liability for mechanical maintenance. The court found that the defendant had signed unconditional delivery acceptance certificates acknowledging satisfactory operational condition. The court held that the borrower cannot evade repayment obligations by asserting unverified defects, and therefore the suit for recovery is decreed with interest.

title: Pankaj Patel v. Rohit Saxena
text_content: The plaintiff banking corporation Pankaj Patel instituted a summary suit under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure against borrower Rohit Saxena before the Commercial Court at Ahmedabad in the year 2015. The plaintiff claimed recovery of a commercial term debt of Rs 2005000 founded upon promissory notes, loan agreements, and continuing personal guarantee deeds. The plaintiff stated that the borrower had availed credit facilities and committed chronic payment defaults. The defendant sought unconditional leave to defend, contending that the suit was barred by limitation under Hindu Marriage Act, asserting that the bank had charged excessive penal interest rates, and disputing the validity of balance confirmation slips. The Bombay High Court examined the loan documentation, the ledger extracts certified under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, and written acknowledgments of debt. The court applied the principles in IDBI Trusteeship Services v Hubtown regarding leave to defend in summary suits. The court found that the defense raised was completely moonshine and lacked any bona fide triable issue of law or fact. The court held that the plaintiff is entitled to judgment forthwith, and therefore leave to defend is refused and the summary suit is decreed for the entire sum.

title: Pushpa Yadav v. Suresh Tripathi
text_content: The plaintiff partner Pushpa Yadav instituted a civil commercial suit against the managing partners Suresh Tripathi before the Commercial Court at Ahmedabad in the year 2015 seeking formal dissolution of the registered partnership firm, rendition of accounts, and distribution of surplus partnership assets. The plaintiff stated that the firm had operated an established industrial manufacturing enterprise with annual commercial turnover exceeding Rs 55000, but the managing partners had systematically excluded the plaintiff from management, refused access to daily books of accounts, diverted lucrative business contracts to their privately owned proprietary firms, and misappropriated partnership revenues. The defendant partners resisted dissolution, asserting that the partnership was a partnership at will under Hindu Marriage Act wherein the plaintiff had retired voluntarily, and claimed that the firm's assets were heavily burdened with commercial debts leaving no distributable surplus. The Bombay High Court examined the partnership deed, audited balance sheets, forensic bank statements, and the provisions of Sections 44 and 48 of the Indian Partnership Act. The court observed that mutual confidence and good faith form the foundation of partnership, and systemic diversion of firm assets creates complete deadlock. The court held that it is just and equitable to dissolve the partnership firm, and therefore a preliminary decree for dissolution and accounting is passed.

title: Priya Chopra v. Ravi Chaturvedi
text_content: The petitioner wife Priya Chopra instituted maintenance proceedings under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against her husband Ravi Chaturvedi before the Family Court at Delhi in the year 2015. The petitioner averred that she had been driven out of the matrimonial home without financial means, had custody of two minor children, and was completely unable to maintain herself, while the husband was an executive earning over Rs 197000 per month. The respondent husband contested the petition, alleging that the wife had deserted him without reasonable cause, asserted that she had private income from freelance consultancy, and produced bank statements to argue that his disposable salary was depleted by housing loans and dependent parents. The Bombay High Court scrutinised the comprehensive income affidavits filed by both spouses in accordance with the mandatory directions in Rajnesh v Neha. The court observed that the purpose of Section 125 CrPC is to prevent vagrancy and ensure that the wife enjoys a standard of living reasonably comparable to that in the matrimonial household. The court held that the respondent husband has neglected to maintain his wife despite possessing sufficient means, and therefore the petition is allowed with maintenance.

title: Ramesh Srivastava v. Vimla Tripathi
text_content: The petitioner Ramesh Srivastava filed this bail application in connection with a case registered under Section 138 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act at Vadodara in the year 2015. The prosecution case against the petitioner, presented by Vimla Tripathi, was that intermediate quantity of psychotropic substance was recovered from a business premise occupied by the applicant. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the recovered quantity did not attract the rigorous threshold of commercial quantity and pointed out that the search was carried out after sunset without obtaining any search authorization or recording grounds of belief under Section 42 of Indian Contract Act. The State argued that the applicant was a repeat offender involved in distribution of prohibited chemical drugs. The court examined the case diary, the seizure memo, and the chemical analysis certificate. The court observed that where recovery falls below commercial quantity, the statutory bar of Section 37 is not attracted and regular bail principles apply. The court held that continued judicial custody is unnecessary for the completion of trial, and therefore bail is granted upon furnishing adequate security.

title: Lata Malhotra v. Pushpa Srivastava
text_content: The petitioner in-laws Lata Malhotra filed a petition seeking quashing of domestic violence proceedings instituted by their daughter-in-law Pushpa Srivastava pending before the magistrate in Lucknow in the year 2015. The petitioners submitted that they had been residing permanently in another state for over a decade, had never shared a household with the complainant, and had been roped in with sweeping and generalized allegations to extract monetary settlement. The complainant opposed quashing, asserting that the in-laws had visited the matrimonial home occasionally and exercised psychological dominance over family affairs. The Bombay High Court reviewed the domestic incident report and evaluated the statutory prerequisites for establishing a domestic relationship in a shared household under Indian Contract Act. The court observed that distant relatives living in separate cities without sharing a domestic household cannot be prosecuted on vague, omnibus averments. The court held that continuing proceedings against the aged in-laws constitutes an abuse of judicial process, and therefore the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Sachin Mehta v. Mahesh Malhotra
text_content: The petitioner enterprise Sachin Mehta approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2015 challenging a penalty order passed under Section 129(3) of the CGST Act by the mobile inspection authority Mahesh Malhotra in Nagpur. The authority had intercepted a commercial consignment valued at Rs 73000 and levied maximum penalty solely because the vehicle registration number on the e-way bill contained a single typographical digit transposition error. The petitioner proved that the tax invoice, consignment value, and destination details were accurate, and argued that minor clerical errors do not justify confiscation. The court referred to the circulars issued by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs regarding minor typographical discrepancies in transit documents. The court observed that penalty cannot be imposed where there is no intention to evade tax and transactions are supported by genuine tax invoices. The court held that the detention and penalty are arbitrary and disproportionate, and therefore the petition is allowed and the penalty is set aside.

title: Pankaj Agarwal v. Anil Srivastava
text_content: The petitioner resident association Pankaj Agarwal filed a PIL before the Bombay High Court in the year 2015 seeking an urgent independent structural safety audit of high-rise residential complexes constructed by the urban development authority Anil Srivastava in Surat. The petitioners showed that multiple newly delivered residential towers exhibited extensive structural beam cracks, spalling concrete, and foundation settlement, threatening the lives of thousands of occupant families. The development authority downplayed the cracks as superficial cosmetic shrinkage. The court constituted an expert committee of senior civil engineering professors from the Indian Institute of Technology to conduct non-destructive testing. The expert report confirmed severe structural integrity compromises and substandard cement quality in load-bearing columns. The court held that the state authority cannot endanger human lives through shoddy construction, and therefore the PIL is allowed directing immediate structural retrofitting.

title: Amit Tiwari v. Amit Chopra
text_content: The petitioner linguistic minority educational society Amit Tiwari filed a writ petition under Article 226 before the Bombay High Court in the year 2015 challenging a government notification issued by the State Department of Higher Education Amit Chopra in Delhi. The impugned notification sought to mandate centralized state counseling for one hundred percent of seats in the petitioner's premier minority professional colleges, abolishing the management quota for minority students. The petitioner society contended that the notification infringed the fundamental right guaranteed to religious and linguistic minorities under Article 30(1) of the Constitution of India to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice without state takeover. The State defended the regulation under Code of Criminal Procedure, submitting that the measure was intended to prevent commercialization and ensure merit-based admissions. The court analyzed the Constitution Bench decisions in TMA Pai Foundation, Islamic Academy, and P.A. Inamdar governing minority institutional autonomy. The court observed that while the state can enforce academic qualifications, it cannot extinguish the minority character by usurping total seat allocation. The court held that the government notification violates Article 30(1) of the Constitution, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and the order is quashed.

title: Meera Mishra v. Pankaj Kapoor
text_content: The petitioner infrastructure company Meera Mishra filed a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the Bombay High Court in the year 2016 challenging an arbitral award passed in Lucknow in a dispute involving Pankaj Kapoor. The arbitral tribunal had awarded claims of Rs 5000000 in favour of the respondent, rejecting the petitioner's counterclaims for liquidated damages. The petitioner contended that the award suffered from patent illegality, argued that the tribunal had rewritten contractual price escalation formulas, and asserted conflict with the public policy of India. The respondent defended the award, submitting that judicial review under Section 34 is strictly circumscribed and does not permit re-appreciation of evidence under Transfer of Property Act. The court examined the principles formulated by the Supreme Court in Associate Builders and Ssangyong Engineering. The court observed that an arbitral tribunal is the ultimate master of factual evidence and contractual interpretation unless its construction is totally perverse. The court held that the arbitral award does not suffer from any patent illegality or public policy violation, and therefore the Section 34 petition is dismissed.

title: Anita Dwivedi v. Deepak Saxena
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant husband Deepak Saxena challenged the judgment of the Family Court in Coimbatore in the year 2016 which awarded monthly maintenance to respondent wife Anita Dwivedi. The appellant argued that the marriage had lasted for barely six months and contended that the maintenance quantum of Rs 997000 was disproportionate to the duration of cohabitation. Learned counsel for the respondent wife demonstrated that the husband was a senior corporate director who traveled internationally and maintained luxury cars, arguing that the award was commensurate with the high socioeconomic status enjoyed during marriage. The Bombay High Court reviewed the precedents under Section 138 and noted that duration of marriage does not diminish the statutory entitlement to dignified maintenance. The court found that the Family Court had carefully balanced the financial capacities and reasonable needs of both parties without imposing punitive burden. The court therefore held that the maintenance award is just, equitable, and appropriate, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Sunita Bhatia v. Rekha Kumar
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant mother Rekha Kumar challenged the order of the Family Court in Bhopal in the year 2016 which had transferred custody of the minor child to the respondent father Sunita Bhatia. The appellant argued that the Family Court had erroneously prioritized the father's luxurious housing over the deep emotional bond between the mother and the young child. Learned counsel for the respondent father submitted that the mother intended to relocate to a foreign jurisdiction which would permanently disrupt the child's education and completely sever contact with the father. The Bombay High Court evaluated the educational records, psychological assessment of the child, and the constitutional principles governing international parental child removal. The court found that uprooting the child from his familiar educational environment in Bhopal was contrary to the best interests of the minor. The court therefore held that the father should retain permanent custody with liberal holiday visitation to the mother, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Pankaj Chaturvedi v. Rekha Agarwal
text_content: The petitioner in-laws Pankaj Chaturvedi filed a petition seeking quashing of domestic violence proceedings instituted by their daughter-in-law Rekha Agarwal pending before the magistrate in Nagpur in the year 2016. The petitioners submitted that they had been residing permanently in another state for over a decade, had never shared a household with the complainant, and had been roped in with sweeping and generalized allegations to extract monetary settlement. The complainant opposed quashing, asserting that the in-laws had visited the matrimonial home occasionally and exercised psychological dominance over family affairs. The Bombay High Court reviewed the domestic incident report and evaluated the statutory prerequisites for establishing a domestic relationship in a shared household under Transfer of Property Act. The court observed that distant relatives living in separate cities without sharing a domestic household cannot be prosecuted on vague, omnibus averments. The court held that continuing proceedings against the aged in-laws constitutes an abuse of judicial process, and therefore the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Pooja Yadav v. Geeta Yadav
text_content: The petitioner Pooja Yadav approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2016 challenging the summary blockage of its electronic credit ledger by the GST Commissioner Geeta Yadav in Agra under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The petitioner argued that the authorities had blocked credit amounting to Rs 499000 without assigning reasons in writing, without providing any pre-decisional hearing, and without establishing reasonable grounds to believe that credit was fraudulently availed. The revenue authority submitted that intelligence inputs suggested circular trading within a shell company network. The court examined the scope of Rule 86A and emphasized that power to block credit is a drastic emergency measure that requires objective satisfaction on record. The court observed that Rule 86A cannot be exercised mechanically as an arm-twisting recovery measure during ordinary audit inquiries. The court held that the blockage order violates principles of natural justice and statutory conditions, and therefore the petition is allowed directing unblocking.

title: Sachin Gupta v. Kavita Tripathi
text_content: The petitioner charitable trust Sachin Gupta approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2016 challenging the cancellation of its registration under Section 12AA and denial of deduction under Section 80G by the Commissioner of Income Tax Kavita Tripathi in Pune. The department alleged that the trust had accumulated surplus revenues of Rs 1497000 from hospital pharmacy operations, which allegedly constituted commercial activity violating the proviso to Section 2(15) of Consumer Protection Act. The petitioner established that the nominal pharmacy margins were deployed exclusively to subsidize medical treatment and free beds for indigent patients. The court examined the statutory definition of charitable purpose and the Supreme Court ruling in Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority. The court observed that incidental commercial receipts that directly subserve the primary charitable object of medical relief do not taint charitable status. The court held that the cancellation of charitable registration is unlawful, and therefore the petition is allowed and the registration is restored.

title: Vikas Srivastava v. Rekha Rastogi
text_content: The petitioner linguistic minority educational society Vikas Srivastava filed a writ petition under Article 226 before the Bombay High Court in the year 2016 challenging a government notification issued by the State Department of Higher Education Rekha Rastogi in Mumbai. The impugned notification sought to mandate centralized state counseling for one hundred percent of seats in the petitioner's premier minority professional colleges, abolishing the management quota for minority students. The petitioner society contended that the notification infringed the fundamental right guaranteed to religious and linguistic minorities under Article 30(1) of the Constitution of India to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice without state takeover. The State defended the regulation under Code of Criminal Procedure, submitting that the measure was intended to prevent commercialization and ensure merit-based admissions. The court analyzed the Constitution Bench decisions in TMA Pai Foundation, Islamic Academy, and P.A. Inamdar governing minority institutional autonomy. The court observed that while the state can enforce academic qualifications, it cannot extinguish the minority character by usurping total seat allocation. The court held that the government notification violates Article 30(1) of the Constitution, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and the order is quashed.

title: Kamla Patel v. Sachin Kapoor
text_content: The plaintiff corporate enterprise Kamla Patel instituted a commercial suit for breach of contract and recovery of liquidated damages against the defendant supplier Sachin Kapoor before the Commercial Court at Delhi in the year 2017. The plaintiff stated that the parties had entered into a binding long-term commercial supply agreement for high-grade industrial alloys, whereunder the defendant was obligated to deliver scheduled monthly consignments. Upon a sudden surge in global commodity market prices, the defendant repudiated the contract and failed to supply raw materials, forcing the plaintiff to procure substitute merchandise from spot markets at exorbitant premiums to fulfill international export commitments, incurring damages of Rs 301000. The defendant contended that the sudden price escalation rendered the contract commercially impracticable and invoked the doctrine of frustration under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act along with force majeure clauses under Indian Penal Code. The Bombay High Court examined the contractual terms, the price variation mechanisms, and the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Energy Watchdog v CERC. The court observed that mere abnormal rise or fall in prices is an ordinary commercial risk that does not frustrate a commercial contract. The court held that the defendant committed a deliberate breach of contract, and therefore the commercial suit is decreed for damages with contractual interest.

title: Rajesh Patel v. Dinesh Saxena
text_content: The plaintiff technology company Rajesh Patel filed a commercial suit against Dinesh Saxena in Agra in the year 2017 claiming damages of Rs 99000 for breach of a software development and master service agreement. The plaintiff established that the defendant had failed to meet core milestone deliverables and had abruptly abandoned software integration midway through the rollout phase. The defendant resisted the claim, alleging that the plaintiff had repeatedly modified project specifications and delayed approval of user acceptance testing under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court analyzed the sprint logs, email correspondence, and the report of an independent technical assessor. The court observed that unilateral abandonment of software commitments without following contractual cure notice procedures constitutes material breach. The court held that the plaintiff is entitled to recover advance milestone payments and consequential damages, and therefore the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

title: Pooja Gupta v. Amit Bhatia
text_content: The petitioner adoptive parents Pooja Gupta filed a civil petition under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act before the district court at Varanasi in the year 2017 seeking a formal declaration of the validity of the adoption of a minor child and registration of the adoption deed. The petitioners established that all essential statutory ceremonies including the actual giving and taking of the child with intent to transfer from the biological family to the adoptive family were duly performed in the presence of relatives. The respondent biological relatives Amit Bhatia contested the adoption, alleging that the consent of the biological mother was procured through misrepresentation and contended that the adoptive parents lacked requisite financial capacity under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The Bombay High Court examined the registered adoption deed, photographs and video recordings of the religious ceremonies, and the testimony of participating elders. The court verified that the child was capable of being adopted, that the adoptive parents possessed sound mind and legal capacity, and that valid consent was executed. The court held that the adoption is legal, valid, and binding on all parties, and therefore the petition is allowed and the adoption is confirmed.

title: Nitin Shah v. Naresh Sharma
text_content: The petitioner wife Nitin Shah filed a civil suit against Naresh Sharma seeking recovery and restitution of her stridhan properties, jewelry, and investments valued at Rs 501000 in Patna in the year 2017. The petitioner alleged that upon the breakdown of the marriage, the husband and his relatives retained all gold ornaments, silverware, and share certificates gifted to her by her parents at the time of wedding. The defendant contended that all wedding gifts were consumed jointly during the marriage and disputed the possession of any separate stridhan articles. The Bombay High Court examined the wedding gift lists signed by both families, jewelers' invoices, and photographs taken during the marriage ceremonies. The court reaffirmed that stridhan is the exclusive absolute property of the woman, and the husband holds it merely as a trustee with an obligation to return on demand. The court held that the defendant is legally bound to restore the stridhan property or pay its equivalent value, and therefore the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

title: Asha Kapoor v. Kavita Pandey
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Asha Kapoor filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India before the Bombay High Court in the year 2017 challenging an order of compulsory retirement passed by the respondent State Government Kavita Pandey in Surat. The petitioner pleaded that he had maintained a distinguished public service record spanning twenty-four years without a single adverse remark, until an abrupt compulsory retirement order was issued under Fundamental Rule 56(j) following a change in political administration. The petitioner contended that the review committee had ignored his consistent outstanding performance ratings and acted on extraneous and collateral considerations, violating principles of natural justice and procedural due process under Code of Criminal Procedure. The State Government justified the premature retirement, asserting that the administration had weeded out deadwood to maintain public efficiency. The court called for the confidential service dossiers, the review committee minutes, and scrutinized the entire service trajectory of the officer. The court observed that compulsory retirement cannot be weaponized as a disguised punitive measure or used to retire efficient officers on subjective whims. The court held that the order of compulsory retirement is arbitrary and perverse, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and reinstatement is ordered.

title: Naresh Chopra v. Suresh Shah
text_content: The public interest litigation was instituted by the environmental action group Naresh Chopra before the Bombay High Court in the year 2017 seeking urgent judicial intervention against the rampant discharge of untreated toxic industrial effluents into the sacred river basin traversing Patna. The petitioners submitted certified water laboratory reports demonstrating that the chemical industrial cluster operated by Suresh Shah was releasing carcinogenic heavy metals and untreated chemical waste directly into the river, contaminating the drinking water supply of two million residents and destroying aquatic fauna. The industrial respondents argued that they had installed effluent treatment plants and contended that stringent judicial directions would cause closure of industries employing thousands of industrial workers under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court appointed an independent court commissioner comprising scientists from the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute and examined the ground data. The court applied the polluter pays principle and the precautionary principle enshrined under Article 21 and international environmental jurisprudence. The court held that industrial profits cannot take precedence over the fundamental right to clean water and public health, and therefore the PIL is allowed with directions.

title: Kavita Malhotra v. Sarla Khanna
text_content: In this commercial appeal, the appellant continuing partner Sarla Khanna challenged the judgment of the High Court at Patna in the year 2018 which directed valuation and division of firm goodwill in favour of retiring partner Kavita Malhotra. The appellant contended that under the partnership deed, a retiring partner was entitled only to the book value of capital contribution without any claim to intangible brand goodwill valued at Rs 1496000. Learned counsel for the retiring partner demonstrated that the restrictive clause in the deed applied only to expulsion for misconduct and argued that under Section 55 of the Indian Partnership Act, in settling accounts upon dissolution or retirement, the goodwill of the firm must be included in the assets. The Bombay High Court analyzed the partnership agreement, the valuation report of the certified valuer, and the statutory scheme under Indian Penal Code. The court found that the firm's prestigious brand name possessed immense commercial value in which the retiring partner had built equity over thirty years. The court therefore held that the retiring partner is entitled to his proportionate share in goodwill, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Mukesh Singh v. Pushpa Chopra
text_content: The petitioner del-credere agent Mukesh Singh filed a commercial suit against the principal corporate enterprise Pushpa Chopra in Bhopal in the year 2019 seeking recovery of commission dues of Rs 145000 and indemnification for customer default payments liquidated by the agent under Consumer Protection Act. The plaintiff established that under the del-credere agency agreement, he had guaranteed customer payments and had remitted full invoice amounts to the principal, yet the principal unlawfully withheld accrued commission incentives on the pretext of general sales target deficits. The defendant enterprise contended that commission was contingent on achieving annual regional sales quotas which the agent failed to meet. The court examined the contract terms, the commission ledger accounts, and the legal obligations of a principal towards a del-credere agent. The court observed that an agent who discharges customer credit defaults is legally entitled to his contractual commission without arbitrary withholding. The court held that the principal is bound to release the commission dues, and therefore the suit is decreed with eighteen percent commercial interest.

title: Dinesh Khanna v. Sarla Tiwari
text_content: In this commercial appeal, the appellant continuing partner Sarla Tiwari challenged the judgment of the High Court at Bengaluru in the year 2019 which directed valuation and division of firm goodwill in favour of retiring partner Dinesh Khanna. The appellant contended that under the partnership deed, a retiring partner was entitled only to the book value of capital contribution without any claim to intangible brand goodwill valued at Rs 197000. Learned counsel for the retiring partner demonstrated that the restrictive clause in the deed applied only to expulsion for misconduct and argued that under Section 55 of the Indian Partnership Act, in settling accounts upon dissolution or retirement, the goodwill of the firm must be included in the assets. The Bombay High Court analyzed the partnership agreement, the valuation report of the certified valuer, and the statutory scheme under Indian Penal Code. The court found that the firm's prestigious brand name possessed immense commercial value in which the retiring partner had built equity over thirty years. The court therefore held that the retiring partner is entitled to his proportionate share in goodwill, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Anil Chopra v. Priya Agarwal
text_content: The applicant Anil Chopra approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2019 seeking regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in connection with an offence registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act in Bengaluru. The prosecution alleged that during a naka checking operation, law enforcement personnel intercepted a motor vehicle and recovered a commercial quantity of contraband substance weighing substantially above the statutory threshold. Learned counsel for the applicant argued that the mandatory provisions regarding search and seizure under Sections 42 and 50 of Indian Contract Act were violated by the seizing officers and stressed that the applicant had undergone prolonged judicial custody without significant progress in trial. Opposing the plea, learned counsel for the respondent State Priya Agarwal contended that the twin statutory conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act impose an absolute bar against release unless the court forms an opinion that the accused is not guilty and is unlikely to commit any offence while on bail. The court scrutinised the chemical examiner report, seizure panchnama, and custodial records. The court held that the applicant failed to satisfy the twin conditions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act, and therefore bail is refused.

title: Vijay Mishra v. Asha Gupta
text_content: The petitioner wife Vijay Mishra instituted maintenance proceedings under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against her husband Asha Gupta before the Family Court at Lucknow in the year 2019. The petitioner averred that she had been driven out of the matrimonial home without financial means, had custody of two minor children, and was completely unable to maintain herself, while the husband was an executive earning over Rs 77000 per month. The respondent husband contested the petition, alleging that the wife had deserted him without reasonable cause, asserted that she had private income from freelance consultancy, and produced bank statements to argue that his disposable salary was depleted by housing loans and dependent parents. The Bombay High Court scrutinised the comprehensive income affidavits filed by both spouses in accordance with the mandatory directions in Rajnesh v Neha. The court observed that the purpose of Section 125 CrPC is to prevent vagrancy and ensure that the wife enjoys a standard of living reasonably comparable to that in the matrimonial household. The court held that the respondent husband has neglected to maintain his wife despite possessing sufficient means, and therefore the petition is allowed with maintenance.

title: Manju Pandey v. Sunita Khanna
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant wife Sunita Khanna assailed the decree of divorce granted in favour of husband Manju Pandey by the Family Court in Coimbatore in the year 2019 on the ground of cruelty under the Hindu Marriage Act. The appellant argued that ordinary wear and tear of married life had been exaggerated into mental cruelty by the trial court, and submitted that reconciliation was still possible in the interest of the minor child. Learned counsel for the respondent husband submitted that the parties had been living separately for more than eight years and pointed out that multiple rounds of court-annexed mediation had completely failed to bridge the profound marital discord. The Bombay High Court examined the judicial guidelines regarding mental cruelty and reviewed the irreversible estrangement between the spouses under Industrial Disputes Act. The court observed that compelling parties to remain legally bound in a dead marriage where emotional bonds have perished causes perpetual agony to both. The court therefore held that the Family Court was fully justified in granting dissolution of marriage, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Rajesh Dwivedi v. Amit Chopra
text_content: The parties Rajesh Dwivedi and Amit Chopra jointly approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2019 seeking dissolution of their marriage by mutual consent under Section 13-B of the Hindu Marriage Act in Jaipur. The parties had executed a comprehensive memorandum of understanding resolving all disputes regarding permanent alimony of Rs 5005000, custody of the minor child, and return of stridhan articles. The parties filed an application praying for waiver of the statutory six months cooling-off period prescribed under Section 13-B(2), citing the Supreme Court judgment in Amardeep Singh v Harveen Kaur. The court examined whether all efforts at conciliation had failed, verified that the parties had lived separately for over eighteen months, and confirmed that the settlement terms were fair and executed without coercion. The court observed that the cooling-off period is directory and can be waived where continuance of the legal tie prolongs human suffering. The court held that all statutory criteria for mutual consent divorce are satisfied, and therefore the cooling-off period is waived and marriage is dissolved.

title: Asha Mishra v. Sunita Khanna
text_content: The petitioner manufacturing firm Asha Mishra approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2019 challenging a best judgment assessment order passed ex-parte under Section 144 of the Income Tax Act by Sunita Khanna assessing authority in Indore. The assessing officer had estimated the petitioner's net profit at twenty percent of gross turnover, making an arbitrary addition of Rs 201000. The petitioner submitted that statutory notices under Section 142(1) were transmitted solely to an obsolete email address during pandemic lockdown disruptions, preventing the assessee from filing books of accounts and audited financial statements. The court examined the service of notices on the ITBA portal and the compliance history of the assessee under Code of Criminal Procedure. The court observed that best judgment assessment cannot be converted into an arbitrary penal assessment without affording fair opportunity to produce accounts. The court held that the assessment order violates principles of natural justice, and therefore the petition is allowed remanding the matter for fresh scrutiny.

title: Seema Sharma v. Rohit Singh
text_content: The petitioner wife Seema Sharma filed a civil suit against Rohit Singh seeking recovery and restitution of her stridhan properties, jewelry, and investments valued at Rs 103000 in Bengaluru in the year 2020. The petitioner alleged that upon the breakdown of the marriage, the husband and his relatives retained all gold ornaments, silverware, and share certificates gifted to her by her parents at the time of wedding. The defendant contended that all wedding gifts were consumed jointly during the marriage and disputed the possession of any separate stridhan articles. The Bombay High Court examined the wedding gift lists signed by both families, jewelers' invoices, and photographs taken during the marriage ceremonies. The court reaffirmed that stridhan is the exclusive absolute property of the woman, and the husband holds it merely as a trustee with an obligation to return on demand. The court held that the defendant is legally bound to restore the stridhan property or pay its equivalent value, and therefore the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

title: Sunita Shah v. Lata Joshi
text_content: The petitioner minority community institution Sunita Shah approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2020 challenging an order passed by the state charity commissioner Lata Joshi in Surat appointing a non-minority administrative receiver over historic religious endowments and community properties valued at Rs 146000. The state authority alleged administrative mismanagement of community funds and sought to reform the trust board under general public trust laws.
