The petitioner contended that Article 26 of the Constitution guarantees religious denominations the fundamental right to manage their own affairs in matters of religion. The court examined the scope of Article 26(b) and the line between secular management and ecclesiastical autonomy under Income Tax Act. The court observed that while secular finances can be audited, the state cannot supplant traditional community management with bureaucratic receivers. The court held that the appointment of an external receiver violates Article 26, and therefore the petition is allowed and the appointment is set aside.

title: Usha Singh v. Mukesh Kapoor
text_content: By this petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the petitioner Usha Singh challenged the summoning order passed by the Metropolitan Magistrate at Bhopal in the year 2021 in a private criminal complaint instituted by Mukesh Kapoor. The complaint alleged that the petitioner had committed offences of criminal breach of trust regarding company machinery worth Rs 1501000. The petitioner submitted that the parties had subsequently resolved all existing disputes through a comprehensive memorandum of settlement and jointly prayed for quashing of all criminal proceedings to restore business harmony. The respondent appeared through counsel and confirmed receipt of agreed settlement amounts and consented to the quashing of the criminal complaint. The Bombay High Court examined whether non-compoundable offences of a predominantly commercial and private nature could be quashed under inherent powers. The court noted that when the underlying commercial dispute is amicably resolved, continuing criminal prosecution would be an exercise in futility. The court therefore held that it is in the interest of justice to quash the proceedings, and accordingly the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Kavita Gupta v. Pooja Sharma
text_content: The complainant Kavita Gupta filed an application under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 against her husband and in-laws Pooja Sharma before the Metropolitan Magistrate at Agra in the year 2021. The complainant alleged that throughout her marital life, she was subjected to persistent physical assaults, verbal degradation, and economic deprivation, culminating in her being locked out of the shared household. The complainant sought statutory protection orders, a residence order under Section 19 to reside in the shared matrimonial home, and monetary relief of Rs 203000. The respondents contested the complaint, asserting that the shared household was the exclusive self-acquired property of the mother-in-law where the complainant had no legal right, and denied all allegations of domestic abuse as fabricated. The Bombay High Court examined the Domestic Incident Report submitted by the Protection Officer, medical emergency room slips, and the Supreme Court ruling in Satish Chander Ahuja. The court observed that the definition of shared household encompasses any house where the aggrieved woman has lived in a domestic relationship irrespective of ownership. The court held that the complainant is entitled to reside in the shared household and receive maintenance, and therefore the domestic violence application is allowed.

title: Nirmala Shah v. Sanjay Mehta
text_content: In this civil appeal, the appellant Sanjay Mehta challenged the judgment of the civil court at Vadodara in the year 2021 which upheld the adoption deed executed by adoptive father Nirmala Shah. The appellant argued that the adoption was void ab initio under Section 11 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act because the adoptive father already had a living biological son at the time of adoption, which acts as an absolute statutory bar against adopting another male child. Learned counsel for the respondent adoptive child submitted that the alleged biological son had been given away in valid adoption decades earlier, thereby removing the bar. The Bombay High Court closely examined the pedigree tables, prior adoption deeds, and the statutory requirements under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The court found that documentary evidence conclusively established the prior adoption of the biological son, leaving the adoptive father free to adopt. The court therefore held that the adoption complies strictly with the statutory mandate, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the adoption is upheld.

title: Ramesh Agarwal v. Sachin Mishra
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the revenue department Sachin Mishra challenged the judgment of the High Court at Chennai in the year 2021 which waived interest levied under Section 234B on public sector enterprise Ramesh Agarwal. The department contended that interest under Section 234B is automatic, mandatory, and compensatory in nature, leaving no room for equitable waiver by judicial authorities regardless of the underlying reasons for shortfall. Learned counsel for the enterprise demonstrated that the shortfall of Rs 753000 occurred because of retrospective statutory amendments to book profit calculations under Section 115JB enacted after the close of the financial year. The Bombay High Court examined the constitutional limits of retrospective taxation and reviewed the landmark judgment in Star India. The court observed that interest for default in payment of advance tax cannot be charged where the tax liability was created by retrospective legislation post factum. The court therefore held that the assessee cannot be deemed in default of advance tax, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Ravi Mishra v. Rohit Chaturvedi
text_content: The petitioner manufacturing firm Ravi Mishra approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2021 challenging a best judgment assessment order passed ex-parte under Section 144 of the Income Tax Act by Rohit Chaturvedi assessing authority in Ahmedabad. The assessing officer had estimated the petitioner's net profit at twenty percent of gross turnover, making an arbitrary addition of Rs 73000. The petitioner submitted that statutory notices under Section 142(1) were transmitted solely to an obsolete email address during pandemic lockdown disruptions, preventing the assessee from filing books of accounts and audited financial statements. The court examined the service of notices on the ITBA portal and the compliance history of the assessee under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The court observed that best judgment assessment cannot be converted into an arbitrary penal assessment without affording fair opportunity to produce accounts. The court held that the assessment order violates principles of natural justice, and therefore the petition is allowed remanding the matter for fresh scrutiny.

title: Rohit Bhatia v. Rekha Dwivedi
text_content: In this commercial first appeal, the appellant debtor Rekha Dwivedi challenged the decree of recovery passed by the Commercial Division at Ahmedabad in the year 2022 in favour of supplier Rohit Bhatia. The appellant contended that the trial court erred in holding that limitation was extended by an informal email correspondence and argued that an unverified electronic email does not constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt in writing under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. Learned counsel for the respondent supplier produced electronic audit certificates under Section 65B of the Evidence Act proving that the email admitting the liability of Rs 1496000 was dispatched by the authorized chief financial officer of the appellant before the expiry of the original limitation period. The Bombay High Court examined the statutory requirements of Section 18 of Industrial Disputes Act in the context of modern electronic commercial communications. The court observed that digital communications admitting subsisting financial obligations satisfy the criteria of written acknowledgment extending limitation. The court therefore held that the recovery suit was filed well within limitation, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Lata Kumar v. Sushma Tiwari
text_content: The plaintiff partner Lata Kumar filed a commercial suit against former partner Sushma Tiwari in Coimbatore in the year 2022 seeking a permanent injunction restraining the defendant from carrying on a competing business using the firm's confidential client database and trade name. The plaintiff proved that upon mutual dissolution of the partnership, the defendant had received substantial monetary compensation of Rs 750000 and had executed a restrictive negative covenant undertaking not to solicit the firm's existing clients for three years within the municipal territory of Coimbatore. The defendant contended that the covenant was void as an unlawful restraint of trade under Section 27 of Income Tax Act. The court examined the statutory exception to Section 27 of the Contract Act and Section 36(2) of the Indian Partnership Act which expressly validates reasonable agreements in restraint of trade upon dissolution or sale of goodwill. The court observed that a reasonable geographic and temporal restriction protecting partnership goodwill is legally enforceable. The court held that the negative covenant is valid and binding, and therefore a permanent injunction is granted restraining client solicitation.

title: Sushma Verma v. Manju Tiwari
text_content: In this commercial arbitration appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, the appellant public undertaking Manju Tiwari challenged the judgment of the High Court at Chennai in the year 2022 which upheld an arbitral award granted to private contractor Sushma Verma. The appellant contended that the sole arbitrator had awarded substantial unliquidated damages of Rs 996000 without any documentary proof of actual loss, and argued that the arbitrator was disqualified under the Seventh Schedule of the Act due to prior professional consultancy relationships. Learned counsel for the contractor demonstrated that the appellant had expressly waived objections under Section 12(5) by participation without protest, and established that the arbitrator had meticulously evaluated chartered accountants' loss certificates. The Bombay High Court analyzed the statutory framework of Section 34 and Section 37 of Hindu Marriage Act and the limits of appellate interference. The court found that the arbitrator's evaluation of commercial losses was grounded upon credible evidence and within arbitral jurisdiction. The court therefore held that no ground for setting aside the arbitral award is established, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Seema Srivastava v. Priya Kapoor
text_content: The plaintiff partner Seema Srivastava filed a commercial suit against former partner Priya Kapoor in Kanpur in the year 2022 seeking a permanent injunction restraining the defendant from carrying on a competing business using the firm's confidential client database and trade name. The plaintiff proved that upon mutual dissolution of the partnership, the defendant had received substantial monetary compensation of Rs 1497000 and had executed a restrictive negative covenant undertaking not to solicit the firm's existing clients for three years within the municipal territory of Kanpur. The defendant contended that the covenant was void as an unlawful restraint of trade under Section 27 of Industrial Disputes Act. The court examined the statutory exception to Section 27 of the Contract Act and Section 36(2) of the Indian Partnership Act which expressly validates reasonable agreements in restraint of trade upon dissolution or sale of goodwill. The court observed that a reasonable geographic and temporal restriction protecting partnership goodwill is legally enforceable. The court held that the negative covenant is valid and binding, and therefore a permanent injunction is granted restraining client solicitation.

title: Sanjay Mehta v. Meera Yadav
text_content: The petitioner Sanjay Mehta invoked the inherent powers of the Bombay High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the year 2022 seeking quashing of the First Information Report registered at Pune for alleged offences of cheating, forgery, and criminal conspiracy. The private respondent Meera Yadav had lodged the complaint alleging that the petitioner had defaulted on a commercial supply agreement valued at Rs 1499000 and had misappropriated advances. The petitioner contended that the dispute was essentially of a civil nature arising out of contractual differences and that the criminal prosecution was initiated maliciously to exert illegitimate pressure for recovery of money. The respondent State asserted that the allegations disclosed prima facie ingredients of criminal breach of trust and cheating from the inception of the contract. The court examined the principles enunciated in Bhajan Lal and analysed the contractual documents executed between the parties under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The court observed that a mere failure to perform a contractual promise does not give rise to criminal liability in the absence of fraudulent intent at the threshold. The court held that the criminal proceedings constitute a manifest abuse of process of the court, and therefore the petition is allowed and the FIR is quashed.

title: Mahesh Gupta v. Mahesh Kapoor
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant mother Mahesh Kapoor challenged the order of the Family Court in Kolkata in the year 2022 which had transferred custody of the minor child to the respondent father Mahesh Gupta. The appellant argued that the Family Court had erroneously prioritized the father's luxurious housing over the deep emotional bond between the mother and the young child. Learned counsel for the respondent father submitted that the mother intended to relocate to a foreign jurisdiction which would permanently disrupt the child's education and completely sever contact with the father. The Bombay High Court evaluated the educational records, psychological assessment of the child, and the constitutional principles governing international parental child removal. The court found that uprooting the child from his familiar educational environment in Kolkata was contrary to the best interests of the minor. The court therefore held that the father should retain permanent custody with liberal holiday visitation to the mother, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Sushma Malhotra v. Pankaj Joshi
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant mother Pankaj Joshi challenged the order of the Family Court in Kolkata in the year 2022 which had transferred custody of the minor child to the respondent father Sushma Malhotra. The appellant argued that the Family Court had erroneously prioritized the father's luxurious housing over the deep emotional bond between the mother and the young child. Learned counsel for the respondent father submitted that the mother intended to relocate to a foreign jurisdiction which would permanently disrupt the child's education and completely sever contact with the father. The Bombay High Court evaluated the educational records, psychological assessment of the child, and the constitutional principles governing international parental child removal. The court found that uprooting the child from his familiar educational environment in Kolkata was contrary to the best interests of the minor. The court therefore held that the father should retain permanent custody with liberal holiday visitation to the mother, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Lata Bhatia v. Lata Shah
text_content: In this GST appeal, the revenue department Lata Shah challenged the judgment of the Appellate Tribunal at Chennai in the year 2022 which allowed input tax credit of Rs 74000 to manufacturing enterprise Lata Bhatia. The department contended that the supplier's registration was canceled retrospectively by anti-evasion intelligence authorities on the ground of issuing bogus invoices without actual movement of goods under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. Learned counsel for the respondent assessee submitted that at the time of purchase transactions, the supplier's GSTIN was active on the government portal, and pointed out that retrospective cancellation of supplier registration cannot invalidate lawful transactions conducted prior to such cancellation. The Bombay High Court examined the documentary trail including weighing slips, transport bilties, toll tax receipts, and audited inventory stock registers. The court found that the assessee had conclusively proved genuine delivery and consumption of raw materials in manufacturing. The court therefore held that retrospective cancellation of supplier's registration cannot extinguish the purchaser's ITC, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Naresh Gupta v. Sanjay Tripathi
text_content: In this writ appeal under Article 226, the State through Sanjay Tripathi challenged the judgment of the Single Judge at Patna in the year 2022 which quashed the punitive transfer of public medical doctor Naresh Gupta. The appellant State contended that transfer is an ordinary incident of service and argued that courts should not interfere with administrative transfers in the absence of proved malice under Hindu Marriage Act. Learned counsel for the doctor demonstrated that the transfer to a remote primary health center was ordered within twenty-four hours of the doctor submitting an official report exposing large-scale procurement irregularities of Rs 204000 involving local politicians. The Bombay High Court examined the sequence of events, the departmental communications, and the settled jurisprudence in Somesh Tiwari v Union of India. The court observed that while transfer is an incident of service, a transfer order passed mala fide as a punitive measure constitutes colorable exercise of power. The court therefore held that the transfer order was passed with collateral malice, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Sachin Yadav v. Deepak Rastogi
text_content: The petitioner government teacher Sachin Yadav approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2022 through a writ petition under Article 226 seeking release of withheld pension and terminal retirement benefits amounting to Rs 75000 against Deepak Rastogi education department in Delhi. The department had withheld pensionary dues for five years after superannuation, citing an unfinalized preliminary audit objection dating back fifteen years. The court referred to the landmark rulings in State of Jharkhand v Jitendra Kumar Srivastava holding that pension is not a bounty but a constitutional property under Article 300A which cannot be withheld without statutory authority. The court observed that an employee cannot be deprived of livelihood in old age based on stale and unadjudicated administrative inquiries. The court held that withholding pension without authority of law violates constitutional guarantees, and therefore the writ petition is allowed with nine percent interest.

title: Sachin Mishra v. Rohit Tiwari
text_content: The petitioner registered political party Sachin Mishra approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2022 challenging the arbitrary rejection of its application for allotment of a reserved common election symbol by the Election Commission of India Rohit Tiwari in Nagpur. The petitioner proved that it had fulfilled all vote share thresholds in the preceding general election under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order. The Election Commission defended its discretion, contending that another splinter faction had asserted competing claims over the registered party name and symbol. The court examined the test of legislative and organizational majority formulated in Sadiq Ali and applied to internal party disputes under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The court found that the petitioner faction demonstrated overwhelming numerical majority in both the legislative wing and the organizational executive committee. The court held that the denial of the common symbol is discriminatory and arbitrary, and therefore the writ petition is allowed directing allotment of the symbol.

title: Ramesh Rastogi v. Renu Tiwari
text_content: The plaintiff technology company Ramesh Rastogi filed a commercial suit against Renu Tiwari in Nagpur in the year 2023 claiming damages of Rs 751000 for breach of a software development and master service agreement. The plaintiff established that the defendant had failed to meet core milestone deliverables and had abruptly abandoned software integration midway through the rollout phase. The defendant resisted the claim, alleging that the plaintiff had repeatedly modified project specifications and delayed approval of user acceptance testing under Consumer Protection Act. The court analyzed the sprint logs, email correspondence, and the report of an independent technical assessor. The court observed that unilateral abandonment of software commitments without following contractual cure notice procedures constitutes material breach. The court held that the plaintiff is entitled to recover advance milestone payments and consequential damages, and therefore the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

title: Renu Bhatia v. Amit Mishra
text_content: The complainant Renu Bhatia instituted criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against Amit Mishra before the trial court in Vadodara in the year 2023. The complainant stated that in discharge of a legally enforceable debt, the accused drawer had issued an account payee cheque of Rs 97000 drawn on a nationalised bank. Upon presentation for encashment through banking channels, the cheque was dishonoured and returned unpaid with the bank memo citing insufficiency of funds. The payee dispatched a statutory notice of demand as mandated by the Negotiable Instruments Act calling upon the drawer to pay within fifteen days. The accused admitted the signatures on the cheque but contended that the instrument had been handed over merely as security and denied the existence of any legally enforceable debt. The Bombay High Court examined the documentary evidence including ledger accounts, the cheque return memo, and legal presumptions under Indian Penal Code. The court held that the accused failed to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and therefore the conviction of the drawer is upheld and the appeal is dismissed.

title: Geeta Kumar v. Manju Tripathi
text_content: The petitioner Geeta Kumar approached the Bombay High Court in the year 2023 challenging the summary blockage of its electronic credit ledger by the GST Commissioner Manju Tripathi in Surat under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The petitioner argued that the authorities had blocked credit amounting to Rs 296000 without assigning reasons in writing, without providing any pre-decisional hearing, and without establishing reasonable grounds to believe that credit was fraudulently availed. The revenue authority submitted that intelligence inputs suggested circular trading within a shell company network. The court examined the scope of Rule 86A and emphasized that power to block credit is a drastic emergency measure that requires objective satisfaction on record. The court observed that Rule 86A cannot be exercised mechanically as an arm-twisting recovery measure during ordinary audit inquiries. The court held that the blockage order violates principles of natural justice and statutory conditions, and therefore the petition is allowed directing unblocking.

title: Kamla Malhotra v. Sarla Mehta
text_content: In this environmental writ appeal, the mining conglomerate Sarla Mehta challenged the judgment of the High Court at Kolkata in the year 2024 which halted open-cast bauxite mining operations inside an eco-sensitive forest zone following a PIL instituted by tribal rights activist Kamla Malhotra. The appellant corporation contended that it held valid environmental clearances granted by the Ministry of Environment and had invested Rs 52000 in infrastructure. Learned counsel for the petitioner established that the mining operations caused massive deforestation, dried up perennial mountain streams, and displaced indigenous tribal communities without obtaining their mandatory consent under the Forest Rights Act and Income Tax Act. The Bombay High Court examined the ecological sensitivity of the Western Ghats and reviewed the constitutional public trust doctrine. The court observed that economic considerations must yield to the imperative need for sustainable development and preservation of fragile ecological biodiversity. The court therefore held that mining in the protected eco-sensitive sanctuary cannot be permitted, and accordingly the mining appeal is dismissed.

title: Ajay Singh v. Priya Saxena
text_content: In this writ appeal, the management Priya Saxena challenged the order of the appellate authority under the Payment of Gratuity Act at Mumbai in the year 2015 which directed payment of enhanced gratuity to employee Ajay Singh. The appellant argued that under the company's internal gratuity scheme, the maximum gratuity was capped at Rs 752000 and contended that the employee was bound by the contractual limit agreed at the time of appointment. Learned counsel for the employee submitted that under Section 4(5) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, an employee is entitled to receive better terms of gratuity under any award, agreement, or contract, but the statutory ceiling prescribed by Parliament acts as the minimum floor below which no employer can contract out. The Central Administrative Tribunal analyzed the overriding effect of Section 14 of the Payment of Gratuity Act over all other contractual agreements or company rules. The court observed that beneficial social legislation must be interpreted to maximize the welfare of the superannuated workman. The court therefore held that the employee is entitled to the full statutory gratuity amount, and accordingly the management appeal is dismissed.

title: Mahesh Chopra v. Sanjay Joshi
text_content: In this service appeal, the State Government through Sanjay Joshi challenged the order of the High Court at Bhopal in the year 2016 directing the retrospective promotion of officer Mahesh Chopra with all consequential monetary benefits. The appellant contended that the High Court in exercise of writ jurisdiction could not usurp the functions of the statutory Departmental Promotion Committee by directing outright promotion instead of remitting the matter for fresh assessment. Learned counsel for the respondent officer demonstrated that the officer had been cleared of all departmental charges in an earlier inquiry and argued that the sealed cover procedure adopted by the DPC was unlawfully maintained for five years after full exoneration. The Central Administrative Tribunal examined the established guidelines in Union of India v K.V. Jankiraman governing the opening of sealed cover recommendations. The court observed that upon complete exoneration in disciplinary proceedings, the sealed cover must be opened and benefits granted from the due date. The court therefore held that the officer is entitled to retrospective promotion from the date his juniors were elevated, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Sunita Chaturvedi v. Prakash Malhotra
text_content: In this civil appeal, the employer bank Prakash Malhotra challenged the judgment of the High Court at Bengaluru in the year 2016 which permitted officer Sunita Chaturvedi to withdraw his application for Voluntary Retirement prior to its effective date of acceptance. The appellant bank contended that under the special terms of the VRS scheme, an application once submitted became irrevocable and could not be rescinded by the employee under any circumstances. Learned counsel for the officer submitted that it is settled law established in Bank of India v O.P. Swarnakar that an application for voluntary retirement is merely an offer by the employee which can be lawfully withdrawn at any time before the contract becomes concluded by formal acceptance and communication by the employer. The Central Administrative Tribunal examined the contract law principles applicable to voluntary retirement schemes under Indian Contract Act. The court observed that the relationship between master and servant continues until the effective date of release, and the locus poenitentiae to withdraw survives until acceptance. The court therefore held that the employee was fully entitled to withdraw his voluntary retirement request, and accordingly the appeal of the bank is dismissed.

title: Mahesh Gupta v. Pankaj Khanna
text_content: The petitioner employee Mahesh Gupta filed a writ petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal in the year 2017 challenging the unilateral rejection of her application for the Voluntary Retirement Scheme by the public sector management Pankaj Khanna in Coimbatore. The petitioner stated that pursuant to an attractive VRS notification promulgated under Consumer Protection Act offering an ex-gratia compensation of Rs 2002000, she submitted her formal option well before the closing date. The management subsequently issued an order declining her voluntary retirement on the asserted ground of administrative exigencies and shortage of specialized staff. The petitioner contended that the management had selectively approved applications of similarly placed junior colleagues while arbitrarily rejecting hers, and argued that the doctrine of promissory estoppel bound the employer once the employee altered her position by opting for the scheme. The court scrutinized the VRS guidelines, the approval roster, and the staffing patterns of the corporation. The court found that the refusal lacked rational criteria and was tainted by arbitrariness, as junior employees in the identical cadre had been relieved under VRS. The court held that the rejection of the VRS application is discriminatory and arbitrary, and therefore the petition is allowed and the employer is directed to relieve the petitioner.

title: Mukesh Agarwal v. Ravi Gupta
text_content: The petitioner retired employee Mukesh Agarwal instituted proceedings under Section 7 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 against the employer Ravi Gupta before the Controlling Authority at Indore in the year 2019. The petitioner claimed statutory gratuity of Rs 497000 based on thirty-two years of continuous service, which the employer had withheld following his superannuation. The employer contended that gratuity was lawfully forfeited under Section 4(6) of the Act because the employee was subjected to disciplinary proceedings on the eve of retirement for alleged administrative negligence resulting in operational financial loss to the enterprise. The employee argued that under Section 4(6) of Industrial Disputes Act, gratuity can be forfeited only where services are terminated for riotous or disorderly conduct or an offence involving moral turpitude, and pointed out that no termination order was ever passed prior to superannuation. The Central Administrative Tribunal examined the statutory provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act and the judicial precedents governing forfeiture of accrued terminal benefits. The court observed that gratuity is a hard-earned statutory entitlement and cannot be withheld or forfeited in the absence of a lawful dismissal order on specified grounds. The court held that the withholding of gratuity is wholly illegal, and therefore directed payment of full gratuity with ten percent compound interest.

title: Seema Saxena v. Sachin Chaturvedi
text_content: In this civil appeal, the employer bank Sachin Chaturvedi challenged the judgment of the High Court at Delhi in the year 2019 which permitted officer Seema Saxena to withdraw his application for Voluntary Retirement prior to its effective date of acceptance. The appellant bank contended that under the special terms of the VRS scheme, an application once submitted became irrevocable and could not be rescinded by the employee under any circumstances. Learned counsel for the officer submitted that it is settled law established in Bank of India v O.P. Swarnakar that an application for voluntary retirement is merely an offer by the employee which can be lawfully withdrawn at any time before the contract becomes concluded by formal acceptance and communication by the employer. The Central Administrative Tribunal examined the contract law principles applicable to voluntary retirement schemes under Hindu Marriage Act. The court observed that the relationship between master and servant continues until the effective date of release, and the locus poenitentiae to withdraw survives until acceptance. The court therefore held that the employee was fully entitled to withdraw his voluntary retirement request, and accordingly the appeal of the bank is dismissed.

title: Pushpa Pandey v. Sarla Srivastava
text_content: The petitioner retired officer Pushpa Pandey approached the Central Administrative Tribunal in the year 2020 seeking direction to Sarla Srivastava public sector enterprise in Kolkata to pay differential pension and ex-gratia benefits of Rs 745000 arising from retrospective wage revision. The petitioner had retired under an early Voluntary Retirement Scheme, and subsequent to his release, a bipartite wage settlement was finalized with retrospective effect covering the period of his active service. The enterprise denied arrears to VRS retirees, contending that voluntary retirees constituted a separate closed class who had received full and final settlement. The court examined the wage revision notification, the terms of the settlement, and constitutional equality under Article 14. The court held that wage revision implemented retrospectively cannot deny accrued benefits to employees who served during the relevant period, and therefore the petition is allowed.

title: Nitin Mishra v. Pankaj Agarwal
text_content: The petitioner nominee Nitin Mishra approached the Central Administrative Tribunal in the year 2021 seeking disbursement of death-cum-retirement gratuity of Rs 48000 due upon the demise of her husband who served as a permanent technician with Pankaj Agarwal in Chennai. The employer resisted payment, alleging that the deceased employee had not completed five years of continuous service as required by Section 4(1) of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and sought to adjust alleged overpayment of salary advances against the terminal gratuity. The court referred to the first proviso to Section 4(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act which explicitly waives the requirement of five years continuous service in cases where employment terminates due to death or disablement of the employee. The court further noted that Section 13 grants absolute immunity to gratuity from attachment in execution of any decree or order of any civil, revenue, or criminal court. The court held that the nominee is entitled to immediate payment of full gratuity without deductions, and therefore the petition is allowed with interest.

title: Sushma Joshi v. Ajay Chopra
text_content: The workman Sushma Joshi raised an industrial dispute challenging the order of dismissal from service passed by the management Ajay Chopra before the Labour Court at Agra in the year 2021. The workman stated that he had served as a permanent machine technician for fifteen years with an unblemished record until he was summarily terminated following an alleged charge of insubordination during a lawful trade union meeting. The workman contended that the domestic enquiry conducted by the management was a sham, wherein he was denied assistance of a co-worker, refused access to documentary exhibits, and condemned unheard in flagrant violation of natural justice under the Industrial Disputes Act. The management defended the dismissal, alleging that the domestic enquiry was conducted strictly in accordance with certified standing orders under Indian Contract Act and contended that the workman's misconduct undermined industrial discipline. The Central Administrative Tribunal examined the enquiry proceedings, the findings of the enquiry officer, and the evidence recorded by the Labour Court. The court found that the enquiry was vitiated by procedural illegality and the punishment of termination was shockingly disproportionate. The court held that the termination is illegal, and therefore directed reinstatement of the workman with fifty percent back wages and continuity of service.

title: Suresh Saxena v. Vimla Patel
text_content: The workman Suresh Saxena raised an industrial dispute challenging the order of dismissal from service passed by the management Vimla Patel before the Labour Court at Coimbatore in the year 2021. The workman stated that he had served as a permanent machine technician for fifteen years with an unblemished record until he was summarily terminated following an alleged charge of insubordination during a lawful trade union meeting. The workman contended that the domestic enquiry conducted by the management was a sham, wherein he was denied assistance of a co-worker, refused access to documentary exhibits, and condemned unheard in flagrant violation of natural justice under the Industrial Disputes Act. The management defended the dismissal, alleging that the domestic enquiry was conducted strictly in accordance with certified standing orders under Hindu Marriage Act and contended that the workman's misconduct undermined industrial discipline. The Central Administrative Tribunal examined the enquiry proceedings, the findings of the enquiry officer, and the evidence recorded by the Labour Court. The court found that the enquiry was vitiated by procedural illegality and the punishment of termination was shockingly disproportionate. The court held that the termination is illegal, and therefore directed reinstatement of the workman with fifty percent back wages and continuity of service.

title: Asha Patel v. Sushma Sharma
text_content: The petitioner employee Asha Patel filed a writ petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal in the year 2023 challenging the unilateral rejection of her application for the Voluntary Retirement Scheme by the public sector management Sushma Sharma in Indore. The petitioner stated that pursuant to an attractive VRS notification promulgated under Code of Criminal Procedure offering an ex-gratia compensation of Rs 250000, she submitted her formal option well before the closing date. The management subsequently issued an order declining her voluntary retirement on the asserted ground of administrative exigencies and shortage of specialized staff. The petitioner contended that the management had selectively approved applications of similarly placed junior colleagues while arbitrarily rejecting hers, and argued that the doctrine of promissory estoppel bound the employer once the employee altered her position by opting for the scheme. The court scrutinized the VRS guidelines, the approval roster, and the staffing patterns of the corporation. The court found that the refusal lacked rational criteria and was tainted by arbitrariness, as junior employees in the identical cadre had been relieved under VRS. The court held that the rejection of the VRS application is discriminatory and arbitrary, and therefore the petition is allowed and the employer is directed to relieve the petitioner.

title: Ravi Kapoor v. Sarla Verma
text_content: The petitioner retired officer Ravi Kapoor approached the Central Administrative Tribunal in the year 2024 seeking direction to Sarla Verma public sector enterprise in Hyderabad to pay differential pension and ex-gratia benefits of Rs 78000 arising from retrospective wage revision. The petitioner had retired under an early Voluntary Retirement Scheme, and subsequent to his release, a bipartite wage settlement was finalized with retrospective effect covering the period of his active service. The enterprise denied arrears to VRS retirees, contending that voluntary retirees constituted a separate closed class who had received full and final settlement. The court examined the wage revision notification, the terms of the settlement, and constitutional equality under Article 14. The court held that wage revision implemented retrospectively cannot deny accrued benefits to employees who served during the relevant period, and therefore the petition is allowed.

title: Asha Verma v. Suresh Gupta
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Asha Verma approached the Central Administrative Tribunal in the year 2024 seeking correction of his date of birth recorded in service records maintained by Suresh Gupta government authority in Ahmedabad. The petitioner produced a certified copy of the municipal birth register showing an age difference of two years and claimed that his retirement date should be extended accordingly with arrears of salary amounting to Rs 55000. The government authority contested the petition, pointing out that the petitioner had entered service thirty years earlier, had recorded his matriculation certificate date of birth without protest, and filed the rectification plea on the verge of superannuation in breach of statutory service regulations under Transfer of Property Act. The court examined the established administrative rules barring entertaining date of birth alteration requests at the fag end of a government servant's career. The court observed that entertained belated alterations of birth dates on the eve of retirement creates chaos in cadre management and deprives juniors of promotion avenues. The court held that the belated application for correction of date of birth is rightly rejected, and therefore the writ petition is dismissed.

title: Sunita Tripathi v. Nitin Patel
text_content: The petitioner workman Sunita Tripathi instituted proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act before the Industrial Tribunal at Kolkata in the year 2016 challenging his abrupt retrenchment by the employer Nitin Patel. The workman averred that he had completed more than 240 days of continuous service in the preceding twelve calendar months, but the management terminated his services without serving any statutory one month notice in writing, without assigning reasons, and without tendering retrenchment compensation computed at fifteen days average pay for each completed year of service as mandated by Section 25-F of Consumer Protection Act. The management contended that the workman was engaged purely as a casual project employee on contractual basis for a specific infrastructure scheme and argued that cessation of employment upon project completion did not constitute retrenchment by virtue of Section 2(oo)(bb). The Calcutta High Court scrutinized the attendance registers, wage payment vouchers, and the continuous nature of work performed across multiple corporate projects. The court found that the artificial breaks in service were deliberate subterfuges to evade the statutory protections of Section 25-F. The court held that the termination amounts to illegal retrenchment void ab initio, and therefore reinstatement with full back wages is ordered.

title: Sarla Malhotra v. Usha Joshi
text_content: The petitioner Sarla Malhotra challenged the revised promotion policy notified by Usha Joshi public financial institution in Surat in the year 2016. The petitioner alleged that the new policy introduced subjective interview marks of forty percent for promotion to senior management cadre, which drastically altered the rules of the game midway through the recruitment cycle and facilitated nepotistic selections. The financial institution justified the policy, submitting that leadership positions in modern banking require high interpersonal and analytical skills best tested in interviews. The court examined the service regulations under Code of Criminal Procedure and reviewed precedents concerning excessive allocation of interview marks in public employment promotions. The court found that allocating disproportionate weight to viva voce in promotion from within an existing workforce creates room for arbitrary favoritism. The court held that the excessive interview weighting is arbitrary and violative of Article 14, and therefore the petition is allowed and promotion criteria are modified.

title: Sachin Yadav v. Ajay Verma
text_content: In this writ appeal under Article 226, the State through Ajay Verma challenged the judgment of the Single Judge at Delhi in the year 2016 which quashed the punitive transfer of public medical doctor Sachin Yadav. The appellant State contended that transfer is an ordinary incident of service and argued that courts should not interfere with administrative transfers in the absence of proved malice under Transfer of Property Act. Learned counsel for the doctor demonstrated that the transfer to a remote primary health center was ordered within twenty-four hours of the doctor submitting an official report exposing large-scale procurement irregularities of Rs 5001000 involving local politicians. The Calcutta High Court examined the sequence of events, the departmental communications, and the settled jurisprudence in Somesh Tiwari v Union of India. The court observed that while transfer is an incident of service, a transfer order passed mala fide as a punitive measure constitutes colorable exercise of power. The court therefore held that the transfer order was passed with collateral malice, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Amit Shah v. Prakash Mishra
text_content: In this writ appeal under Article 226, the State through Prakash Mishra challenged the judgment of the Single Judge at Indore in the year 2016 which quashed the punitive transfer of public medical doctor Amit Shah. The appellant State contended that transfer is an ordinary incident of service and argued that courts should not interfere with administrative transfers in the absence of proved malice under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. Learned counsel for the doctor demonstrated that the transfer to a remote primary health center was ordered within twenty-four hours of the doctor submitting an official report exposing large-scale procurement irregularities of Rs 250000 involving local politicians. The Calcutta High Court examined the sequence of events, the departmental communications, and the settled jurisprudence in Somesh Tiwari v Union of India. The court observed that while transfer is an incident of service, a transfer order passed mala fide as a punitive measure constitutes colorable exercise of power. The court therefore held that the transfer order was passed with collateral malice, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Meera Pandey v. Priya Chaturvedi
text_content: In this service appeal, the direct recruit appellants Priya Chaturvedi challenged the judgment of the High Court at Mumbai in the year 2017 which quashed their seniority over promotee officers Meera Pandey. The appellants contended that their selection process had commenced prior to the promotion of the respondents and argued that delayed issuance of appointment orders due to administrative processing should not deprive them of their rightful cadre seniority. Learned counsel for the promotee officers submitted that seniority in service law cannot be claimed from a date prior to birth in the cadre through formal appointment. The Calcutta High Court reviewed the Constitution Bench judgments in Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers Association and K. Meghachandra Singh v Ningam Siro. The court observed that no person can be granted seniority from a date when he was not even borne in the cadre or appointed to the post. The court therefore held that the direct recruits can claim seniority only from the date of their actual appointment, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Prakash Tiwari v. Asha Verma
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the State Government through Asha Verma challenged the judgment of the High Court at Surat in the year 2017 which struck down statutory provisions restricting the right of minority religious trusts represented by Prakash Tiwari to appoint headmasters and teaching faculty. The State contended that setting up a state selection commission for all government-aided schools was necessary to maintain uniform pedagogical excellence under Hindu Marriage Act. Learned counsel for the minority institution submitted that the choice of headmaster is the key to administering an educational institution and preserving its ethos. The Calcutta High Court examined the distinction between regulatory measures promoting educational standards and administrative interference destroying institutional autonomy. The court found that divesting minority managements of the power to appoint principal faculty alters the core character of the institution. The court therefore held that the statutory restriction infringes Article 30(1) of the Constitution, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Sunita Agarwal v. Priya Singh
text_content: The petitioner retired employee Sunita Agarwal instituted proceedings under Section 7 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 against the employer Priya Singh before the Controlling Authority at Delhi in the year 2018. The petitioner claimed statutory gratuity of Rs 95000 based on thirty-two years of continuous service, which the employer had withheld following his superannuation. The employer contended that gratuity was lawfully forfeited under Section 4(6) of the Act because the employee was subjected to disciplinary proceedings on the eve of retirement for alleged administrative negligence resulting in operational financial loss to the enterprise. The employee argued that under Section 4(6) of Industrial Disputes Act, gratuity can be forfeited only where services are terminated for riotous or disorderly conduct or an offence involving moral turpitude, and pointed out that no termination order was ever passed prior to superannuation. The Calcutta High Court examined the statutory provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act and the judicial precedents governing forfeiture of accrued terminal benefits. The court observed that gratuity is a hard-earned statutory entitlement and cannot be withheld or forfeited in the absence of a lawful dismissal order on specified grounds. The court held that the withholding of gratuity is wholly illegal, and therefore directed payment of full gratuity with ten percent compound interest.

title: Vimla Patel v. Rajesh Saxena
text_content: In this infrastructure writ appeal, the municipal corporation Rajesh Saxena challenged the judgment of the High Court at Indore in the year 2018 which directed the municipal body to provide potable piped drinking water to unregularized resettlement colonies following a PIL filed by community activist Vimla Patel. The municipal body argued that municipal bylaws restricted water supply infrastructure to authorized planned layouts and contended that laying pipelines would cost Rs 46000 which was commercially unviable under Hindu Marriage Act. Learned counsel for the residents demonstrated that families were compelled to consume contaminated borewell water resulting in widespread waterborne epidemics among children. The Calcutta High Court examined the international covenant on economic and social rights and the extensive domestic jurisprudence recognizing the right to safe drinking water under Article 21. The court observed that access to clean drinking water is a basic human right that cannot be conditioned upon property regularisation or layout legality. The court therefore held that the municipal corporation is constitutionally bound to supply potable water, and accordingly the municipal appeal is dismissed.

title: Kavita Kapoor v. Pooja Bhatia
text_content: In this writ appeal, the management Pooja Bhatia challenged the judgment of the Single Judge at Chennai in the year 2019 which upheld the award of the Industrial Tribunal ordering full reinstatement with back wages for employee Kavita Kapoor. The management argued that the employee had lost the confidence of the employer due to financial irregularities involving company inventory worth Rs 501000 and contended that monetary compensation was the only proper remedy. Learned counsel for the workman demonstrated that the criminal court had completely acquitted the workman on the identical set of allegations, and established that the management had initiated disciplinary action solely as an act of anti-union victimization. The Calcutta High Court examined the scope of judicial review under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act and reviewed the findings of the tribunal. The court observed that where an enquiry is found to be mala fide and punitive, reinstatement with back wages is the standard statutory remedy. The court therefore held that the order of reinstatement is just and lawful, and accordingly the management appeal is dismissed.

title: Usha Pandey v. Nitin Patel
text_content: In this writ appeal, the management Nitin Patel challenged the order of the appellate authority under the Payment of Gratuity Act at Kolkata in the year 2020 which directed payment of enhanced gratuity to employee Usha Pandey. The appellant argued that under the company's internal gratuity scheme, the maximum gratuity was capped at Rs 105000 and contended that the employee was bound by the contractual limit agreed at the time of appointment. Learned counsel for the employee submitted that under Section 4(5) of Indian Contract Act, an employee is entitled to receive better terms of gratuity under any award, agreement, or contract, but the statutory ceiling prescribed by Parliament acts as the minimum floor below which no employer can contract out. The Calcutta High Court analyzed the overriding effect of Section 14 of the Payment of Gratuity Act over all other contractual agreements or company rules. The court observed that beneficial social legislation must be interpreted to maximize the welfare of the superannuated workman. The court therefore held that the employee is entitled to the full statutory gratuity amount, and accordingly the management appeal is dismissed.

title: Kavita Verma v. Pooja Verma
text_content: In this service appeal, the State Government through Pooja Verma challenged the order of the High Court at Surat in the year 2020 directing the retrospective promotion of officer Kavita Verma with all consequential monetary benefits. The appellant contended that the High Court in exercise of writ jurisdiction could not usurp the functions of the statutory Departmental Promotion Committee by directing outright promotion instead of remitting the matter for fresh assessment. Learned counsel for the respondent officer demonstrated that the officer had been cleared of all departmental charges in an earlier inquiry and argued that the sealed cover procedure adopted by the DPC was unlawfully maintained for five years after full exoneration. The Calcutta High Court examined the established guidelines in Union of India v K.V. Jankiraman governing the opening of sealed cover recommendations. The court observed that upon complete exoneration in disciplinary proceedings, the sealed cover must be opened and benefits granted from the due date. The court therefore held that the officer is entitled to retrospective promotion from the date his juniors were elevated, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Renu Mehta v. Deepak Tiwari
text_content: In this civil appeal, the employer bank Deepak Tiwari challenged the judgment of the High Court at Delhi in the year 2021 which permitted officer Renu Mehta to withdraw his application for Voluntary Retirement prior to its effective date of acceptance. The appellant bank contended that under the special terms of the VRS scheme, an application once submitted became irrevocable and could not be rescinded by the employee under any circumstances. Learned counsel for the officer submitted that it is settled law established in Bank of India v O.P. Swarnakar that an application for voluntary retirement is merely an offer by the employee which can be lawfully withdrawn at any time before the contract becomes concluded by formal acceptance and communication by the employer. The Calcutta High Court examined the contract law principles applicable to voluntary retirement schemes under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The court observed that the relationship between master and servant continues until the effective date of release, and the locus poenitentiae to withdraw survives until acceptance. The court therefore held that the employee was fully entitled to withdraw his voluntary retirement request, and accordingly the appeal of the bank is dismissed.

title: Kavita Tripathi v. Asha Malhotra
text_content: The workman Kavita Tripathi approached the Calcutta High Court in the year 2022 alleging violation of Section 25-H of the Industrial Disputes Act by Asha Malhotra in Jaipur. The petitioner established that he was retrenched two years earlier after receiving retrenchment compensation of Rs 499000. He alleged that when the employer subsequently revived industrial operations and recruited fresh personnel for identical technician posts, the management failed to offer him preferential re-employment as mandated by statutory provisions. The employer contended that fresh hiring was conducted through a third-party manpower outsourcing agency and argued that Section 25-H applied only to direct recruitment. The court examined the scope of Section 25-H of Negotiable Instruments Act designed to protect experienced retrenched workers against indirect replacement. The court observed that employers cannot circumvent statutory re-employment obligations through outsourcing subterfuges when regular work is resumed. The court held that the retrenched workman is entitled to preferential re-employment, and therefore the petition is allowed with directions to absorb the petitioner.

title: Vijay Kumar v. Lata Kapoor
text_content: In this writ appeal, the management Lata Kapoor challenged the judgment of the Single Judge at Kolkata in the year 2022 which upheld the award of the Industrial Tribunal ordering full reinstatement with back wages for employee Vijay Kumar. The management argued that the employee had lost the confidence of the employer due to financial irregularities involving company inventory worth Rs 502000 and contended that monetary compensation was the only proper remedy. Learned counsel for the workman demonstrated that the criminal court had completely acquitted the workman on the identical set of allegations, and established that the management had initiated disciplinary action solely as an act of anti-union victimization. The Calcutta High Court examined the scope of judicial review under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act and reviewed the findings of the tribunal. The court observed that where an enquiry is found to be mala fide and punitive, reinstatement with back wages is the standard statutory remedy. The court therefore held that the order of reinstatement is just and lawful, and accordingly the management appeal is dismissed.

title: Deepak Saxena v. Pankaj Gupta
text_content: In this infrastructure writ appeal, the municipal corporation Pankaj Gupta challenged the judgment of the High Court at Varanasi in the year 2022 which directed the municipal body to provide potable piped drinking water to unregularized resettlement colonies following a PIL filed by community activist Deepak Saxena. The municipal body argued that municipal bylaws restricted water supply infrastructure to authorized planned layouts and contended that laying pipelines would cost Rs 295000 which was commercially unviable under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. Learned counsel for the residents demonstrated that families were compelled to consume contaminated borewell water resulting in widespread waterborne epidemics among children. The Calcutta High Court examined the international covenant on economic and social rights and the extensive domestic jurisprudence recognizing the right to safe drinking water under Article 21. The court observed that access to clean drinking water is a basic human right that cannot be conditioned upon property regularisation or layout legality. The court therefore held that the municipal corporation is constitutionally bound to supply potable water, and accordingly the municipal appeal is dismissed.

title: Nitin Patel v. Deepak Agarwal
text_content: In this environmental writ appeal, the mining conglomerate Deepak Agarwal challenged the judgment of the High Court at Patna in the year 2023 which halted open-cast bauxite mining operations inside an eco-sensitive forest zone following a PIL instituted by tribal rights activist Nitin Patel. The appellant corporation contended that it held valid environmental clearances granted by the Ministry of Environment and had invested Rs 51000 in infrastructure. Learned counsel for the petitioner established that the mining operations caused massive deforestation, dried up perennial mountain streams, and displaced indigenous tribal communities without obtaining their mandatory consent under the Forest Rights Act and Negotiable Instruments Act. The Calcutta High Court examined the ecological sensitivity of the Western Ghats and reviewed the constitutional public trust doctrine. The court observed that economic considerations must yield to the imperative need for sustainable development and preservation of fragile ecological biodiversity. The court therefore held that mining in the protected eco-sensitive sanctuary cannot be permitted, and accordingly the mining appeal is dismissed.

title: Seema Khanna v. Amit Kumar
text_content: The petitioner workman Seema Khanna instituted proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act before the Industrial Tribunal at Bengaluru in the year 2024 challenging his abrupt retrenchment by the employer Amit Kumar. The workman averred that he had completed more than 240 days of continuous service in the preceding twelve calendar months, but the management terminated his services without serving any statutory one month notice in writing, without assigning reasons, and without tendering retrenchment compensation computed at fifteen days average pay for each completed year of service as mandated by Section 25-F of Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The management contended that the workman was engaged purely as a casual project employee on contractual basis for a specific infrastructure scheme and argued that cessation of employment upon project completion did not constitute retrenchment by virtue of Section 2(oo)(bb). The Calcutta High Court scrutinized the attendance registers, wage payment vouchers, and the continuous nature of work performed across multiple corporate projects. The court found that the artificial breaks in service were deliberate subterfuges to evade the statutory protections of Section 25-F. The court held that the termination amounts to illegal retrenchment void ab initio, and therefore reinstatement with full back wages is ordered.

title: Vimla Verma v. Sunita Verma
text_content: By this petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the petitioner Vimla Verma challenged the summoning order passed by the Metropolitan Magistrate at Varanasi in the year 2015 in a private criminal complaint instituted by Sunita Verma. The complaint alleged that the petitioner had committed offences of criminal breach of trust regarding company machinery worth Rs 54000. The petitioner submitted that the parties had subsequently resolved all existing disputes through a comprehensive memorandum of settlement and jointly prayed for quashing of all criminal proceedings to restore business harmony. The respondent appeared through counsel and confirmed receipt of agreed settlement amounts and consented to the quashing of the criminal complaint. The Delhi High Court examined whether non-compoundable offences of a predominantly commercial and private nature could be quashed under inherent powers. The court noted that when the underlying commercial dispute is amicably resolved, continuing criminal prosecution would be an exercise in futility. The court therefore held that it is in the interest of justice to quash the proceedings, and accordingly the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Deepak Singh v. Asha Yadav
text_content: In this regular first appeal, the appellant husband Asha Yadav challenged the preliminary decree passed by the civil court at Ahmedabad in the year 2015 declaring that the respondent wife Deepak Singh was a joint owner of two commercial apartments purchased during cohabitation. The appellant contended that the trial court had erroneously applied community of property concepts that are alien to the general matrimonial law of India outside Goa. Learned counsel for the wife demonstrated that the mortgage loan was sanctioned jointly, that rental revenues were deposited into a joint account, and that the wife had pledged her ancestral gold ornaments to secure initial bridge financing. The Delhi High Court scrutinized the loan sanction agreements, banking records, and property tax assessments. The court observed that where property is acquired jointly through mutual contributions of spouses, neither party can unilaterally exclude the other. The court therefore held that the wife is a bona fide co-owner of the disputed properties, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Kavita Khanna v. Amit Kumar
text_content: The petitioner candidate Kavita Khanna filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Delhi High Court in the year 2015 challenging an order passed by the Returning Officer Amit Kumar in Indore rejecting his nomination papers for the legislative assembly constituency under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Returning Officer had rejected the nomination paper on the hyper-technical ground of a minor clerical omission in the accompanying electoral affidavit, despite the petitioner submitting a rectification affidavit before the deadline for scrutiny. The Election Commission raised a preliminary objection, arguing that under Article 329(b) of the Constitution, all electoral disputes must await completion of the election and can only be adjudicated through an election petition under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The court examined the narrow exceptions where writ intervention is permissible to facilitate rather than stall the democratic election process. The court observed that where rejection of nomination is patently arbitrary and perverse, leaving a candidate remediless until post-election defeats democracy. The court held that the rejection of nomination was wholly arbitrary, and therefore the writ petition is allowed directing acceptance of nomination.

title: Ramesh Kapoor v. Mahesh Patel
text_content: The petitioner environmentalist Ramesh Kapoor filed a PIL before the Delhi High Court in the year 2015 challenging the commercial felling of thousands of heritage trees in Pune for constructing an elevated highway project by the infrastructure corporation Mahesh Patel. The petitioner showed that the environmental impact assessment was flawed and demonstrated that viable alternative civil engineering alignments could save the tree canopy. The infrastructure agency contended that the road was essential to decongest vehicular traffic and promised compensatory afforestation of saplings. The court reviewed international protocols on urban forestry, the right to clean air under Article 21, and the recommendations of the Tree Authority. The court observed that planting distant saplings cannot instantly replace century-old oxygen-generating heritage trees that combat severe urban air pollution. The court held that the infrastructure authority must redesign the project alignment to preserve the heritage trees, and therefore the PIL is allowed.

title: Vimla Singh v. Anita Malhotra
text_content: The petitioner adoptive parents Vimla Singh filed a civil petition under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act before the district court at Lucknow in the year 2016 seeking a formal declaration of the validity of the adoption of a minor child and registration of the adoption deed. The petitioners established that all essential statutory ceremonies including the actual giving and taking of the child with intent to transfer from the biological family to the adoptive family were duly performed in the presence of relatives. The respondent biological relatives Anita Malhotra contested the adoption, alleging that the consent of the biological mother was procured through misrepresentation and contended that the adoptive parents lacked requisite financial capacity under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The Delhi High Court examined the registered adoption deed, photographs and video recordings of the religious ceremonies, and the testimony of participating elders. The court verified that the child was capable of being adopted, that the adoptive parents possessed sound mind and legal capacity, and that valid consent was executed. The court held that the adoption is legal, valid, and binding on all parties, and therefore the petition is allowed and the adoption is confirmed.

title: Ravi Mishra v. Kamla Sharma
text_content: The petitioner nominee Ravi Mishra approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2016 seeking disbursement of death-cum-retirement gratuity of Rs 253000 due upon the demise of her husband who served as a permanent technician with Kamla Sharma in Jaipur. The employer resisted payment, alleging that the deceased employee had not completed five years of continuous service as required by Section 4(1) of Indian Contract Act and sought to adjust alleged overpayment of salary advances against the terminal gratuity. The court referred to the first proviso to Section 4(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act which explicitly waives the requirement of five years continuous service in cases where employment terminates due to death or disablement of the employee. The court further noted that Section 13 grants absolute immunity to gratuity from attachment in execution of any decree or order of any civil, revenue, or criminal court. The court held that the nominee is entitled to immediate payment of full gratuity without deductions, and therefore the petition is allowed with interest.

title: Naresh Malhotra v. Renu Dwivedi
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the State authority Renu Dwivedi challenged the judgment of the High Court at Vadodara in the year 2016 which declared a state policy discriminating against transgender persons in public employment as violative of Articles 14 and 16 in a challenge by Naresh Malhotra. The appellant contended that service recruitment rules under Central Goods and Services Tax Act historically recognized only binary gender categories and pleaded administrative convenience. Learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the landmark Supreme Court ruling in NALSA v Union of India and argued that denying public employment on the ground of gender identity violates fundamental equality and personal autonomy under Articles 14, 19, and 21. The Delhi High Court examined the constitutional framework of substantive equality and reviewed the statutory provisions of the Transgender Persons Act. The court observed that administrative convenience can never be an acceptable justification for perpetuating institutional discrimination against marginalized citizens. The court therefore held that exclusion of transgender citizens from public employment is unconstitutional, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Lata Malhotra v. Sunita Kapoor
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Lata Malhotra filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India before the Delhi High Court in the year 2016 challenging an order of compulsory retirement passed by the respondent State Government Sunita Kapoor in Hyderabad. The petitioner pleaded that he had maintained a distinguished public service record spanning twenty-four years without a single adverse remark, until an abrupt compulsory retirement order was issued under Fundamental Rule 56(j) following a change in political administration. The petitioner contended that the review committee had ignored his consistent outstanding performance ratings and acted on extraneous and collateral considerations, violating principles of natural justice and procedural due process under Hindu Marriage Act. The State Government justified the premature retirement, asserting that the administration had weeded out deadwood to maintain public efficiency. The court called for the confidential service dossiers, the review committee minutes, and scrutinized the entire service trajectory of the officer. The court observed that compulsory retirement cannot be weaponized as a disguised punitive measure or used to retire efficient officers on subjective whims. The court held that the order of compulsory retirement is arbitrary and perverse, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and reinstatement is ordered.

title: Meera Khanna v. Sarla Verma
text_content: The petitioner government teacher Meera Khanna approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2016 through a writ petition under Article 226 seeking release of withheld pension and terminal retirement benefits amounting to Rs 1499000 against Sarla Verma education department in Lucknow. The department had withheld pensionary dues for five years after superannuation, citing an unfinalized preliminary audit objection dating back fifteen years. The court referred to the landmark rulings in State of Jharkhand v Jitendra Kumar Srivastava holding that pension is not a bounty but a constitutional property under Article 300A which cannot be withheld without statutory authority. The court observed that an employee cannot be deprived of livelihood in old age based on stale and unadjudicated administrative inquiries. The court held that withholding pension without authority of law violates constitutional guarantees, and therefore the writ petition is allowed with nine percent interest.

title: Deepak Joshi v. Vimla Bhatia
text_content: The petitioner registered political party Deepak Joshi approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2016 challenging the arbitrary rejection of its application for allotment of a reserved common election symbol by the Election Commission of India Vimla Bhatia in Lucknow. The petitioner proved that it had fulfilled all vote share thresholds in the preceding general election under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order. The Election Commission defended its discretion, contending that another splinter faction had asserted competing claims over the registered party name and symbol. The court examined the test of legislative and organizational majority formulated in Sadiq Ali and applied to internal party disputes under Consumer Protection Act. The court found that the petitioner faction demonstrated overwhelming numerical majority in both the legislative wing and the organizational executive committee. The court held that the denial of the common symbol is discriminatory and arbitrary, and therefore the writ petition is allowed directing allotment of the symbol.

title: Anita Rastogi v. Amit Rastogi
text_content: The revisionist tenant Anita Rastogi approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2017 assailing an order of eviction passed under summary eviction provisions of the Rent Control Act in Lucknow. The respondent landlord Amit Rastogi had sought recovery of immediate possession of the residential property on the ground of personal requirement as a retired senior citizen needing ground-floor accommodation due to medical infirmities. The tenant sought leave to defend under Section 192, contending that the landlord owned multiple alternative residential flats in Lucknow and argued that the eviction petition was a stratagem to coerce enhanced rent. The court examined whether the affidavit filed by the tenant disclosed any triable issue of law or fact warranting a full-fledged trial. The court noted that vague assertions regarding alternative accommodation without specific property identification do not constitute triable issues. The court held that the landlord's need is genuine and pressing, and therefore the revision petition is dismissed and the tenant is directed to vacate.

title: Pankaj Gupta v. Deepak Agarwal
text_content: The plaintiff Pankaj Gupta filed a civil suit for partition against Deepak Agarwal seeking metes and bounds division of an ancestral residential building in Varanasi in the year 2017. Following the preliminary decree determining one-half share each, disputes arose during final decree proceedings regarding the feasibility of physical division of the single compact residential structure. The court commissioner submitted a report stating that dividing the small structure into two separate residential units would render both portions uninhabitable and destroy their economic value. The plaintiff moved an application under the Partition Act seeking public auction of the property and division of sale proceeds, which the defendant opposed. The Delhi High Court examined Sections 2 and 3 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act governing sale in lieu of partition where physical division cannot reasonably be made. The court observed that where metes and bounds partition destroys utility, court-directed sale amongst co-owners or public auction is the sole practical remedy. The court held that the property shall be put to sale with first option to co-sharers, and therefore the final decree application is allowed with directions.

title: Amit Gupta v. Vijay Kumar
text_content: In this first appeal, the appellant mortgagor Vijay Kumar challenged the final decree for foreclosure and sale passed in favour of mortgagee Amit Gupta by the civil court in Patna in the year 2017. The appellant contended that under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, the equity of redemption remained alive until the confirmation of court auction sale and tendered a partial payment of Rs 4999000 in court while praying for rescheduling of dues. Learned counsel for the respondent mortgagee submitted that the mortgagor had failed to deposit the full redemption amount within the six months granted under the preliminary decree and argued that the right to redeem stood legally extinguished upon final decree. The Delhi High Court examined the statutory scheme of Order XXXIV Rules 4 and 5 of CPC and the judicial precedents governing mortgagor's right to redeem prior to sale confirmation. The court noted that equity of redemption is an inviolable statutory right which can be exercised upon depositing the entire outstanding debt with costs prior to auction. The court held that upon failure to tender the complete mortgage debt, foreclosure must proceed, and therefore the appeal is dismissed.

title: Sachin Shah v. Prakash Gupta
text_content: In this commercial appeal, the appellant contractor Prakash Gupta challenged the decree of damages passed in favour of project owner Sachin Shah by the Commercial Division of the High Court at Coimbatore in the year 2017.
