The appellant contended that the project owner had contributed to construction delays by failing to provide unencumbered site access, delayed architectural drawings, and argued that the liquidated damages clause of Rs 303000 was a punitive penalty unenforceable under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act without proof of actual pecuniary loss. Learned counsel for the respondent project owner demonstrated that the contractual completion schedule was agreed as essential, that site access was timely provided, and pointed out that the liquidated damages represented a genuine pre-estimate of loss incurred due to delayed commercial operations. The Delhi High Court reviewed the landmark principles laid down in Kailash Nath Associates v DDA regarding liquidated damages under Section 74. The court found that the pre-estimated liquidated damages were reasonable and commensurate with the commercial loss suffered by the owner. The court therefore held that the contractor is liable for contractual delay damages, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Suresh Mishra v. Vikas Bhatia
text_content: The financial creditor financial institution Suresh Mishra filed an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 before the National Company Law Tribunal at Surat in the year 2017 seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the corporate debtor Vikas Bhatia. The financial creditor established that it had disbursed a consortium credit facility of Rs 98000 for constructing an industrial manufacturing plant, and demonstrated that the corporate debtor had committed continuous payment defaults exceeding the statutory threshold of one crore rupees, with default conclusively proved by the record of default certified by the Information Utility (NeSL). The corporate debtor resisted admission, contending that default was occasioned by macroeconomic factors, arguing that the loan agreement was unstamped under Indian Penal Code, and asserting that ongoing debt restructuring negotiations precluded the initiation of corporate insolvency. The Delhi High Court examined the landmark Supreme Court judgments in Innoventive Industries and Swiss Ribbons. The court observed that under Section 7, the adjudicating authority is only required to satisfy itself whether a financial debt exists and default has occurred. The court held that debt and default stand indisputably established, and therefore the Section 7 petition is admitted and moratorium is declared.

title: Meera Mishra v. Manju Shah
text_content: The applicant wife Meera Mishra instituted proceedings claiming maintenance from her husband Manju Shah before the Family Court at Delhi in the year 2017. The applicant stated that following grave matrimonial discord, she was forced to leave the matrimonial domicile with her infant child, possessed no independent financial assets, and required monthly maintenance of Rs 47000 to meet living and medical expenses. The respondent husband opposed the application, alleging that the applicant was gainfully employed as a commercial designer and argued that his own net salary was insufficient to bear the claimed maintenance after meeting obligations towards his aged parents under Indian Penal Code. The Delhi High Court examined the detailed assets and liabilities affidavits submitted by both spouses along with bank statements and income tax disclosures. The court observed that the husband had suppressed supplementary allowances and investment portfolios, and noted that maintenance under social welfare legislation is intended to prevent destitution and maintain parity of living standard. The court held that the wife and infant child are entitled to reasonable maintenance, and therefore directed payment of monthly maintenance and allowed the petition.

title: Renu Verma v. Mahesh Joshi
text_content: The petitioner single female Renu Verma approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2017 seeking directions to the Central Adoption Resource Authority and local welfare agency Mahesh Joshi to finalize the domestic adoption of a surrendered child in Hyderabad. The authorities had delayed issuance of the final no-objection certificate, questioning the eligibility of an unmarried working professional under Industrial Disputes Act and seeking additional financial guarantees of Rs 505000. The petitioner submitted that she satisfied all criteria under the Juvenile Justice Act and Adoption Regulations, having an established career and strong support system. The court examined the home study report, the psychological fitness evaluation, and the constitutional guarantee of non-discrimination. The court observed that unmarried women have an equal legal right to adopt and provide loving parental care to orphaned children without arbitrary impediments. The court held that the delay caused by the authorities is unjustified, and therefore the petition is allowed and the authorities are directed to finalize the adoption.

title: Prakash Patel v. Dinesh Srivastava
text_content: The petitioner workman Prakash Patel approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2017 seeking enforcement of an industrial award directing reinstatement passed against the public sector corporation Dinesh Srivastava in Bengaluru. The petitioner submitted that despite the award attaining finality following the dismissal of the employer's special leave petition, the management refused to permit him to rejoin duties or disburse wages under Section 17-B of Negotiable Instruments Act. The corporation pleaded corporate restructuring and abolition of the operational cadre, offering to pay a lumpsum ex-gratia amount of Rs 5003000 in lieu of job. The court observed that public sector undertakings cannot defy binding awards of competent industrial adjudicators under the pretext of restructuring. The court reiterated that an award for reinstatement must be implemented in letter and spirit unless modified by a superior court. The court held that the respondent corporation is bound to reinstate the petitioner forthwith, and therefore the contempt and writ petition is allowed.

title: Nirmala Verma v. Nitin Yadav
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Nirmala Verma approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2017 seeking correction of his date of birth recorded in service records maintained by Nitin Yadav government authority in Kolkata. The petitioner produced a certified copy of the municipal birth register showing an age difference of two years and claimed that his retirement date should be extended accordingly with arrears of salary amounting to Rs 48000. The government authority contested the petition, pointing out that the petitioner had entered service thirty years earlier, had recorded his matriculation certificate date of birth without protest, and filed the rectification plea on the verge of superannuation in breach of statutory service regulations under Indian Contract Act. The court examined the established administrative rules barring entertaining date of birth alteration requests at the fag end of a government servant's career. The court observed that entertained belated alterations of birth dates on the eve of retirement creates chaos in cadre management and deprives juniors of promotion avenues. The court held that the belated application for correction of date of birth is rightly rejected, and therefore the writ petition is dismissed.

title: Pooja Mehta v. Mahesh Tiwari
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the State authority Mahesh Tiwari challenged the judgment of the High Court at Jaipur in the year 2017 which declared a state policy discriminating against transgender persons in public employment as violative of Articles 14 and 16 in a challenge by Pooja Mehta. The appellant contended that service recruitment rules under Indian Penal Code historically recognized only binary gender categories and pleaded administrative convenience. Learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the landmark Supreme Court ruling in NALSA v Union of India and argued that denying public employment on the ground of gender identity violates fundamental equality and personal autonomy under Articles 14, 19, and 21. The Delhi High Court examined the constitutional framework of substantive equality and reviewed the statutory provisions of the Transgender Persons Act. The court observed that administrative convenience can never be an acceptable justification for perpetuating institutional discrimination against marginalized citizens. The court therefore held that exclusion of transgender citizens from public employment is unconstitutional, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Manju Shah v. Meera Tiwari
text_content: The citizen welfare forum Manju Shah instituted a public interest litigation before the Delhi High Court in the year 2017 highlighting the catastrophic dilapidation of municipal roads, open sewer trenches, and ubiquitous potholes across the metropolitan area of Lucknow. The petitioners placed on record photographic documentation and hospital statistics showing that over two hundred commuters had suffered fatal accidents or permanent spinal disabilities during the monsoon season due to unpaved roads and uncovered drainage manholes maintained by the Municipal Corporation Meera Tiwari. The municipal body pleaded financial constraints, shortage of bituminous asphalt, and delays in processing maintenance tenders under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The court examined the statutory duties imposed upon municipal authorities under the Municipal Corporation Act and the constitutional dimensions of Article 21. The court observed that citizens who pay municipal taxes possess an inalienable fundamental right to safe, motorable, and dignified public roads. The court held that the municipal corporation has failed miserably in discharging its statutory obligations, and therefore the PIL is allowed with time-bound repair directions.

title: Asha Khanna v. Asha Verma
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Asha Khanna filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India before the Delhi High Court in the year 2017 challenging an order of compulsory retirement passed by the respondent State Government Asha Verma in Delhi. The petitioner pleaded that he had maintained a distinguished public service record spanning twenty-four years without a single adverse remark, until an abrupt compulsory retirement order was issued under Fundamental Rule 56(j) following a change in political administration. The petitioner contended that the review committee had ignored his consistent outstanding performance ratings and acted on extraneous and collateral considerations, violating principles of natural justice and procedural due process under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The State Government justified the premature retirement, asserting that the administration had weeded out deadwood to maintain public efficiency. The court called for the confidential service dossiers, the review committee minutes, and scrutinized the entire service trajectory of the officer. The court observed that compulsory retirement cannot be weaponized as a disguised punitive measure or used to retire efficient officers on subjective whims. The court held that the order of compulsory retirement is arbitrary and perverse, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and reinstatement is ordered.

title: Ajay Khanna v. Prakash Malhotra
text_content: The petitioner registered political party Ajay Khanna approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2018 challenging the arbitrary rejection of its application for allotment of a reserved common election symbol by the Election Commission of India Prakash Malhotra in Kanpur. The petitioner proved that it had fulfilled all vote share thresholds in the preceding general election under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order. The Election Commission defended its discretion, contending that another splinter faction had asserted competing claims over the registered party name and symbol. The court examined the test of legislative and organizational majority formulated in Sadiq Ali and applied to internal party disputes under Code of Criminal Procedure. The court found that the petitioner faction demonstrated overwhelming numerical majority in both the legislative wing and the organizational executive committee. The court held that the denial of the common symbol is discriminatory and arbitrary, and therefore the writ petition is allowed directing allotment of the symbol.

title: Kamla Sharma v. Anita Shah
text_content: The plaintiff Kamla Sharma filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable residential property in Vadodara executed in the year 2019 against Anita Shah. In the alternative, the plaintiff claimed refund of earnest money with twenty-four percent interest and substantial damages. During trial, it emerged that the defendant vendor did not possess sole transferable title to the suit property, which was co-owned by his estranged siblings who were not signatories to the agreement to sell. The Delhi High Court examined Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act governing specific performance of a part of contract and evaluated whether the purchaser was willing to accept the vendor's undivided fractional share without claiming abatement of price. The court found that the contract could not be specifically enforced in its entirety without infringing third-party rights of non-signatory co-owners. The court held that decreeing specific performance would be inequitable, and therefore the alternative relief of refund of earnest money with interest is granted.

title: Kamla Agarwal v. Suresh Chaturvedi
text_content: The plaintiff Kamla Agarwal instituted a civil suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell against the defendant vendor Suresh Chaturvedi before the civil court at Nagpur in the year 2019. The plaintiff stated that the parties had entered into a registered agreement to sell an immovable commercial property for a total sale consideration of Rs 998000, whereof a substantial earnest money deposit was duly paid upon execution. The plaintiff averred that he was always ready and willing to perform his part of the contract by paying the balance consideration and obtaining the sale deed. The defendant resisted the suit, contending that time was of the essence of the contract and claiming that the plaintiff had defaulted in paying the balance amount within the agreed ninety days, thereby forfeiting the earnest money deposit under Income Tax Act. The Delhi High Court examined the correspondence between parties, the bank solvency certificates produced by the plaintiff, and the terms of the agreement. The court reiterated the settled legal principle that in agreements for sale of immovable property, time is ordinarily not the essence of the contract unless explicitly so stipulated. The court held that the plaintiff has established continuous readiness and willingness throughout, and therefore the suit for specific performance is decreed.

title: Sarla Sharma v. Ramesh Saxena
text_content: In this company appeal under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the suspended director Ramesh Saxena challenged the order of the NCLT at Vadodara in the year 2019 which admitted a Section 9 application filed by operational creditor Sarla Sharma. The appellant contended that the operational creditor's claim of Rs 105000 was subject to a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods raised in email correspondence long prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice under Section 8 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act. Learned counsel for the operational creditor submitted that the alleged dispute was a spurious defense raised after demand notice to evade insolvency proceedings. The Delhi High Court examined the email exchanges, the rejection notes, and the seminal ruling in Mobilox Innovations v Kirusa Software. The court found that contemporaneous communications revealed that the corporate debtor had rejected the consignments and raised debit notes prior to notice. The court therefore held that a genuine pre-existing dispute exists barring Section 9 insolvency, and accordingly the appeal is allowed and CIRP is quashed.

title: Pankaj Rastogi v. Rohit Kapoor
text_content: The resolution applicant Pankaj Rastogi approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2019 challenging an order passed by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal at Coimbatore which rejected its approved resolution plan for corporate debtor Rohit Kapoor involving a total financial outlay of Rs 300000. The NCLAT had set aside the plan on the ground that it offered differential settlement percentages between financial creditors and operational creditors. The petitioner contended that the resolution plan had received unanimous ninety-eight percent voting approval from the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom. The court examined Section 30 and Section 31 of Transfer of Property Act and reviewed the Constitution Bench rulings in Essar Steel and Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel. The court observed that the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is non-justiciable unless the plan violates specific statutory provisions. The court held that the resolution plan complies with all statutory requirements, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the resolution plan is reinstated.

title: Vimla Gupta v. Sarla Chaturvedi
text_content: In this service appeal, the direct recruit appellants Sarla Chaturvedi challenged the judgment of the High Court at Coimbatore in the year 2019 which quashed their seniority over promotee officers Vimla Gupta. The appellants contended that their selection process had commenced prior to the promotion of the respondents and argued that delayed issuance of appointment orders due to administrative processing should not deprive them of their rightful cadre seniority. Learned counsel for the promotee officers submitted that seniority in service law cannot be claimed from a date prior to birth in the cadre through formal appointment. The Delhi High Court reviewed the Constitution Bench judgments in Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers Association and K. Meghachandra Singh v Ningam Siro. The court observed that no person can be granted seniority from a date when he was not even borne in the cadre or appointed to the post. The court therefore held that the direct recruits can claim seniority only from the date of their actual appointment, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Asha Tripathi v. Naresh Mishra
text_content: The petitioner environmentalist Asha Tripathi filed a PIL before the Delhi High Court in the year 2019 challenging the commercial felling of thousands of heritage trees in Chennai for constructing an elevated highway project by the infrastructure corporation Naresh Mishra. The petitioner showed that the environmental impact assessment was flawed and demonstrated that viable alternative civil engineering alignments could save the tree canopy. The infrastructure agency contended that the road was essential to decongest vehicular traffic and promised compensatory afforestation of saplings. The court reviewed international protocols on urban forestry, the right to clean air under Article 21, and the recommendations of the Tree Authority. The court observed that planting distant saplings cannot instantly replace century-old oxygen-generating heritage trees that combat severe urban air pollution. The court held that the infrastructure authority must redesign the project alignment to preserve the heritage trees, and therefore the PIL is allowed.

title: Vimla Chopra v. Pushpa Sharma
text_content: The petitioner Vimla Chopra filed this petition for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC before the Delhi High Court in 2020 apprehending arrest in an FIR lodged at Hyderabad by Pushpa Sharma arising out of a matrimonial dispute under Section 226 of Indian Penal Code. The allegations related to harassment for dowry and unlawful retention of stridhan ornaments valued at approximately Rs 1000000. Counsel for the petitioner submitted that omnibus allegations were made against the entire family, that the marriage had broken down irretrievably, and that the petitioner was willing to deposit the value of stridhan articles in an escrow account to demonstrate bona fides. The State submitted that recovery of the stridhan property was yet to be completed and opposed pre-arrest protection. The court reiterated that arrest in matrimonial conflicts should be an exception rather than a routine measure to prevent abuse of criminal law. The court held that custodial interrogation of the petitioner is not necessary for the recovery of stridhan, and therefore anticipatory bail is granted.

title: Sachin Khanna v. Ravi Tripathi
text_content: In this criminal appeal, the appellant Sachin Khanna challenged the judgment of conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code recorded by the Sessions Court at Lucknow in the year 2020. The prosecution case against the appellant rested entirely on circumstantial evidence as deposed by witness Ravi Tripathi. The circumstantial links relied upon were the last seen theory, motive relating to disputed business accounts of Rs 1499000, and recovery of the weapon of offence pursuant to a disclosure statement recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. The appellant contended that the chain of circumstantial evidence was fragmented, pointing out that an interval of over twelve hours elapsed between the last seen encounter and the estimated time of death, and alleged that the weapon recovery was planted by investigating officials. The Delhi High Court examined the golden principles governing circumstantial evidence and evaluated whether every link pointed unerringly to the guilt of the accused. The court found that the prosecution had conclusively established every link in the chain leaving no room for any hypothesis of innocence. The court therefore held that the circumstantial evidence conclusively proves the guilt of the appellant, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Kavita Agarwal v. Rohit Tiwari
text_content: In this criminal appeal under the Domestic Violence Act, the appellant husband Rohit Tiwari assailed the monetary relief order passed by the magistrate in Agra in the year 2020 directing him to pay Rs 151000 per month towards alternative rented accommodation for aggrieved wife Kavita Agarwal. The appellant contended that the wife was residing with her affluent parents and suffered no financial distress, arguing that the award was punitive. Learned counsel for the wife submitted that under Section 19(1)(f) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, the magistrate possesses explicit statutory power to direct the respondent to secure the same level of alternative accommodation for the aggrieved person as enjoyed in the shared household. The Delhi High Court evaluated the lifestyle of the husband, the rental value of residential premises in Agra, and the legislative object of the enactment. The court found that the monetary provision for alternative accommodation was strictly in accordance with statutory guidelines and proportional to the respondent's income. The court therefore held that the order of the magistrate is unassailable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the order is confirmed.

title: Geeta Tiwari v. Pooja Rastogi
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant husband Pooja Rastogi challenged the judgment of the Family Court in Varanasi in the year 2020 which awarded monthly maintenance to respondent wife Geeta Tiwari. The appellant argued that the marriage had lasted for barely six months and contended that the maintenance quantum of Rs 1501000 was disproportionate to the duration of cohabitation. Learned counsel for the respondent wife demonstrated that the husband was a senior corporate director who traveled internationally and maintained luxury cars, arguing that the award was commensurate with the high socioeconomic status enjoyed during marriage. The Delhi High Court reviewed the precedents under Section 143 and noted that duration of marriage does not diminish the statutory entitlement to dignified maintenance. The court found that the Family Court had carefully balanced the financial capacities and reasonable needs of both parties without imposing punitive burden. The court therefore held that the maintenance award is just, equitable, and appropriate, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Renu Malhotra v. Kavita Gupta
text_content: The petitioner Renu Malhotra approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2020 seeking enforcement and recovery of accumulated maintenance arrears of Rs 296000 awarded by the Family Court at Hyderabad against Kavita Gupta. The petitioner submitted that the husband had wilfully failed to pay monthly maintenance for over two years despite coercive recovery notices and attachment warrants issued under Consumer Protection Act. The respondent husband pleaded business insolvency and offered to liquidate the arrears in nominal monthly instalments of negligible value. The court scrutinized the husband's company accounts, credit card statements, and recent foreign travel expenditures. The court observed that deliberate refusal to comply with maintenance orders cannot be tolerated, as it defeats the benevolent purpose of the statute. The court held that coercive measures including attachment of bank accounts and civil imprisonment must follow upon continued default, and therefore the execution petition is allowed.

title: Anita Tiwari v. Ajay Dwivedi
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Anita Tiwari filed a service writ petition before the Delhi High Court in the year 2020 challenging the proceedings of the Departmental Promotion Committee convened by the respondent department Ajay Dwivedi in Pune. The petitioner contended that he was senior in the feeder cadre of Executive Engineers and possessed outstanding annual performance appraisal reports, yet his junior colleagues were promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer while his candidature was superseded without any communicating reason. The respondent department defended the promotion orders, contending that promotions were governed by the principle of merit-cum-seniority under Indian Contract Act and stated that the DPC had evaluated the relative merit of all officers within the zone of consideration based on benchmark gradings. The court called for the original DPC minutes, the appraisal dossiers, and examined the criteria applied during selection. The court found that uncommunicated below-benchmark remarks in the petitioner's appraisal reports had been taken into consideration by the DPC in violation of the law laid down in Dev Dutt v Union of India. The court held that consideration of uncommunicated adverse remarks vitiates the promotion process, and therefore the petition is allowed directing a review DPC.

title: Meera Srivastava v. Nitin Gupta
text_content: The petitioner promotee officers Meera Srivastava filed a service writ petition before the Delhi High Court in the year 2020 challenging the final seniority list promulgated by the respondent department Nitin Gupta in Lucknow. The petitioners contended that they were substantively promoted to the cadre of Assistant Commissioners against regular promotional quota vacancies and had continuously officiated for over seven years before the direct recruits were recruited. The impugned seniority list placed newly appointed direct recruit respondents above the petitioners by assigning them notional seniority from the year of vacancy under a flawed application of the quota-rota rule under Negotiable Instruments Act. The direct recruits argued that recruitment rules mandated a fifty-fifty quota between direct recruitment and promotion, and contended that vacancies must be filled rota-wise. The court examined the breakdown of the quota-rota rule over several years due to inordinate delays in conducting direct recruitment examinations. The court reiterated the settled legal principle that when the quota-rota rule breaks down, continuous officiation in substantive capacity must determine inter-se seniority. The court held that the promotees are entitled to seniority from the date of continuous substantive officiation, and therefore the seniority list is quashed and petition is allowed.

title: Meera Khanna v. Ravi Chopra
text_content: The petitioner workman Meera Khanna approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2020 seeking enforcement of an industrial award directing reinstatement passed against the public sector corporation Ravi Chopra in Ahmedabad. The petitioner submitted that despite the award attaining finality following the dismissal of the employer's special leave petition, the management refused to permit him to rejoin duties or disburse wages under Section 17-B of Code of Criminal Procedure. The corporation pleaded corporate restructuring and abolition of the operational cadre, offering to pay a lumpsum ex-gratia amount of Rs 253000 in lieu of job. The court observed that public sector undertakings cannot defy binding awards of competent industrial adjudicators under the pretext of restructuring. The court reiterated that an award for reinstatement must be implemented in letter and spirit unless modified by a superior court. The court held that the respondent corporation is bound to reinstate the petitioner forthwith, and therefore the contempt and writ petition is allowed.

title: Sunita Kumar v. Pooja Dwivedi
text_content: The petitioner nominee Sunita Kumar approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2020 seeking disbursement of death-cum-retirement gratuity of Rs 1999000 due upon the demise of her husband who served as a permanent technician with Pooja Dwivedi in Coimbatore. The employer resisted payment, alleging that the deceased employee had not completed five years of continuous service as required by Section 4(1) of Indian Contract Act and sought to adjust alleged overpayment of salary advances against the terminal gratuity. The court referred to the first proviso to Section 4(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act which explicitly waives the requirement of five years continuous service in cases where employment terminates due to death or disablement of the employee. The court further noted that Section 13 grants absolute immunity to gratuity from attachment in execution of any decree or order of any civil, revenue, or criminal court. The court held that the nominee is entitled to immediate payment of full gratuity without deductions, and therefore the petition is allowed with interest.

title: Deepak Patel v. Naresh Kumar
text_content: In this tax appeal, the revenue department Naresh Kumar challenged the decision of the ITAT at Chennai in the year 2020 deleting a TDS default demand raised against employer corporation Deepak Patel. The department had demanded tax and interest of Rs 247000 for alleged failure to deduct TDS under Section 192 on perquisites provided to executive employees by way of interest-free housing loans and stock options. Learned counsel for the assessee corporation demonstrated that the recipient employees had already declared the full value of the benefits in their individual income tax returns and had paid due income taxes thereon. The Delhi High Court examined the first proviso to Section 201(1) of Consumer Protection Act which incorporates the principle laid down in Hindustan Coca-Cola. The court noted that where the payee has furnished return of income, accounted for the payment, and discharged taxes, the payer cannot be treated as an assessee-in-default. The court therefore held that the revenue cannot recover the tax a second time from the deductor, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Rekha Bhatia v. Sunita Joshi
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the elected legislator Sunita Joshi challenged the judgment of the High Court at Lucknow in the year 2020 which declared his election to Parliament void under Section 100 of the Representation of the People Act upon an election petition filed by rival candidate Rekha Bhatia. The High Court had found that the elected member had failed to disclose multiple pending criminal charges and substantial commercial assets of Rs 79000 in his affidavit. The appellant contended that the omissions were unintentional inadvertent oversights that did not materially affect the result of the election under Code of Criminal Procedure. The Delhi High Court examined the landmark ruling in Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms regarding voters' fundamental right to know under Article 19(1)(a). The court observed that non-disclosure of criminal antecedents and assets taints the purity of the electoral process and constitutes a corrupt practice. The court therefore held that the election was rightly set aside, and accordingly the appeal of the disqualified member is dismissed.

title: Rohit Malhotra v. Deepak Gupta
text_content: This application under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act was filed by Rohit Malhotra through counsel before the Delhi High Court in 2021. The applicant had been arrested at Hyderabad following an alleged seizure of narcotic contraband valued at Rs 503000 in the illicit market. The respondent State represented by Deepak Gupta opposed the grant of regular bail, highlighting that the quantity recovered fell within the commercial bracket. The applicant contended that no contraband was recovered from his conscious possession and submitted that his name surfaced solely on the basis of an inadmissible confessional disclosure made by a co-accused while in police custody. The court examined the constitutional guarantee of speedy trial under Article 21 vis-a-vis the legislative restrictions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act. The court noted that the prosecution had not produced any independent corroborative evidence connecting the applicant with the alleged drug syndicate. The court therefore held that reasonable grounds exist for believing that the accused is not guilty, and consequently bail is granted subject to stringent conditions.

title: Mukesh Agarwal v. Nirmala Gupta
text_content: The plaintiff wife Mukesh Agarwal instituted a civil suit for declaration of title, partition, and separate possession in respect of the matrimonial residence against her estranged husband Nirmala Gupta before the civil court at Patna in the year 2021. The plaintiff stated that the luxury residential property valued at Rs 1498000 was purchased during the subsistence of the marriage, and although the registered title deed stood exclusively in the husband's name, she had contributed fifty percent of the initial down payment from her stridhan and savings, while also managing the domestic household for two decades. The defendant husband resisted the suit, claiming that he had financed the entire purchase through personal commercial borrowings and argued that under the Benami Transactions Prohibition Act as amended, the wife could not assert any equitable or beneficial title against the recorded owner. The Delhi High Court examined the banking transactions, the source of funds for down payment, and emerging jurisprudence recognizing homemakers' economic contributions. The court held that the plaintiff has established direct financial contribution and beneficial ownership, and therefore the suit is decreed granting a half share.

title: Rohit Chaturvedi v. Ravi Rastogi
text_content: The petitioner company Rohit Chaturvedi approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2021 challenging an order passed by the Chief Commissioner of Income Tax Ravi Rastogi in Mumbai rejecting its statutory application for waiver of interest under Section 234A, 234B, and 234C of Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The petitioner had suffered extensive flood damage destroying manufacturing operations and had applied for waiver of interest amounting to Rs 98000 under the benevolent notification issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes empowering Commissioners to grant relief in cases of natural disasters. The Commissioner had rejected the application mechanically, stating that interest is statutory and non-discretionary. The court examined the CBDT circulars issued under Section 119(2)(a) and evaluated the financial hardship and destruction caused by the natural disaster. The court observed that statutory authorities must exercise benevolent powers with empathy and sound discretion rather than arbitrary administrative apathy. The court held that the rejection of waiver is arbitrary and perverse, and therefore the petition is allowed remitting the matter for waiver of interest.

title: Amit Tiwari v. Rohit Chaturvedi
text_content: The petitioner registered taxpayer Amit Tiwari filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court in the year 2021 challenging an order passed by the respondent GST revenue authority Rohit Chaturvedi in Indore disallowing Input Tax Credit amounting to Rs 301000. The department had blocked the petitioner's electronic credit ledger and issued a demand notice with interest and penalties on the ground that the input tax credit availed by the petitioner in return Form GSTR-3B did not match the auto-populated details reflected in Form GSTR-2A, alleging that the selling suppliers had failed to remit the collected tax to the government exchequer. The petitioner demonstrated that he had purchased goods under genuine tax invoices, paid the entire value along with applicable GST through banking channels, and possessed valid e-way bills establishing actual receipt of physical goods. The court examined Section 16(2) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act and reviewed precedents including Bharti Airtel and Arise India. The court observed that a bona fide purchasing dealer who has satisfied all conditions cannot be penalized for subsequent tax remittance defaults of registered suppliers. The court held that the denial of Input Tax Credit is legally unsustainable, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and the demand order is quashed.

title: Dinesh Sharma v. Anil Saxena
text_content: The petitioner corporate enterprise Dinesh Sharma filed an income tax appeal before the Delhi High Court in the year 2021 assailing an order passed by the Assessing Officer (TDS) Anil Saxena in Kolkata under Section 201(1) and Section 201(1A) of the Income Tax Act. The assessing officer had treated the company as an assessee-in-default for alleged short-deduction of tax at source amounting to Rs 72000, holding that payments made to software developers and cloud hosting platforms were fees for technical services attracting ten percent TDS under Section 194J rather than contractual work payments attracting two percent TDS under Section 194C of Hindu Marriage Act. The petitioner contended that standard cloud hosting and automated data bandwidth services do not involve human intellectual intervention and therefore cannot be categorized as managerial or technical services under the statute. The court examined the scope of technical services under Section 194J and reviewed the authoritative Supreme Court rulings in Kotak Securities and Engineering Analysis. The court observed that automated standard computing facilities without customized human technical expertise do not constitute technical services. The court held that the payments fall appropriately under Section 194C, and therefore the demand order under Section 201 is quashed and the appeal is allowed.

title: Manju Chopra v. Pushpa Dwivedi
text_content: In this first appeal, the appellant vendor Pushpa Dwivedi assailed the decree of specific performance granted to purchaser Manju Chopra by the civil court in Patna in the year 2022. The agreement to sell pertained to agricultural land situated in the outskirts of Patna with consideration amounting to Rs 196000. The appellant argued that the contract had become frustrated and unenforceable due to subsequent notification of the land for industrial development and contended that escalating market valuations rendered the grant of specific performance inequitable under Section 20 of Transfer of Property Act. Learned counsel for the respondent purchaser submitted that the purchaser had deposited the entire balance consideration in court and insisted that subsequent price inflation cannot be a ground to deny specific relief. The Delhi High Court balanced equitable principles with contractual sanctity and reviewed the conduct of the vendor who delayed obtaining requisite revenue clearances. The court observed that a defaulting vendor cannot be permitted to take advantage of his own default and market appreciation during litigation. The court therefore held that the trial court rightly exercised judicial discretion, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Anita Singh v. Usha Dwivedi
text_content: The plaintiff partner Anita Singh instituted a civil commercial suit against the managing partners Usha Dwivedi before the Commercial Court at Pune in the year 2022 seeking formal dissolution of the registered partnership firm, rendition of accounts, and distribution of surplus partnership assets. The plaintiff stated that the firm had operated an established industrial manufacturing enterprise with annual commercial turnover exceeding Rs 45000, but the managing partners had systematically excluded the plaintiff from management, refused access to daily books of accounts, diverted lucrative business contracts to their privately owned proprietary firms, and misappropriated partnership revenues. The defendant partners resisted dissolution, asserting that the partnership was a partnership at will under Income Tax Act wherein the plaintiff had retired voluntarily, and claimed that the firm's assets were heavily burdened with commercial debts leaving no distributable surplus. The Delhi High Court examined the partnership deed, audited balance sheets, forensic bank statements, and the provisions of Sections 44 and 48 of the Indian Partnership Act. The court observed that mutual confidence and good faith form the foundation of partnership, and systemic diversion of firm assets creates complete deadlock. The court held that it is just and equitable to dissolve the partnership firm, and therefore a preliminary decree for dissolution and accounting is passed.

title: Nirmala Singh v. Sachin Singh
text_content: The State prosecuted the accused appellant Nirmala Singh for committing the offence of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code arising out of an incident that occurred at Surat in the year 2022. The prosecution alleged that due to longstanding animosity over partition of ancestral land, the accused assaulted the deceased with a lethal sharp-edged weapon, intentionally inflicting fatal injuries. The prosecution examined eyewitnesses including Sachin Singh, whose testimony was corroborated by the post-mortem report confirming that the cranial injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The defence contended that the incident occurred during a sudden fight without premeditation, argued that the witnesses were interested family members, and pleaded that the offence at most attracted Exception 4 of Section 300 punishable under Section 304 Part I of Transfer of Property Act. The Delhi High Court meticulously analysed the medical evidence, the nature of weapon employed, and the multiplicity of brutal blows directed at vital body parts. The court noted that the repeated infliction of forceful blows on the head ruled out any plea of sudden fight or absence of intention to kill. The court held that the prosecution has established the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore the conviction is confirmed and the appeal is dismissed.

title: Sanjay Joshi v. Pushpa Dwivedi
text_content: In this criminal revision petition, the husband Pushpa Dwivedi assailed the order passed under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the Family Court at Agra in the year 2022, which directed payment of monthly maintenance of Rs 298000 to his estranged wife Sanjay Joshi. The revisionist argued that the maintenance quantum was arbitrary, unsupported by documentary proof of his actual business revenues, and exceeded his paying capacity. Learned counsel for the respondent wife submitted that the husband had deliberately suppressed substantial rental incomes from commercial properties and pointed out that the maintenance amount was barely adequate to meet escalating rental and medical expenses in Agra. The Delhi High Court examined the tax returns, balance sheets of the husband's proprietary enterprise, and lifestyle expenditures disclosed during cross-examination. The court noted that maintenance should not be excessive but must guarantee that the dependent spouse lives with dignity rather than mere subsistence. The court held that the quantum determined by the trial magistrate was fair, equitable, and proportional, and therefore the revision petition is dismissed.

title: Mukesh Agarwal v. Dinesh Tripathi
text_content: The revisionist Mukesh Agarwal approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2022 assailing the conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act recorded by the appellate court in Vadodara. The complainant payee Dinesh Tripathi alleged that the accused had borrowed a friendly financial accommodation of Rs 300000 and issued a cheque towards the discharge of the said legally enforceable debt. The cheque on presentation was dishonoured and returned by the banker due to account closed by drawer. The statutory notice of demand was dispatched by registered post with acknowledgement due and was returned with postal endorsement of refusal. The drawer contended that he had lost the signed blank cheque and claimed that the statutory notice was never tendered to him. The court referred to settled judicial precedents holding that endorsement of refusal constitutes valid tender and deemed service under the General Clauses Act. The court observed that no police complaint was ever lodged regarding the alleged loss of the negotiable instrument. The court held that the accused drawer is guilty of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and therefore the petition is dismissed.

title: Pankaj Mishra v. Vikas Sharma
text_content: The revisionist Pankaj Mishra approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2022 assailing the conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act recorded by the appellate court in Pune. The complainant payee Vikas Sharma alleged that the accused had borrowed a friendly financial accommodation of Rs 1498000 and issued a cheque towards the discharge of the said legally enforceable debt. The cheque on presentation was dishonoured and returned by the banker due to account closed by drawer. The statutory notice of demand was dispatched by registered post with acknowledgement due and was returned with postal endorsement of refusal. The drawer contended that he had lost the signed blank cheque and claimed that the statutory notice was never tendered to him. The court referred to settled judicial precedents holding that endorsement of refusal constitutes valid tender and deemed service under the General Clauses Act. The court observed that no police complaint was ever lodged regarding the alleged loss of the negotiable instrument. The court held that the accused drawer is guilty of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and therefore the petition is dismissed.

title: Usha Dwivedi v. Sunita Chopra
text_content: This anticipatory bail application under Section 438 of CrPC was moved by Usha Dwivedi before the Delhi High Court in the year 2022 in relation to an FIR registered at Kanpur alleging economic offences under Sections 420 and 409 involving misappropriation of public funds amounting to Rs 504000. The State represented by Sunita Chopra contended that the applicant was the principal custodian of the government welfare treasury and had orchestrated fictitious payments to non-existent beneficiaries. The applicant asserted that he was merely a subordinate officer who signed disbursement vouchers on instructions of superior administrative authorities and volunteered to surrender his passport and join the probe daily. The court examined the special audit reports, the transaction logs, and the statements of treasury officials implicating the applicant directly. The court observed that economic offences involving large-scale siphoning of public money require thorough custodial examination and unhindered investigation. The court therefore held that the grant of anticipatory bail in such grave economic offences would prejudice investigation, and accordingly the application is dismissed.

title: Suresh Kapoor v. Vijay Khanna
text_content: The petitioner Suresh Kapoor challenged the revised promotion policy notified by Vijay Khanna public financial institution in Pune in the year 2022. The petitioner alleged that the new policy introduced subjective interview marks of forty percent for promotion to senior management cadre, which drastically altered the rules of the game midway through the recruitment cycle and facilitated nepotistic selections. The financial institution justified the policy, submitting that leadership positions in modern banking require high interpersonal and analytical skills best tested in interviews. The court examined the service regulations under Consumer Protection Act and reviewed precedents concerning excessive allocation of interview marks in public employment promotions. The court found that allocating disproportionate weight to viva voce in promotion from within an existing workforce creates room for arbitrary favoritism. The court held that the excessive interview weighting is arbitrary and violative of Article 14, and therefore the petition is allowed and promotion criteria are modified.

title: Rohit Malhotra v. Deepak Singh
text_content: The petitioner workman Rohit Malhotra instituted proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act before the Industrial Tribunal at Chennai in the year 2022 challenging his abrupt retrenchment by the employer Deepak Singh. The workman averred that he had completed more than 240 days of continuous service in the preceding twelve calendar months, but the management terminated his services without serving any statutory one month notice in writing, without assigning reasons, and without tendering retrenchment compensation computed at fifteen days average pay for each completed year of service as mandated by Section 25-F of Consumer Protection Act. The management contended that the workman was engaged purely as a casual project employee on contractual basis for a specific infrastructure scheme and argued that cessation of employment upon project completion did not constitute retrenchment by virtue of Section 2(oo)(bb). The Delhi High Court scrutinized the attendance registers, wage payment vouchers, and the continuous nature of work performed across multiple corporate projects. The court found that the artificial breaks in service were deliberate subterfuges to evade the statutory protections of Section 25-F. The court held that the termination amounts to illegal retrenchment void ab initio, and therefore reinstatement with full back wages is ordered.

title: Sachin Tripathi v. Kamla Srivastava
text_content: The petitioner charitable trust Sachin Tripathi approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2022 challenging the cancellation of its registration under Section 12AA and denial of deduction under Section 80G by the Commissioner of Income Tax Kamla Srivastava in Chennai. The department alleged that the trust had accumulated surplus revenues of Rs 1500000 from hospital pharmacy operations, which allegedly constituted commercial activity violating the proviso to Section 2(15) of Consumer Protection Act. The petitioner established that the nominal pharmacy margins were deployed exclusively to subsidize medical treatment and free beds for indigent patients. The court examined the statutory definition of charitable purpose and the Supreme Court ruling in Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority. The court observed that incidental commercial receipts that directly subserve the primary charitable object of medical relief do not taint charitable status. The court held that the cancellation of charitable registration is unlawful, and therefore the petition is allowed and the registration is restored.

title: Naresh Mishra v. Kamla Chaturvedi
text_content: In this tax appeal, the revenue department Kamla Chaturvedi challenged the order of the High Court at Surat in the year 2022 which deleted a penalty of Rs 996000 imposed under Section 271D of the Income Tax Act against partnership firm Naresh Mishra. The penalty was levied for accepting cash loans exceeding twenty thousand rupees in alleged contravention of Section 269SS of Indian Penal Code. Learned counsel for the partnership firm submitted that under Section 273B, no penalty can be imposed if the assessee proves reasonable cause for the failure, and established that the cash was accepted on a bank holiday to meet emergency hospitalisation expenses of an injured factory worker. The Delhi High Court examined the medical discharge bills, the contemporaneous cash ledger entries, and the legislative purpose of Section 269SS. The court found that the emergency medical exigency constituted genuine and bona fide reasonable cause within the statutory framework of Section 273B. The court therefore held that penalty under Section 271D cannot be sustained in the presence of reasonable cause, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Mahesh Shah v. Naresh Verma
text_content: The petitioner journalist Mahesh Shah filed a writ petition under Article 226 before the Delhi High Court in the year 2022 challenging an order of preventive detention passed against him by the district magistrate Naresh Verma in Bengaluru under the National Security Act. The detention order was grounded upon investigative articles published by the petitioner reporting on municipal corruption in medical supplies during a public health emergency. The State argued that the publications incited public disorder and justified detention under Arbitration and Conciliation Act to maintain public order. The court examined the grounds of detention, the constitutional safeguards under Article 22(5), and the fundamental right to free expression under Article 19(1)(a). The court observed that legitimate criticism of public administration cannot be conflated with a threat to public order or national security. The court held that the detention order is an impermissible muzzling of free press, and therefore the petition is allowed and the detenu is directed to be released.

title: Lata Malhotra v. Pankaj Tiwari
text_content: The plaintiff Lata Malhotra instituted a civil suit for permanent injunction against the defendant Pankaj Tiwari before the civil court at Surat in the year 2023. The plaintiff averred that he was the absolute owner and in lawful settled possession of the suit parcel of land by virtue of a registered conveyance deed executed under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant, who was an adjoining landholder possessing no lawful title or interest, had attempted to forcibly trespass into the property, damage the boundary wall, and dispossess the plaintiff without due process of law. The defendant filed a written statement asserting competing ownership over a common pathway and claimed customary easement rights over the disputed boundary strip. The Delhi High Court examined the chain of title deeds, revenue khasra entries, electricity meter connections, and the report of the local commissioner. The court applied the classical tests under the Specific Relief Act governing grant of perpetual injunction to protect settled peaceful possession against unlawful interference. The court observed that a person in peaceful settled possession is entitled to protect his holding even against lawful owners except through due process. The court held that the plaintiff has established lawful possession and threatened invasion, and therefore the suit for permanent injunction is decreed.

title: Suresh Kumar v. Mukesh Yadav
text_content: The plaintiff partner Suresh Kumar instituted a civil commercial suit against the managing partners Mukesh Yadav before the Commercial Court at Varanasi in the year 2023 seeking formal dissolution of the registered partnership firm, rendition of accounts, and distribution of surplus partnership assets. The plaintiff stated that the firm had operated an established industrial manufacturing enterprise with annual commercial turnover exceeding Rs 48000, but the managing partners had systematically excluded the plaintiff from management, refused access to daily books of accounts, diverted lucrative business contracts to their privately owned proprietary firms, and misappropriated partnership revenues. The defendant partners resisted dissolution, asserting that the partnership was a partnership at will under Industrial Disputes Act wherein the plaintiff had retired voluntarily, and claimed that the firm's assets were heavily burdened with commercial debts leaving no distributable surplus. The Delhi High Court examined the partnership deed, audited balance sheets, forensic bank statements, and the provisions of Sections 44 and 48 of the Indian Partnership Act. The court observed that mutual confidence and good faith form the foundation of partnership, and systemic diversion of firm assets creates complete deadlock. The court held that it is just and equitable to dissolve the partnership firm, and therefore a preliminary decree for dissolution and accounting is passed.

title: Pooja Mishra v. Mahesh Malhotra
text_content: The plaintiff partner Pooja Mishra filed a commercial suit against former partner Mahesh Malhotra in Surat in the year 2023 seeking a permanent injunction restraining the defendant from carrying on a competing business using the firm's confidential client database and trade name. The plaintiff proved that upon mutual dissolution of the partnership, the defendant had received substantial monetary compensation of Rs 504000 and had executed a restrictive negative covenant undertaking not to solicit the firm's existing clients for three years within the municipal territory of Surat. The defendant contended that the covenant was void as an unlawful restraint of trade under Section 27 of Code of Criminal Procedure. The court examined the statutory exception to Section 27 of the Contract Act and Section 36(2) of the Indian Partnership Act which expressly validates reasonable agreements in restraint of trade upon dissolution or sale of goodwill. The court observed that a reasonable geographic and temporal restriction protecting partnership goodwill is legally enforceable. The court held that the negative covenant is valid and binding, and therefore a permanent injunction is granted restraining client solicitation.

title: Mukesh Chopra v. Meera Mehta
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant wife Meera Mehta assailed the decree of divorce granted in favour of husband Mukesh Chopra by the Family Court in Kanpur in the year 2023 on the ground of cruelty under the Hindu Marriage Act. The appellant argued that ordinary wear and tear of married life had been exaggerated into mental cruelty by the trial court, and submitted that reconciliation was still possible in the interest of the minor child. Learned counsel for the respondent husband submitted that the parties had been living separately for more than eight years and pointed out that multiple rounds of court-annexed mediation had completely failed to bridge the profound marital discord. The Delhi High Court examined the judicial guidelines regarding mental cruelty and reviewed the irreversible estrangement between the spouses under Hindu Marriage Act. The court observed that compelling parties to remain legally bound in a dead marriage where emotional bonds have perished causes perpetual agony to both. The court therefore held that the Family Court was fully justified in granting dissolution of marriage, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Pooja Tiwari v. Prakash Patel
text_content: The petitioner citizen Pooja Tiwari approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2023 invoking Article 226 of the Constitution of India to challenge a summary demolition order issued by the municipal development authority Prakash Patel in Ahmedabad. The authority had arrived with bulldozers and demolished the petitioner's residential premises and commercial shop without serving any prior statutory show-cause notice, without affording an opportunity of hearing, and without allowing time to seek judicial redress, alleging that the structure was an illegal encroachment on public land. The petitioner proved registered ownership deeds, continuous property tax receipts dating back thirty years, and asserted gross violation of Article 21. The municipal authority contended that encroachments on public pathways could be removed summarily without prior notice under Hindu Marriage Act. The court examined the constitutional jurisprudence on shelter as an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21 and the necessity of procedural fairness. The court observed that executive bulldozing of homes without notice and hearing is completely antithetical to the rule of law and constitutional governance. The court held that the demolition was unlawful and unconstitutional, and therefore directed restitution, interim compensation of Rs 2001000, and allowed the petition.

title: Amit Sharma v. Rekha Sharma
text_content: In this infrastructure writ appeal, the municipal corporation Rekha Sharma challenged the judgment of the High Court at Lucknow in the year 2023 which directed the municipal body to provide potable piped drinking water to unregularized resettlement colonies following a PIL filed by community activist Amit Sharma. The municipal body argued that municipal bylaws restricted water supply infrastructure to authorized planned layouts and contended that laying pipelines would cost Rs 153000 which was commercially unviable under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. Learned counsel for the residents demonstrated that families were compelled to consume contaminated borewell water resulting in widespread waterborne epidemics among children. The Delhi High Court examined the international covenant on economic and social rights and the extensive domestic jurisprudence recognizing the right to safe drinking water under Article 21. The court observed that access to clean drinking water is a basic human right that cannot be conditioned upon property regularisation or layout legality. The court therefore held that the municipal corporation is constitutionally bound to supply potable water, and accordingly the municipal appeal is dismissed.

title: Meera Mishra v. Manju Kumar
text_content: The petitioner minority community institution Meera Mishra approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2023 challenging an order passed by the state charity commissioner Manju Kumar in Coimbatore appointing a non-minority administrative receiver over historic religious endowments and community properties valued at Rs 299000. The state authority alleged administrative mismanagement of community funds and sought to reform the trust board under general public trust laws. The petitioner contended that Article 26 of the Constitution guarantees religious denominations the fundamental right to manage their own affairs in matters of religion. The court examined the scope of Article 26(b) and the line between secular management and ecclesiastical autonomy under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The court observed that while secular finances can be audited, the state cannot supplant traditional community management with bureaucratic receivers. The court held that the appointment of an external receiver violates Article 26, and therefore the petition is allowed and the appointment is set aside.

title: Ravi Gupta v. Rohit Chopra
text_content: The plaintiff Ravi Gupta instituted a comprehensive suit for partition and separate possession of ancestral joint family properties against the defendant coparceners Rohit Chopra before the civil court at Kanpur in the year 2024. The suit properties comprised agricultural holdings, residential premises, and commercial shops valued at over Rs 5001000. The plaintiff claimed a one-fourth undivided share in all properties, asserting that the joint family had continued undivided and that no formal severance of status had taken place. The defendants resisted partition, contending that a prior oral family settlement had taken place three decades ago followed by separate revenue entries, and argued that certain prime commercial shops were their self-acquired properties funded through independent business revenues rather than HUF nucleus. The Delhi High Court scrutinized the ancestral title deeds, mutation records, income tax returns of the Hindu Undivided Family, and oral evidence. The court noted that when ancestral nucleus is established, the burden shifts heavily onto the coparcener asserting self-acquisition to prove independent funds. The court held that the defendants failed to establish prior oral partition or independent acquisition, and therefore a preliminary decree for partition is granted.

title: Manju Chopra v. Dinesh Agarwal
text_content: The petitioner infrastructure company Manju Chopra filed a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the Delhi High Court in the year 2024 challenging an arbitral award passed in Varanasi in a dispute involving Dinesh Agarwal. The arbitral tribunal had awarded claims of Rs 996000 in favour of the respondent, rejecting the petitioner's counterclaims for liquidated damages. The petitioner contended that the award suffered from patent illegality, argued that the tribunal had rewritten contractual price escalation formulas, and asserted conflict with the public policy of India. The respondent defended the award, submitting that judicial review under Section 34 is strictly circumscribed and does not permit re-appreciation of evidence under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court examined the principles formulated by the Supreme Court in Associate Builders and Ssangyong Engineering. The court observed that an arbitral tribunal is the ultimate master of factual evidence and contractual interpretation unless its construction is totally perverse. The court held that the arbitral award does not suffer from any patent illegality or public policy violation, and therefore the Section 34 petition is dismissed.

title: Nitin Chopra v. Vikas Dwivedi
text_content: The parties Nitin Chopra and Vikas Dwivedi jointly approached the Delhi High Court in the year 2024 seeking dissolution of their marriage by mutual consent under Section 13-B of the Hindu Marriage Act in Indore. The parties had executed a comprehensive memorandum of understanding resolving all disputes regarding permanent alimony of Rs 5000000, custody of the minor child, and return of stridhan articles. The parties filed an application praying for waiver of the statutory six months cooling-off period prescribed under Section 13-B(2), citing the Supreme Court judgment in Amardeep Singh v Harveen Kaur. The court examined whether all efforts at conciliation had failed, verified that the parties had lived separately for over eighteen months, and confirmed that the settlement terms were fair and executed without coercion. The court observed that the cooling-off period is directory and can be waived where continuance of the legal tie prolongs human suffering. The court held that all statutory criteria for mutual consent divorce are satisfied, and therefore the cooling-off period is waived and marriage is dissolved.

title: Vikas Chaturvedi v. Vikas Verma
text_content: The complainant Vikas Chaturvedi filed a complaint against Vikas Verma diagnostic pathology center in Kanpur in the year 2015 claiming damages of Rs 76000 for issuing an erroneous and false negative biopsy report regarding a malignant tumor. The complainant alleged that the inaccurate diagnostic report delayed vital oncological chemotherapy by fourteen months, allowing the cancer to metastasize into advanced Stage IV. The diagnostic center pleaded human error in slide preparation and claimed limitation of liability under the disclaimer printed on the report. The court examined the revised histopathology findings from two independent oncology institutes confirming obvious presence of malignant cells in the original slides. The court observed that diagnostic laboratories hold patients' lives in their hands and cannot escape liability for gross diagnostic blunders through preprinted disclaimers. The court held that the diagnostic center is guilty of egregious medical negligence, and therefore the complaint is allowed with compensatory damages.

title: Lata Mishra v. Vimla Yadav
text_content: In this consumer appeal, the appellant real estate developer Vimla Yadav challenged the order of the State Commission at Surat in the year 2015 directing delayed possession compensation to homebuyer Lata Mishra. The developer argued that the buyer had agreed to contractual compensation of five rupees per square foot per month under the standard allotment agreement, and contended that the consumer court had no jurisdiction to award higher statutory interest rates. Learned counsel for the homebuyer submitted that standard pre-printed builder contracts are one-sided adhesion contracts wherein the developer charges eighteen percent for payment defaults while providing nominal pennies for years of delivery delay. The Delhi SCDRC examined the doctrine of unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act and reviewed Supreme Court precedents on unconscionable contractual clauses. The court observed that one-sided penalty clauses in builder agreements constitute unfair trade practices and are not binding on consumer adjudicators. The court therefore held that the allottee is entitled to reasonable interest for prolonged delay, and accordingly the builder's appeal is dismissed.

title: Amit Malhotra v. Vijay Pandey
text_content: The complainant Amit Malhotra approached the Delhi SCDRC in the year 2018 claiming product liability compensation against Vijay Pandey pharmaceutical manufacturer in Bhopal. The complainant established that a batch of contaminated intravenous fluids manufactured by the respondent and administered during surgery caused severe endotoxic shock, organ impairment, and medical rehabilitation expenses of Rs 301000. The drug manufacturer contended that the contamination was caused by improper storage conditions at the local retail chemist and denied manufacturing culpability. The court examined the government drug testing laboratory report which confirmed bacterial endotoxin contamination in unopened ampoules from the identical manufacturing batch. The court applied the strict product liability framework codified under Negotiable Instruments Act holding manufacturers liable for defective and harmful goods. The court held that the pharmaceutical manufacturer is strictly liable for marketing defective medicinal goods, and therefore the complaint is allowed with damages.

title: Lata Agarwal v. Anil Rastogi
text_content: The complainant Lata Agarwal approached the Delhi SCDRC in the year 2020 alleging unfair trade practice and deficiency in service against Anil Rastogi bank for failing to return original title deeds of residential property mortgaged for a housing loan in Kanpur. The complainant established that he had fully repaid the entire housing loan along with interest amounting to Rs 1002000 and obtained a formal no-dues certificate, yet the bank failed to return the original registered sale deeds, subsequently admitting that the documents were misplaced from the central repository. The bank offered token compensation of five thousand rupees and suggested obtaining certified copies from the sub-registrar office at bank expense. The court observed that loss of original title deeds permanently impairs the marketability and resale value of real estate and causes extreme mental agony. The court held that losing property documents is gross negligence and deficiency in service, and therefore awarded substantial compensation and allowed the complaint.

title: Geeta Srivastava v. Sunita Gupta
text_content: The complainant Geeta Srivastava approached the Delhi SCDRC in the year 2024 claiming product liability compensation against Sunita Gupta pharmaceutical manufacturer in Surat. The complainant established that a batch of contaminated intravenous fluids manufactured by the respondent and administered during surgery caused severe endotoxic shock, organ impairment, and medical rehabilitation expenses of Rs 305000. The drug manufacturer contended that the contamination was caused by improper storage conditions at the local retail chemist and denied manufacturing culpability. The court examined the government drug testing laboratory report which confirmed bacterial endotoxin contamination in unopened ampoules from the identical manufacturing batch. The court applied the strict product liability framework codified under Income Tax Act holding manufacturers liable for defective and harmful goods. The court held that the pharmaceutical manufacturer is strictly liable for marketing defective medicinal goods, and therefore the complaint is allowed with damages.

title: Asha Dwivedi v. Sunita Mishra
text_content: The complainant association of apartment owners Asha Dwivedi filed a class-action consumer complaint against Sunita Mishra builder in Ahmedabad in the year 2024. The allottees alleged that the builder had illegally converted designated common green areas and community clubhouse spaces into commercial retail shops valued at Rs 197000 in brazen violation of the sanctioned master plan and brochures. The developer contended that the agreement empowered the promoter to carry out modifications and revisions in building plans until final completion. The court examined the original sanctioned layout, the RERA registration disclosures, and the statutory obligations of promoters under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court found that unilateral alterations of common amenities without two-thirds consent of allottees is completely prohibited by law. The court held that the developer must demolish commercial encroachments and restore common facilities, and therefore the complaint is allowed with punitive costs.

title: Suresh Mishra v. Mukesh Sharma
text_content: The plaintiff Suresh Mishra instituted a civil suit for permanent injunction against the defendant Mukesh Sharma before the civil court at Mumbai in the year 2016. The plaintiff averred that he was the absolute owner and in lawful settled possession of the suit parcel of land by virtue of a registered conveyance deed executed under Income Tax Act. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant, who was an adjoining landholder possessing no lawful title or interest, had attempted to forcibly trespass into the property, damage the boundary wall, and dispossess the plaintiff without due process of law. The defendant filed a written statement asserting competing ownership over a common pathway and claimed customary easement rights over the disputed boundary strip. The Gujarat High Court examined the chain of title deeds, revenue khasra entries, electricity meter connections, and the report of the local commissioner. The court applied the classical tests under the Specific Relief Act governing grant of perpetual injunction to protect settled peaceful possession against unlawful interference. The court observed that a person in peaceful settled possession is entitled to protect his holding even against lawful owners except through due process. The court held that the plaintiff has established lawful possession and threatened invasion, and therefore the suit for permanent injunction is decreed.

title: Anil Malhotra v. Sachin Chopra
text_content: In this civil appeal, the appellant Sachin Chopra challenged the decree of permanent injunction granted by the trial court in Varanasi in the year 2016 restraining the appellant from constructing on a disputed vacant plot measuring five hundred square yards. The respondent plaintiff Anil Malhotra had established continuous possession and produced municipal sanction plans for development. The appellant contended that the trial court erred in granting permanent injunction without requiring the plaintiff to seek a declaration of title, pointing out that a genuine cloud was cast over the plaintiff's ownership by an rival agreement to sell. The Gujarat High Court examined the law laid down in Anathula Sudhakar v P. Buchi Reddy regarding suits for injunction simpliciter versus suits requiring declaratory relief. The court found that the defendant had merely raised bare denials without producing any registered document of title capable of casting a real cloud. The court therefore held that the suit for permanent injunction simpliciter is fully maintainable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the injunction is upheld.

title: Pankaj Agarwal v. Manju Sharma
text_content: The plaintiff Pankaj Agarwal filed a commercial suit for permanent injunction against Manju Sharma before the Gujarat High Court in the year 2016 seeking to restrain the defendant from infringing registered trademarks and passing off goods using deceptively similar brand packaging in Hyderabad. The plaintiff proved long-standing commercial use and substantial advertising expenditure of Rs 204000 establishing immense consumer goodwill in the market. The defendant contended that the disputed mark was generic and descriptive, claiming prior user in a localized rural market prior to the plaintiff's registration. The court evaluated the phonetic, visual, and conceptual similarity between the rival trademarks under Consumer Protection Act and assessed the likelihood of public confusion. The court observed that registration confers an exclusive statutory monopoly and noted that the defendant's packaging was a deceptive imitation designed to mislead consumers. The court held that the defendant is guilty of trademark infringement and passing off, and therefore a permanent injunction is granted with compensatory damages.

title: Priya Kapoor v. Kamla Patel
text_content: The plaintiff landlord Priya Kapoor instituted an eviction suit against the tenant defendant Kamla Patel under the provisions of the relevant Rent Control Act before the civil court at Hyderabad in the year 2016. The plaintiff pleaded that the tenanted commercial premises were let out on monthly tenancy and that the tenant had committed wilful default in payment of rent, accumulating substantial arrears of rent amounting to Rs 1501000 despite repeated demands. The landlord further established bona fide personal requirement, stating that he required the suit premises to establish an independent commercial consultancy for his unemployed son who possessed professional qualifications.
