The defendant tenant resisted eviction, claiming protection under Indian Penal Code, asserting that rent was regularly tendered by money order which the landlord maliciously refused to accept, and disputing the genuine nature of the landlord's bona fide requirement. The Gujarat High Court evaluated the oral testimonies, the rent counterfoils, postal refusal receipts, and municipal records. The court observed that the tenant failed to deposit the arrears of rent in court within the statutory cure period and noted that the landlord is the best judge of his commercial requirements. The court held that the tenant has committed wilful default and the landlord's requirement is bona fide, and therefore the eviction decree is confirmed.

title: Dinesh Sharma v. Asha Patel
text_content: The plaintiff Dinesh Sharma instituted a comprehensive suit for partition and separate possession of ancestral joint family properties against the defendant coparceners Asha Patel before the civil court at Indore in the year 2017. The suit properties comprised agricultural holdings, residential premises, and commercial shops valued at over Rs 502000. The plaintiff claimed a one-fourth undivided share in all properties, asserting that the joint family had continued undivided and that no formal severance of status had taken place. The defendants resisted partition, contending that a prior oral family settlement had taken place three decades ago followed by separate revenue entries, and argued that certain prime commercial shops were their self-acquired properties funded through independent business revenues rather than HUF nucleus. The Gujarat High Court scrutinized the ancestral title deeds, mutation records, income tax returns of the Hindu Undivided Family, and oral evidence. The court noted that when ancestral nucleus is established, the burden shifts heavily onto the coparcener asserting self-acquisition to prove independent funds. The court held that the defendants failed to establish prior oral partition or independent acquisition, and therefore a preliminary decree for partition is granted.

title: Lata Gupta v. Nitin Mishra
text_content: In this regular civil appeal, the appellant tenant Nitin Mishra challenged the decree of eviction passed in favour of landlord Lata Gupta by the appellate rent tribunal in Patna in the year 2018. The eviction proceedings were grounded upon unauthorised subletting of the demised premises and material impairment of property value under the Rent Control Act. The landlord established that the tenant had parted with exclusive possession of a substantial portion of the premises to a third party without obtaining prior written consent as mandated by Negotiable Instruments Act. The tenant argued that the third party was merely an employee and business associate assisting in daily operations and not an unauthorised subtenant. The Gujarat High Court examined the report of the local commissioner appointed to inspect the premises, the electricity bills, and the partnership agreement. The court found that exclusive commercial control over the subdivided portion was transferred to a stranger without landlord approval. The court therefore held that unlawful subletting stands conclusively established, and accordingly the tenant's appeal is dismissed.

title: Manju Rastogi v. Deepak Agarwal
text_content: The plaintiff financial institution Manju Rastogi instituted a mortgage suit for foreclosure and sale of hypothecated immovable property against the defendant mortgagor Deepak Agarwal before the civil court at Kolkata in the year 2018. The plaintiff stated that the defendant had borrowed a commercial term loan facility of Rs 1999000 and executed a registered simple mortgage deed over his prime commercial building to secure repayment with agreed interest. Upon persistent default in servicing quarterly interest instalments, the loan account was classified as non-performing and statutory recall notices were dispatched. The defendant contested the foreclosure suit, claiming that the penal interest rates charged by the mortgagee were usurious, asserting that the bank had failed to adjust insurance proceeds following a warehouse fire, and seeking extension of the equity of redemption under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The Gujarat High Court examined the loan sanction letter, registered mortgage deed, audited account statements, and the provisions of Order XXXIV of the Code of Civil Procedure. The court found that the mortgage debt remained unpaid despite valid demand and noted that interest was computed in conformity with contractual terms. The court held that the mortgagee is entitled to realize its debt through foreclosure, and therefore a preliminary decree for foreclosure and sale is passed.

title: Vimla Chopra v. Sushma Malhotra
text_content: The land reference arose out of an acquisition of agricultural holdings in Coimbatore undertaken by the State Government through Sushma Malhotra for an urban infrastructure corridor in the year 2019. The Land Acquisition Collector had awarded compensation at the rate of Rs 304000 per acre, which the claimant landowners Vimla Chopra rejected under protest as grossly inadequate compared to prevailing open-market commercial values. The claimants produced registered sale deeds of adjacent parcels executed shortly prior to the Section 4 notification, valuation reports of certified experts, and demonstrated that the acquired land enjoyed immediate potential for high-density residential and industrial development. The acquiring authority opposed enhancement, submitting that the sale instances relied upon pertained to small developed plots which could not serve as comparables for large tracts of undeveloped agricultural land, and demanded a forty percent deduction for developmental expenditure. The Gujarat High Court analyzed the comparable sale exemplars, the distance from arterial highways, and the development potential under Indian Contract Act. The court observed that fair market value must reflect potential value while allowing reasonable deductions for internal roads and amenities. The court held that the compensation awarded by the collector is insufficient and must be enhanced, and therefore the reference petition is allowed with statutory solatium.

title: Rohit Kapoor v. Sushma Saxena
text_content: The plaintiff Rohit Kapoor filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable residential property in Kanpur executed in the year 2019 against Sushma Saxena. In the alternative, the plaintiff claimed refund of earnest money with twenty-four percent interest and substantial damages. During trial, it emerged that the defendant vendor did not possess sole transferable title to the suit property, which was co-owned by his estranged siblings who were not signatories to the agreement to sell. The Gujarat High Court examined Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act governing specific performance of a part of contract and evaluated whether the purchaser was willing to accept the vendor's undivided fractional share without claiming abatement of price. The court found that the contract could not be specifically enforced in its entirety without infringing third-party rights of non-signatory co-owners. The court held that decreeing specific performance would be inequitable, and therefore the alternative relief of refund of earnest money with interest is granted.

title: Rekha Khanna v. Mahesh Bhatia
text_content: The petitioner corporate enterprise Rekha Khanna filed an income tax appeal before the ITAT Delhi in the year 2015 assailing an order passed by the Assessing Officer (TDS) Mahesh Bhatia in Bhopal under Section 201(1) and Section 201(1A) of the Income Tax Act. The assessing officer had treated the company as an assessee-in-default for alleged short-deduction of tax at source amounting to Rs 748000, holding that payments made to software developers and cloud hosting platforms were fees for technical services attracting ten percent TDS under Section 194J rather than contractual work payments attracting two percent TDS under Section 194C of Negotiable Instruments Act. The petitioner contended that standard cloud hosting and automated data bandwidth services do not involve human intellectual intervention and therefore cannot be categorized as managerial or technical services under the statute. The court examined the scope of technical services under Section 194J and reviewed the authoritative Supreme Court rulings in Kotak Securities and Engineering Analysis. The court observed that automated standard computing facilities without customized human technical expertise do not constitute technical services. The court held that the payments fall appropriately under Section 194C, and therefore the demand order under Section 201 is quashed and the appeal is allowed.

title: Anil Joshi v. Prakash Tiwari
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the Commissioner of Income Tax Prakash Tiwari challenged the order of the Tribunal at Jaipur in the year 2015 which allowed deduction under Section 80-IA of the Income Tax Act to infrastructure corporation Anil Joshi. The revenue argued that the assessee was merely a works contractor executing government road development tenders and not an infrastructure enterprise developing, maintaining, and operating an infrastructure facility within the statutory scheme. Learned counsel for the assessee demonstrated that the enterprise had assumed complete financial, technical, and operational risks under a Public-Private Partnership concession agreement, having invested Rs 78000 in constructing arterial bridges. The ITAT Delhi analyzed the concession terms, the statutory language of Section 80-IA, and the explanation inserted by Finance Act. The court found that the assessee was an infrastructure developer assuming entrepreneurial risk rather than a simple supply contractor. The court therefore held that the assessee is entitled to the ten-year tax holiday deduction, and accordingly the revenue's appeal is dismissed.

title: Pankaj Sharma v. Pooja Shah
text_content: The petitioner assessee Pankaj Sharma filed a writ petition before the ITAT Delhi in the year 2016 challenging the validity of a notice issued under Section 148 and the reassessment order passed under Section 147 of the Income Tax Act by the respondent Assessing Officer Pooja Shah in Bengaluru. The assessing officer had reopened the concluded regular assessment after four years, alleging that taxable income amounting to Rs 1001000 had escaped assessment on account of unexplained accommodation entries and share capital received at substantial premium. The petitioner demonstrated that during the original scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3), full disclosures regarding share capital, bank statements, and investor confirmations had been furnished and examined, rendering the reopening a mere impermissible change of opinion without new tangible material. The court scrutinized the reasons recorded for reopening, the audit objections, and the statutory requirements under Industrial Disputes Act. The court reiterated the settled legal position in Kelvinator of India that reassessment cannot be initiated on the basis of a mere change of opinion. The court held that the reopening is devoid of new tangible material and lacks jurisdiction, and therefore the petition is allowed and reassessment is quashed.

title: Sarla Bhatia v. Meera Verma
text_content: The petitioner registered taxpayer Sarla Bhatia filed a writ petition before the ITAT Delhi in the year 2017 challenging an order passed by the respondent GST revenue authority Meera Verma in Kolkata disallowing Input Tax Credit amounting to Rs 76000. The department had blocked the petitioner's electronic credit ledger and issued a demand notice with interest and penalties on the ground that the input tax credit availed by the petitioner in return Form GSTR-3B did not match the auto-populated details reflected in Form GSTR-2A, alleging that the selling suppliers had failed to remit the collected tax to the government exchequer. The petitioner demonstrated that he had purchased goods under genuine tax invoices, paid the entire value along with applicable GST through banking channels, and possessed valid e-way bills establishing actual receipt of physical goods. The court examined Section 16(2) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act and reviewed precedents including Bharti Airtel and Arise India. The court observed that a bona fide purchasing dealer who has satisfied all conditions cannot be penalized for subsequent tax remittance defaults of registered suppliers. The court held that the denial of Input Tax Credit is legally unsustainable, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and the demand order is quashed.

title: Rohit Patel v. Rohit Saxena
text_content: In this tax appeal, the revenue department Rohit Saxena challenged the decision of the ITAT at Bengaluru in the year 2017 deleting a TDS default demand raised against employer corporation Rohit Patel. The department had demanded tax and interest of Rs 96000 for alleged failure to deduct TDS under Section 192 on perquisites provided to executive employees by way of interest-free housing loans and stock options. Learned counsel for the assessee corporation demonstrated that the recipient employees had already declared the full value of the benefits in their individual income tax returns and had paid due income taxes thereon. The ITAT Delhi examined the first proviso to Section 201(1) of Consumer Protection Act which incorporates the principle laid down in Hindustan Coca-Cola. The court noted that where the payee has furnished return of income, accounted for the payment, and discharged taxes, the payer cannot be treated as an assessee-in-default. The court therefore held that the revenue cannot recover the tax a second time from the deductor, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Anita Pandey v. Sarla Chaturvedi
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the Commissioner of Income Tax Sarla Chaturvedi challenged the order of the Appellate Tribunal at Jaipur in the year 2017 which deleted an addition of Rs 501000 made under Section 68 of the Income Tax Act as unexplained cash credits against assessee Anita Pandey. The revenue contended that the corporate assessee had raised unsecured loans from shell companies lacking genuine creditworthiness. Learned counsel for the assessee demonstrated that the assessee had furnished PAN details, audited balance sheets, bank statements showing banking channel transfers, and affidavits from the directors of the creditor companies confirming the transactions. The ITAT Delhi examined the burden of proof under Section 68 of Industrial Disputes Act and reviewed the principles governing identity, creditworthiness, and genuineness of transactions. The court found that the assessee had successfully discharged the initial statutory onus, while the assessing officer failed to conduct any independent inquiry. The court therefore held that the addition under Section 68 was rightly deleted by the Tribunal, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Rajesh Kumar v. Geeta Khanna
text_content: The appellant assessee Rajesh Kumar approached the ITAT Delhi in the year 2018 challenging the order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal at Surat which upheld the disallowance of business expenditure amounting to Rs 54000 made by the Assessing Officer Geeta Khanna. The Assessing Officer had treated the expenditure incurred on software development, digital system migration, and cloud infrastructure as capital expenditure, disallowing the deduction claimed as revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act. The assessee contended that software licenses and digital upgrades do not create an enduring capital asset in modern computing environments but merely facilitate efficient operation of existing business processes, thereby qualifying fully as revenue expenditure under Industrial Disputes Act. The ITAT Delhi examined the commercial nature of software licensing agreements and reviewed the leading precedents distinguishing capital from revenue expenditure. The court observed that in the fast-evolving technology sector, expenditures incurred to update and maintain digital systems are essential running operational costs. The court held that the expenditure on software upgrades is deductible as revenue expenditure, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the disallowance is set aside.

title: Prakash Mehta v. Sachin Mishra
text_content: The petitioner hospital Prakash Mehta approached the ITAT Delhi in the year 2019 challenging a TDS demand notice issued by Sachin Mishra Income Tax Officer in Indore. The department contended that retainer consultancy payments made to visiting specialist medical doctors should have been subjected to salary TDS under Section 192 rather than professional fee TDS under Section 194J, raising a differential demand of Rs 2005000. The hospital produced consultancy contracts demonstrating that the doctors were independent practitioners who received fixed retainers plus revenue shares, did not receive provident fund or leave benefits, and were not bound by master-servant employment rules. The court evaluated the tests distinguishing contract of service from contract for services under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The court found that the professional arrangements established independent consultancy rather than employer-employee relationship. The court held that TDS was correctly deducted under Section 194J, and therefore the demand treating the hospital as in default is quashed.

title: Nirmala Chopra v. Manju Rastogi
text_content: The petitioner company Nirmala Chopra approached the ITAT Delhi in the year 2020 challenging an order passed by the Chief Commissioner of Income Tax Manju Rastogi in Surat rejecting its statutory application for waiver of interest under Section 234A, 234B, and 234C of Indian Penal Code. The petitioner had suffered extensive flood damage destroying manufacturing operations and had applied for waiver of interest amounting to Rs 747000 under the benevolent notification issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes empowering Commissioners to grant relief in cases of natural disasters. The Commissioner had rejected the application mechanically, stating that interest is statutory and non-discretionary. The court examined the CBDT circulars issued under Section 119(2)(a) and evaluated the financial hardship and destruction caused by the natural disaster. The court observed that statutory authorities must exercise benevolent powers with empathy and sound discretion rather than arbitrary administrative apathy. The court held that the rejection of waiver is arbitrary and perverse, and therefore the petition is allowed remitting the matter for waiver of interest.

title: Pankaj Mishra v. Sachin Tripathi
text_content: In this tax appeal, the revenue department Sachin Tripathi challenged the order of the High Court at Bengaluru in the year 2022 which deleted a penalty of Rs 101000 imposed under Section 271D of the Income Tax Act against partnership firm Pankaj Mishra. The penalty was levied for accepting cash loans exceeding twenty thousand rupees in alleged contravention of Section 269SS of Code of Criminal Procedure. Learned counsel for the partnership firm submitted that under Section 273B, no penalty can be imposed if the assessee proves reasonable cause for the failure, and established that the cash was accepted on a bank holiday to meet emergency hospitalisation expenses of an injured factory worker. The ITAT Delhi examined the medical discharge bills, the contemporaneous cash ledger entries, and the legislative purpose of Section 269SS. The court found that the emergency medical exigency constituted genuine and bona fide reasonable cause within the statutory framework of Section 273B. The court therefore held that penalty under Section 271D cannot be sustained in the presence of reasonable cause, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Mahesh Tiwari v. Suresh Chopra
text_content: The petitioner manufacturing firm Mahesh Tiwari approached the ITAT Delhi in the year 2022 challenging a best judgment assessment order passed ex-parte under Section 144 of the Income Tax Act by Suresh Chopra assessing authority in Hyderabad. The assessing officer had estimated the petitioner's net profit at twenty percent of gross turnover, making an arbitrary addition of Rs 149000. The petitioner submitted that statutory notices under Section 142(1) were transmitted solely to an obsolete email address during pandemic lockdown disruptions, preventing the assessee from filing books of accounts and audited financial statements. The court examined the service of notices on the ITBA portal and the compliance history of the assessee under Transfer of Property Act. The court observed that best judgment assessment cannot be converted into an arbitrary penal assessment without affording fair opportunity to produce accounts. The court held that the assessment order violates principles of natural justice, and therefore the petition is allowed remanding the matter for fresh scrutiny.

title: Kavita Malhotra v. Kamla Shah
text_content: In this GST appeal, the revenue department Kamla Shah challenged the judgment of the Appellate Tribunal at Patna in the year 2023 which allowed input tax credit of Rs 995000 to manufacturing enterprise Kavita Malhotra. The department contended that the supplier's registration was canceled retrospectively by anti-evasion intelligence authorities on the ground of issuing bogus invoices without actual movement of goods under Code of Criminal Procedure. Learned counsel for the respondent assessee submitted that at the time of purchase transactions, the supplier's GSTIN was active on the government portal, and pointed out that retrospective cancellation of supplier registration cannot invalidate lawful transactions conducted prior to such cancellation. The ITAT Delhi examined the documentary trail including weighing slips, transport bilties, toll tax receipts, and audited inventory stock registers. The court found that the assessee had conclusively proved genuine delivery and consumption of raw materials in manufacturing. The court therefore held that retrospective cancellation of supplier's registration cannot extinguish the purchaser's ITC, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Pankaj Shah v. Seema Rastogi
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the Commissioner of Income Tax Seema Rastogi challenged the order of the Appellate Tribunal at Bengaluru in the year 2024 which deleted an addition of Rs 152000 made under Section 68 of the Income Tax Act as unexplained cash credits against assessee Pankaj Shah. The revenue contended that the corporate assessee had raised unsecured loans from shell companies lacking genuine creditworthiness. Learned counsel for the assessee demonstrated that the assessee had furnished PAN details, audited balance sheets, bank statements showing banking channel transfers, and affidavits from the directors of the creditor companies confirming the transactions. The ITAT Delhi examined the burden of proof under Section 68 of Income Tax Act and reviewed the principles governing identity, creditworthiness, and genuineness of transactions. title: Anil Gupta v. Dinesh Singh
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the Commissioner of Income Tax Dinesh Singh challenged the order of the Appellate Tribunal at Nagpur in the year 2024 which deleted an addition of Rs 4996000 made under Section 68 of the Income Tax Act as unexplained cash credits against assessee Anil Gupta. Learned counsel for the assessee demonstrated that the assessee had furnished PAN details, audited balance sheets, bank statements showing banking channel transfers, and affidavits from the directors of the creditor companies confirming the transactions. The ITAT Delhi examined the burden of proof under Section 68 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act and reviewed the principles governing identity, creditworthiness, and genuineness of transactions. The court found that the assessee had successfully discharged the initial statutory onus, while the assessing officer failed to conduct any independent inquiry. The court therefore held that the addition under Section 68 was rightly deleted by the Tribunal, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Meera Malhotra v. Renu Kumar
text_content: The petitioner corporate enterprise Meera Malhotra filed an income tax appeal before the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2016 assailing an order passed by the Assessing Officer (TDS) Renu Kumar in Pune under Section 201(1) and Section 201(1A) of the Income Tax Act. The assessing officer had treated the company as an assessee-in-default for alleged short-deduction of tax at source amounting to Rs 1499000, holding that payments made to software developers and cloud hosting platforms were fees for technical services attracting ten percent TDS under Section 194J rather than contractual work payments attracting two percent TDS under Section 194C of Arbitration and Conciliation Act. title: Anita Kapoor v. Rajesh Saxena
text_content: The petitioner hospital Anita Kapoor approached the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2017 challenging a TDS demand notice issued by Rajesh Saxena Income Tax Officer in Varanasi. The hospital produced consultancy contracts demonstrating that the doctors were independent practitioners who received fixed retainers plus revenue shares, did not receive provident fund or leave benefits, and were not bound by master-servant employment rules. title: Nitin Singh v. Rajesh Shah
text_content: The petitioner assessee Nitin Singh filed a writ petition before the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2017 challenging the validity of a notice issued under Section 148 and the reassessment order passed under Section 147 of the Income Tax Act by the respondent Assessing Officer Rajesh Shah in Indore. title: Nirmala Tiwari v. Kamla Pandey
text_content: The appellant assessee Nirmala Tiwari filed an income tax appeal before the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2019 challenging an order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal at Hyderabad which confirmed a penalty of Rs 746000 levied under Section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act by the assessing authority Kamla Pandey. The penalty was imposed following the disallowance of a depreciation claim on commercial wind energy equipment in regular assessment proceedings. The appellant contended that full and accurate details of the capital expenditure, equipment installation certificates, and depreciation rates were openly disclosed in the return of income, and argued that a bona fide legal claim rejected by the revenue cannot be equated with concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars. The court reviewed the statutory provisions of Section 271(1)(c) of Code of Criminal Procedure and the seminal Supreme Court ruling in CIT v Reliance Petroproducts. The court observed that mere making of a claim that is not accepted by the Assessing Officer does not attract penalty when all facts are fully disclosed. The court held that the levy of penalty is wholly unjustified and untenable, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the penalty order is deleted.

title: Ajay Chopra v. Lata Pandey
text_content: In this tax appeal, the revenue department Lata Pandey challenged the order of the High Court at Agra in the year 2020 which deleted a penalty of Rs 151000 imposed under Section 271D of the Income Tax Act against partnership firm Ajay Chopra. The penalty was levied for accepting cash loans exceeding twenty thousand rupees in alleged contravention of Section 269SS of Central Goods and Services Tax Act. title: Renu Singh v. Anil Yadav
text_content: The appellant assessee Renu Singh filed a tax appeal before the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2021 challenging the levy of mandatory interest under Section 234B and Section 234C of the Income Tax Act confirmed by the Tribunal at Hyderabad in proceedings initiated by the revenue Anil Yadav. The assessing officer had charged interest of Rs 4995000 for shortfall in payment of advance tax instalments, which arose entirely because the assessee had received substantial unexpected capital gains from compulsory land acquisition on the final week of the financial year. The assessee argued that under the proviso to Section 234C of Indian Contract Act, no interest can be charged for shortfall in advance tax where the shortfall arises on account of unforeseen capital gains and the assessee discharges the remaining tax liability in subsequent instalments. The court examined the dates of compensation disbursement, the advance tax challans, and the statutory relief provided in the proviso to Section 234C. The court observed that the law does not compel an assessee to perform the impossible task of anticipating unexpected capital gains before they arise. The court held that the assessee is entitled to statutory relief from interest, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the interest levy is cancelled.

title: Pooja Pandey v. Sarla Rastogi
text_content: The petitioner enterprise Pooja Pandey approached the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2022 challenging a penalty order passed under Section 129(3) of the CGST Act by the mobile inspection authority Sarla Rastogi in Varanasi. The authority had intercepted a commercial consignment valued at Rs 303000 and levied maximum penalty solely because the vehicle registration number on the e-way bill contained a single typographical digit transposition error. The petitioner proved that the tax invoice, consignment value, and destination details were accurate, and argued that minor clerical errors do not justify confiscation. The court referred to the circulars issued by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs regarding minor typographical discrepancies in transit documents. The court observed that penalty cannot be imposed where there is no intention to evade tax and transactions are supported by genuine tax invoices. The court held that the detention and penalty are arbitrary and disproportionate, and therefore the petition is allowed and the penalty is set aside.

title: Rekha Agarwal v. Suresh Gupta
text_content: The petitioner charitable trust Rekha Agarwal approached the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2023 challenging the cancellation of its registration under Section 12AA and denial of deduction under Section 80G by the Commissioner of Income Tax Suresh Gupta in Kanpur. The department alleged that the trust had accumulated surplus revenues of Rs 253000 from hospital pharmacy operations, which allegedly constituted commercial activity violating the proviso to Section 2(15) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The petitioner established that the nominal pharmacy margins were deployed exclusively to subsidize medical treatment and free beds for indigent patients. The court examined the statutory definition of charitable purpose and the Supreme Court ruling in Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority. The court observed that incidental commercial receipts that directly subserve the primary charitable object of medical relief do not taint charitable status. The court held that the cancellation of charitable registration is unlawful, and therefore the petition is allowed and the registration is restored.

title: Usha Sharma v. Nirmala Rastogi
text_content: The appellant assessee Usha Sharma filed an income tax appeal before the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2023 challenging an order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal at Hyderabad which confirmed a penalty of Rs 152000 levied under Section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act by the assessing authority Nirmala Rastogi. title: Sunita Rastogi v. Nitin Patel
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the revenue department Nitin Patel challenged the judgment of the High Court at Hyderabad in the year 2023 which waived interest levied under Section 234B on public sector enterprise Sunita Rastogi. The department contended that interest under Section 234B is automatic, mandatory, and compensatory in nature, leaving no room for equitable waiver by judicial authorities regardless of the underlying reasons for shortfall. Learned counsel for the enterprise demonstrated that the shortfall of Rs 999000 occurred because of retrospective statutory amendments to book profit calculations under Section 115JB enacted after the close of the financial year. The ITAT Mumbai examined the constitutional limits of retrospective taxation and reviewed the landmark judgment in Star India. The court observed that interest for default in payment of advance tax cannot be charged where the tax liability was created by retrospective legislation post factum. The court therefore held that the assessee cannot be deemed in default of advance tax, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

text_content: The appellant assessee Asha Saxena approached the ITAT Mumbai in the year 2024 challenging the order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal at Bengaluru which upheld the disallowance of business expenditure amounting to Rs 4995000 made by the Assessing Officer Priya Tripathi. The assessee contended that software licenses and digital upgrades do not create an enduring capital asset in modern computing environments but merely facilitate efficient operation of existing business processes, thereby qualifying fully as revenue expenditure under Code of Criminal Procedure.
