title: Rohit Sharma v. Rajesh Joshi
text_content: The petitioner in-laws Rohit Sharma filed a petition seeking quashing of domestic violence proceedings instituted by their daughter-in-law Rajesh Joshi pending before the magistrate in Coimbatore in the year 2015. The petitioners submitted that they had been residing permanently in another state for over a decade, had never shared a household with the complainant, and had been roped in with sweeping and generalized allegations to extract monetary settlement. The complainant opposed quashing, asserting that the in-laws had visited the matrimonial home occasionally and exercised psychological dominance over family affairs. The Karnataka High Court reviewed the domestic incident report and evaluated the statutory prerequisites for establishing a domestic relationship in a shared household under Indian Contract Act. The court observed that distant relatives living in separate cities without sharing a domestic household cannot be prosecuted on vague, omnibus averments. The court held that continuing proceedings against the aged in-laws constitutes an abuse of judicial process, and therefore the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Ajay Bhatia v. Pushpa Patel
text_content: The petitioner Ajay Bhatia approached the Karnataka High Court in the year 2018 seeking enforcement and recovery of accumulated maintenance arrears of Rs 505000 awarded by the Family Court at Coimbatore against Pushpa Patel. The petitioner submitted that the husband had wilfully failed to pay monthly maintenance for over two years despite coercive recovery notices and attachment warrants issued under Indian Penal Code. The respondent husband pleaded business insolvency and offered to liquidate the arrears in nominal monthly instalments of negligible value. The court scrutinized the husband's company accounts, credit card statements, and recent foreign travel expenditures. The court observed that deliberate refusal to comply with maintenance orders cannot be tolerated, as it defeats the benevolent purpose of the statute. The court held that coercive measures including attachment of bank accounts and civil imprisonment must follow upon continued default, and therefore the execution petition is allowed.

title: Usha Tripathi v. Meera Gupta
text_content: The applicant wife Usha Tripathi instituted proceedings claiming maintenance from her husband Meera Gupta before the Family Court at Kanpur in the year 2018. The applicant stated that following grave matrimonial discord, she was forced to leave the matrimonial domicile with her infant child, possessed no independent financial assets, and required monthly maintenance of Rs 295000 to meet living and medical expenses. The respondent husband opposed the application, alleging that the applicant was gainfully employed as a commercial designer and argued that his own net salary was insufficient to bear the claimed maintenance after meeting obligations towards his aged parents under Indian Penal Code. The Karnataka High Court examined the detailed assets and liabilities affidavits submitted by both spouses along with bank statements and income tax disclosures. The court observed that the husband had suppressed supplementary allowances and investment portfolios, and noted that maintenance under social welfare legislation is intended to prevent destitution and maintain parity of living standard. The court held that the wife and infant child are entitled to reasonable maintenance, and therefore directed payment of monthly maintenance and allowed the petition.

title: Sachin Malhotra v. Pankaj Yadav
text_content: The petitioner husband Sachin Malhotra filed a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce against the respondent wife Pankaj Yadav under Section 13(1)(ia) and (ib) of the Hindu Marriage Act before the Family Court at Vadodara in the year 2019. The petitioner alleged that the respondent had treated him with continuous mental cruelty by leveling false and scandalous allegations against his character, instituting frivolous criminal complaints under Section 498A which resulted in his discharge, and deserting the matrimonial home for over three years without justification. The respondent wife contested the petition, asserting that she was subjected to persistent dowry harassment, denied having deserted the home voluntarily, and stated that she was always ready to resume cohabitation subject to separate accommodation. The Karnataka High Court evaluated the documentary records of the criminal litigation, the exchange of legal notices, and the oral testimonies of family members. The court noted that filing unproven and defamatory criminal charges that humiliate a spouse in society constitutes mental cruelty of the highest degree under Hindu Marriage Act. The court held that the marriage has broken down irretrievably on account of cruelty and desertion, and therefore the petition is allowed and divorce is decreed.

title: Dinesh Chaturvedi v. Ajay Patel
text_content: The petitioner father Dinesh Chaturvedi instituted guardianship and custody proceedings under the Guardians and Wards Act against the respondent mother Ajay Patel before the Family Court at Bengaluru in the year 2019. The petitioner sought permanent custody of the minor child aged eight years, contending that he was better equipped financially and emotionally to cater to the child's premier schooling and extracurricular development with an annual income of Rs 5002000. The respondent mother opposed custody, asserting that she had been the primary caregiver since birth, that the father had remained detached due to extensive corporate travel, and that the child's tender age demanded maternal care and stability under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The Karnataka High Court conducted an interactive session in chambers with the minor child and considered the detailed home evaluation report submitted by the court welfare officer. The court observed that in custody disputes, the welfare of the child is the paramount consideration, overriding financial superiority of one parent over the other. The court held that custody should remain with the mother while granting extensive weekend visitation rights to the father, and therefore the petition is disposed of.

title: Sachin Saxena v. Nitin Bhatia
text_content: The petitioner Sachin Saxena filed a habeas corpus writ petition before the Karnataka High Court in the year 2019 alleging that his minor child was being illegally detained by the respondent maternal grandparents Nitin Bhatia in Hyderabad following the tragic demise of the child's mother. The petitioner asserted that as the surviving biological father, he was the natural guardian under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act and entitled to immediate custody. The grandparents resisted the petition, arguing that the father had neglected the mother during her prolonged terminal illness and pointed out that the child had resided exclusively with them since infancy. The court examined the scope of habeas corpus in custody matters and reiterated that natural guardianship must yield to the welfare of the minor. The court observed that a sudden change of custody from loving grandparents would cause severe emotional trauma to the young child. The court held that interim custody shall remain with the grandparents pending final decision by the Family Court, and therefore the writ petition is dismissed.

title: Nitin Rastogi v. Nitin Sharma
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant wife Nitin Sharma assailed the decree of divorce granted in favour of husband Nitin Rastogi by the Family Court in Varanasi in the year 2020 on the ground of cruelty under the Hindu Marriage Act. The appellant argued that ordinary wear and tear of married life had been exaggerated into mental cruelty by the trial court, and submitted that reconciliation was still possible in the interest of the minor child. Learned counsel for the respondent husband submitted that the parties had been living separately for more than eight years and pointed out that multiple rounds of court-annexed mediation had completely failed to bridge the profound marital discord. The Karnataka High Court examined the judicial guidelines regarding mental cruelty and reviewed the irreversible estrangement between the spouses under Indian Penal Code. The court observed that compelling parties to remain legally bound in a dead marriage where emotional bonds have perished causes perpetual agony to both. The court therefore held that the Family Court was fully justified in granting dissolution of marriage, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Naresh Chaturvedi v. Usha Bhatia
text_content: The parties Naresh Chaturvedi and Usha Bhatia jointly approached the Karnataka High Court in the year 2021 seeking dissolution of their marriage by mutual consent under Section 13-B of the Hindu Marriage Act in Chennai. The parties had executed a comprehensive memorandum of understanding resolving all disputes regarding permanent alimony of Rs 151000, custody of the minor child, and return of stridhan articles. The parties filed an application praying for waiver of the statutory six months cooling-off period prescribed under Section 13-B(2), citing the Supreme Court judgment in Amardeep Singh v Harveen Kaur. The court examined whether all efforts at conciliation had failed, verified that the parties had lived separately for over eighteen months, and confirmed that the settlement terms were fair and executed without coercion. The court observed that the cooling-off period is directory and can be waived where continuance of the legal tie prolongs human suffering. The court held that all statutory criteria for mutual consent divorce are satisfied, and therefore the cooling-off period is waived and marriage is dissolved.

title: Manju Pandey v. Ajay Malhotra
text_content: The complainant Manju Pandey filed an application under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 against her husband and in-laws Ajay Malhotra before the Metropolitan Magistrate at Nagpur in the year 2021. The complainant alleged that throughout her marital life, she was subjected to persistent physical assaults, verbal degradation, and economic deprivation, culminating in her being locked out of the shared household. The complainant sought statutory protection orders, a residence order under Section 19 to reside in the shared matrimonial home, and monetary relief of Rs 5004000. The respondents contested the complaint, asserting that the shared household was the exclusive self-acquired property of the mother-in-law where the complainant had no legal right, and denied all allegations of domestic abuse as fabricated. The Karnataka High Court examined the Domestic Incident Report submitted by the Protection Officer, medical emergency room slips, and the Supreme Court ruling in Satish Chander Ahuja. The court observed that the definition of shared household encompasses any house where the aggrieved woman has lived in a domestic relationship irrespective of ownership. The court held that the complainant is entitled to reside in the shared household and receive maintenance, and therefore the domestic violence application is allowed.

title: Pankaj Verma v. Vikas Khanna
text_content: In this regular first appeal, the appellant husband Vikas Khanna challenged the preliminary decree passed by the civil court at Kanpur in the year 2022 declaring that the respondent wife Pankaj Verma was a joint owner of two commercial apartments purchased during cohabitation. The appellant contended that the trial court had erroneously applied community of property concepts that are alien to the general matrimonial law of India outside Goa. Learned counsel for the wife demonstrated that the mortgage loan was sanctioned jointly, that rental revenues were deposited into a joint account, and that the wife had pledged her ancestral gold ornaments to secure initial bridge financing. The Karnataka High Court scrutinized the loan sanction agreements, banking records, and property tax assessments. The court observed that where property is acquired jointly through mutual contributions of spouses, neither party can unilaterally exclude the other. The court therefore held that the wife is a bona fide co-owner of the disputed properties, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Amit Verma v. Lata Agarwal
text_content: In this criminal appeal under the Domestic Violence Act, the appellant husband Lata Agarwal assailed the monetary relief order passed by the magistrate in Kanpur in the year 2022 directing him to pay Rs 5000000 per month towards alternative rented accommodation for aggrieved wife Amit Verma. The appellant contended that the wife was residing with her affluent parents and suffered no financial distress, arguing that the award was punitive. Learned counsel for the wife submitted that under Section 19(1)(f) of Code of Criminal Procedure, the magistrate possesses explicit statutory power to direct the respondent to secure the same level of alternative accommodation for the aggrieved person as enjoyed in the shared household. The Karnataka High Court evaluated the lifestyle of the husband, the rental value of residential premises in Kanpur, and the legislative object of the enactment. The court found that the monetary provision for alternative accommodation was strictly in accordance with statutory guidelines and proportional to the respondent's income. The court therefore held that the order of the magistrate is unassailable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the order is confirmed.

title: Priya Tripathi v. Naresh Kapoor
text_content: The petitioner Priya Tripathi filed a habeas corpus writ petition before the Karnataka High Court in the year 2023 alleging that his minor child was being illegally detained by the respondent maternal grandparents Naresh Kapoor in Agra following the tragic demise of the child's mother. The petitioner asserted that as the surviving biological father, he was the natural guardian under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act and entitled to immediate custody. The grandparents resisted the petition, arguing that the father had neglected the mother during her prolonged terminal illness and pointed out that the child had resided exclusively with them since infancy. The court examined the scope of habeas corpus in custody matters and reiterated that natural guardianship must yield to the welfare of the minor. The court observed that a sudden change of custody from loving grandparents would cause severe emotional trauma to the young child. The court held that interim custody shall remain with the grandparents pending final decision by the Family Court, and therefore the writ petition is dismissed.

title: Kamla Rastogi v. Lata Gupta
text_content: The petitioner husband Kamla Rastogi filed a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce against the respondent wife Lata Gupta under Section 13(1)(ia) and (ib) of the Hindu Marriage Act before the Family Court at Chennai in the year 2021. The petitioner alleged that the respondent had treated him with continuous mental cruelty by leveling false and scandalous allegations against his character, instituting frivolous criminal complaints under Section 498A which resulted in his discharge, and deserting the matrimonial home for over three years without justification. The respondent wife contested the petition, asserting that she was subjected to persistent dowry harassment, denied having deserted the home voluntarily, and stated that she was always ready to resume cohabitation subject to separate accommodation. The Kerala High Court evaluated the documentary records of the criminal litigation, the exchange of legal notices, and the oral testimonies of family members. The court noted that filing unproven and defamatory criminal charges that humiliate a spouse in society constitutes mental cruelty of the highest degree under Income Tax Act. The court held that the marriage has broken down irretrievably on account of cruelty and desertion, and therefore the petition is allowed and divorce is decreed.

title: Anil Chopra v. Sarla Agarwal
text_content: The plaintiff wife Anil Chopra instituted a civil suit for declaration of title, partition, and separate possession in respect of the matrimonial residence against her estranged husband Sarla Agarwal before the civil court at Patna in the year 2021. The plaintiff stated that the luxury residential property valued at Rs 251000 was purchased during the subsistence of the marriage, and although the registered title deed stood exclusively in the husband's name, she had contributed fifty percent of the initial down payment from her stridhan and savings, while also managing the domestic household for two decades. The defendant husband resisted the suit, claiming that he had financed the entire purchase through personal commercial borrowings and argued that under the Benami Transactions Prohibition Act as amended, the wife could not assert any equitable or beneficial title against the recorded owner. The Kerala High Court examined the banking transactions, the source of funds for down payment, and emerging jurisprudence recognizing homemakers' economic contributions. The court held that the plaintiff has established direct financial contribution and beneficial ownership, and therefore the suit is decreed granting a half share.

title: Seema Verma v. Priya Gupta
text_content: The petitioner adoptive parents Seema Verma filed a civil petition under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act before the district court at Ahmedabad in the year 2021 seeking a formal declaration of the validity of the adoption of a minor child and registration of the adoption deed. The petitioners established that all essential statutory ceremonies including the actual giving and taking of the child with intent to transfer from the biological family to the adoptive family were duly performed in the presence of relatives. The respondent biological relatives Priya Gupta contested the adoption, alleging that the consent of the biological mother was procured through misrepresentation and contended that the adoptive parents lacked requisite financial capacity under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The Kerala High Court examined the registered adoption deed, photographs and video recordings of the religious ceremonies, and the testimony of participating elders. The court verified that the child was capable of being adopted, that the adoptive parents possessed sound mind and legal capacity, and that valid consent was executed. The court held that the adoption is legal, valid, and binding on all parties, and therefore the petition is allowed and the adoption is confirmed.

title: Manju Malhotra v. Asha Chaturvedi
text_content: The petitioner father Manju Malhotra instituted guardianship and custody proceedings under the Guardians and Wards Act against the respondent mother Asha Chaturvedi before the Family Court at Varanasi in the year 2022. The petitioner sought permanent custody of the minor child aged eight years, contending that he was better equipped financially and emotionally to cater to the child's premier schooling and extracurricular development with an annual income of Rs 1504000. The respondent mother opposed custody, asserting that she had been the primary caregiver since birth, that the father had remained detached due to extensive corporate travel, and that the child's tender age demanded maternal care and stability under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The Kerala High Court conducted an interactive session in chambers with the minor child and considered the detailed home evaluation report submitted by the court welfare officer. The court observed that in custody disputes, the welfare of the child is the paramount consideration, overriding financial superiority of one parent over the other. The court held that custody should remain with the mother while granting extensive weekend visitation rights to the father, and therefore the petition is disposed of.

title: Prakash Saxena v. Lata Chopra
text_content: In this matrimonial appeal, the appellant husband Lata Chopra challenged the judgment of the Family Court in Chennai in the year 2023 which awarded monthly maintenance to respondent wife Prakash Saxena. The appellant argued that the marriage had lasted for barely six months and contended that the maintenance quantum of Rs 253000 was disproportionate to the duration of cohabitation. Learned counsel for the respondent wife demonstrated that the husband was a senior corporate director who traveled internationally and maintained luxury cars, arguing that the award was commensurate with the high socioeconomic status enjoyed during marriage. The Kerala High Court reviewed the precedents under Section 304 and noted that duration of marriage does not diminish the statutory entitlement to dignified maintenance. The court found that the Family Court had carefully balanced the financial capacities and reasonable needs of both parties without imposing punitive burden. The court therefore held that the maintenance award is just, equitable, and appropriate, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Pooja Patel v. Priya Mishra
text_content: The petitioner husband Pooja Patel filed a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce against the respondent wife Priya Mishra under Section 13(1)(ia) and (ib) of the Hindu Marriage Act before the Family Court at Kolkata in the year 2023. The petitioner alleged that the respondent had treated him with continuous mental cruelty by leveling false and scandalous allegations against his character, instituting frivolous criminal complaints under Section 498A which resulted in his discharge, and deserting the matrimonial home for over three years without justification. The respondent wife contested the petition, asserting that she was subjected to persistent dowry harassment, denied having deserted the home voluntarily, and stated that she was always ready to resume cohabitation subject to separate accommodation. The Kerala High Court evaluated the documentary records of the criminal litigation, the exchange of legal notices, and the oral testimonies of family members. The court noted that filing unproven and defamatory criminal charges that humiliate a spouse in society constitutes mental cruelty of the highest degree under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court held that the marriage has broken down irretrievably on account of cruelty and desertion, and therefore the petition is allowed and divorce is decreed.

title: Rekha Chaturvedi v. Dinesh Saxena
text_content: In this civil appeal, the appellant Dinesh Saxena challenged the judgment of the civil court at Bengaluru in the year 2024 which upheld the adoption deed executed by adoptive father Rekha Chaturvedi. The appellant argued that the adoption was void ab initio under Section 11 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act because the adoptive father already had a living biological son at the time of adoption, which acts as an absolute statutory bar against adopting another male child. Learned counsel for the respondent adoptive child submitted that the alleged biological son had been given away in valid adoption decades earlier, thereby removing the bar. The Kerala High Court closely examined the pedigree tables, prior adoption deeds, and the statutory requirements under Indian Penal Code. The court found that documentary evidence conclusively established the prior adoption of the biological son, leaving the adoptive father free to adopt. The court therefore held that the adoption complies strictly with the statutory mandate, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the adoption is upheld.

title: Prakash Rastogi v. Amit Pandey
text_content: In this criminal revision petition, the husband Amit Pandey assailed the order passed under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the Family Court at Chennai in the year 2015, which directed payment of monthly maintenance of Rs 50000 to his estranged wife Prakash Rastogi. The revisionist argued that the maintenance quantum was arbitrary, unsupported by documentary proof of his actual business revenues, and exceeded his paying capacity. Learned counsel for the respondent wife submitted that the husband had deliberately suppressed substantial rental incomes from commercial properties and pointed out that the maintenance amount was barely adequate to meet escalating rental and medical expenses in Chennai. The Madras High Court examined the tax returns, balance sheets of the husband's proprietary enterprise, and lifestyle expenditures disclosed during cross-examination. The court noted that maintenance should not be excessive but must guarantee that the dependent spouse lives with dignity rather than mere subsistence. The court held that the quantum determined by the trial magistrate was fair, equitable, and proportional, and therefore the revision petition is dismissed.

title: Deepak Kumar v. Nirmala Khanna
text_content: By this petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the petitioner Deepak Kumar challenged the summoning order passed by the Metropolitan Magistrate at Agra in the year 2017 in a private criminal complaint instituted by Nirmala Khanna. The complaint alleged that the petitioner had committed offences of criminal breach of trust regarding company machinery worth Rs 205000. The petitioner submitted that the parties had subsequently resolved all existing disputes through a comprehensive memorandum of settlement and jointly prayed for quashing of all criminal proceedings to restore business harmony. The respondent appeared through counsel and confirmed receipt of agreed settlement amounts and consented to the quashing of the criminal complaint. The Madras High Court examined whether non-compoundable offences of a predominantly commercial and private nature could be quashed under inherent powers. The court noted that when the underlying commercial dispute is amicably resolved, continuing criminal prosecution would be an exercise in futility. The court therefore held that it is in the interest of justice to quash the proceedings, and accordingly the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Renu Dwivedi v. Renu Mishra
text_content: In this environmental writ appeal, the mining conglomerate Renu Mishra challenged the judgment of the High Court at Mumbai in the year 2017 which halted open-cast bauxite mining operations inside an eco-sensitive forest zone following a PIL instituted by tribal rights activist Renu Dwivedi. The appellant corporation contended that it held valid environmental clearances granted by the Ministry of Environment and had invested Rs 1499000 in infrastructure. Learned counsel for the petitioner established that the mining operations caused massive deforestation, dried up perennial mountain streams, and displaced indigenous tribal communities without obtaining their mandatory consent under the Forest Rights Act and Consumer Protection Act. The Madras High Court examined the ecological sensitivity of the Western Ghats and reviewed the constitutional public trust doctrine. The court observed that economic considerations must yield to the imperative need for sustainable development and preservation of fragile ecological biodiversity. The court therefore held that mining in the protected eco-sensitive sanctuary cannot be permitted, and accordingly the mining appeal is dismissed.

title: Ajay Tripathi v. Vikas Chopra
text_content: The petitioner Ajay Tripathi filed this bail application in connection with a case registered under Section 138 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act at Kolkata in the year 2018. The prosecution case against the petitioner, presented by Vikas Chopra, was that intermediate quantity of psychotropic substance was recovered from a business premise occupied by the applicant. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the recovered quantity did not attract the rigorous threshold of commercial quantity and pointed out that the search was carried out after sunset without obtaining any search authorization or recording grounds of belief under Section 42 of Code of Criminal Procedure. The State argued that the applicant was a repeat offender involved in distribution of prohibited chemical drugs. The court examined the case diary, the seizure memo, and the chemical analysis certificate. The court observed that where recovery falls below commercial quantity, the statutory bar of Section 37 is not attracted and regular bail principles apply. The court held that continued judicial custody is unnecessary for the completion of trial, and therefore bail is granted upon furnishing adequate security.

title: Anil Tripathi v. Sachin Srivastava
text_content: The petitioner Anil Tripathi filed this petition for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC before the Madras High Court in 2018 apprehending arrest in an FIR lodged at Ahmedabad by Sachin Srivastava arising out of a matrimonial dispute under Section 34 of Code of Criminal Procedure. The allegations related to harassment for dowry and unlawful retention of stridhan ornaments valued at approximately Rs 499000. Counsel for the petitioner submitted that omnibus allegations were made against the entire family, that the marriage had broken down irretrievably, and that the petitioner was willing to deposit the value of stridhan articles in an escrow account to demonstrate bona fides. The State submitted that recovery of the stridhan property was yet to be completed and opposed pre-arrest protection. The court reiterated that arrest in matrimonial conflicts should be an exception rather than a routine measure to prevent abuse of criminal law. The court held that custodial interrogation of the petitioner is not necessary for the recovery of stridhan, and therefore anticipatory bail is granted.

title: Lata Mishra v. Kavita Agarwal
text_content: The petitioner single female Lata Mishra approached the Madras High Court in the year 2018 seeking directions to the Central Adoption Resource Authority and local welfare agency Kavita Agarwal to finalize the domestic adoption of a surrendered child in Nagpur. The authorities had delayed issuance of the final no-objection certificate, questioning the eligibility of an unmarried working professional under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and seeking additional financial guarantees of Rs 1500000. The petitioner submitted that she satisfied all criteria under the Juvenile Justice Act and Adoption Regulations, having an established career and strong support system. The court examined the home study report, the psychological fitness evaluation, and the constitutional guarantee of non-discrimination. The court observed that unmarried women have an equal legal right to adopt and provide loving parental care to orphaned children without arbitrary impediments. The court held that the delay caused by the authorities is unjustified, and therefore the petition is allowed and the authorities are directed to finalize the adoption.

title: Nirmala Pandey v. Naresh Khanna
text_content: This application under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act was filed by Nirmala Pandey through counsel before the Madras High Court in 2019. The applicant had been arrested at Mumbai following an alleged seizure of narcotic contraband valued at Rs 78000 in the illicit market. The respondent State represented by Naresh Khanna opposed the grant of regular bail, highlighting that the quantity recovered fell within the commercial bracket. The applicant contended that no contraband was recovered from his conscious possession and submitted that his name surfaced solely on the basis of an inadmissible confessional disclosure made by a co-accused while in police custody. The court examined the constitutional guarantee of speedy trial under Article 21 vis-a-vis the legislative restrictions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act. The court noted that the prosecution had not produced any independent corroborative evidence connecting the applicant with the alleged drug syndicate. The court therefore held that reasonable grounds exist for believing that the accused is not guilty, and consequently bail is granted subject to stringent conditions.

title: Amit Shah v. Mahesh Tiwari
text_content: In this civil appeal, the appellant Mahesh Tiwari challenged the judgment of the civil court at Coimbatore in the year 2019 which upheld the adoption deed executed by adoptive father Amit Shah. The appellant argued that the adoption was void ab initio under Section 11 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act because the adoptive father already had a living biological son at the time of adoption, which acts as an absolute statutory bar against adopting another male child. Learned counsel for the respondent adoptive child submitted that the alleged biological son had been given away in valid adoption decades earlier, thereby removing the bar. The Madras High Court closely examined the pedigree tables, prior adoption deeds, and the statutory requirements under Transfer of Property Act. The court found that documentary evidence conclusively established the prior adoption of the biological son, leaving the adoptive father free to adopt. The court therefore held that the adoption complies strictly with the statutory mandate, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the adoption is upheld.

title: Vimla Khanna v. Rajesh Mehta
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the elected legislator Rajesh Mehta challenged the judgment of the High Court at Kolkata in the year 2019 which declared his election to Parliament void under Section 100 of the Representation of the People Act upon an election petition filed by rival candidate Vimla Khanna. The High Court had found that the elected member had failed to disclose multiple pending criminal charges and substantial commercial assets of Rs 300000 in his affidavit. The appellant contended that the omissions were unintentional inadvertent oversights that did not materially affect the result of the election under Industrial Disputes Act. The Madras High Court examined the landmark ruling in Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms regarding voters' fundamental right to know under Article 19(1)(a). The court observed that non-disclosure of criminal antecedents and assets taints the purity of the electoral process and constitutes a corrupt practice. The court therefore held that the election was rightly set aside, and accordingly the appeal of the disqualified member is dismissed.

title: Geeta Singh v. Deepak Srivastava
text_content: The applicant wife Geeta Singh instituted proceedings claiming maintenance from her husband Deepak Srivastava before the Family Court at Pune in the year 2020. The applicant stated that following grave matrimonial discord, she was forced to leave the matrimonial domicile with her infant child, possessed no independent financial assets, and required monthly maintenance of Rs 304000 to meet living and medical expenses. The respondent husband opposed the application, alleging that the applicant was gainfully employed as a commercial designer and argued that his own net salary was insufficient to bear the claimed maintenance after meeting obligations towards his aged parents under Income Tax Act. The Madras High Court examined the detailed assets and liabilities affidavits submitted by both spouses along with bank statements and income tax disclosures. The court observed that the husband had suppressed supplementary allowances and investment portfolios, and noted that maintenance under social welfare legislation is intended to prevent destitution and maintain parity of living standard. The court held that the wife and infant child are entitled to reasonable maintenance, and therefore directed payment of monthly maintenance and allowed the petition.

title: Vimla Saxena v. Meera Tiwari
text_content: The petitioner candidate Vimla Saxena filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Madras High Court in the year 2020 challenging an order passed by the Returning Officer Meera Tiwari in Indore rejecting his nomination papers for the legislative assembly constituency under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Returning Officer had rejected the nomination paper on the hyper-technical ground of a minor clerical omission in the accompanying electoral affidavit, despite the petitioner submitting a rectification affidavit before the deadline for scrutiny. The Election Commission raised a preliminary objection, arguing that under Article 329(b) of the Constitution, all electoral disputes must await completion of the election and can only be adjudicated through an election petition under Transfer of Property Act. The court examined the narrow exceptions where writ intervention is permissible to facilitate rather than stall the democratic election process. The court observed that where rejection of nomination is patently arbitrary and perverse, leaving a candidate remediless until post-election defeats democracy. The court held that the rejection of nomination was wholly arbitrary, and therefore the writ petition is allowed directing acceptance of nomination.

title: Suresh Gupta v. Anil Mishra
text_content: In this criminal appeal arising out of proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the appellant Suresh Gupta assailed the concurrent findings of guilt recorded by the appellate court at Mumbai in the year 2021. The respondent payee Anil Mishra had supplied commercial inventory and received an account payee cheque for Rs 754000 towards discharge of the outstanding commercial invoices. Upon presentation to the drawee bank, the instrument was dishonoured with the remark stop payment instructions. A formal statutory notice was served upon the drawer within the prescribed period of limitation, yet the drawer failed to make payment. The appellant drawer claimed that the goods delivered were defective and argued that the statutory presumption had been successfully rebutted. The Madras High Court reviewed the trial court record and noted that the drawer had neither returned the supplied merchandise nor sent any contemporaneous protest communication prior to the dishonour of the negotiable instrument. The court observed that mere oral assertions unsupported by documentary proof cannot displace the statutory presumption operating in favour of the payee. The court therefore held that the complainant has established the existence of a legally enforceable debt, and accordingly the conviction is confirmed.

title: Vikas Singh v. Sarla Saxena
text_content: In this criminal appeal, the appellant Vikas Singh challenged the judgment of conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code recorded by the Sessions Court at Pune in the year 2021. The prosecution case against the appellant rested entirely on circumstantial evidence as deposed by witness Sarla Saxena. The circumstantial links relied upon were the last seen theory, motive relating to disputed business accounts of Rs 70000, and recovery of the weapon of offence pursuant to a disclosure statement recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. The appellant contended that the chain of circumstantial evidence was fragmented, pointing out that an interval of over twelve hours elapsed between the last seen encounter and the estimated time of death, and alleged that the weapon recovery was planted by investigating officials. The Madras High Court examined the golden principles governing circumstantial evidence and evaluated whether every link pointed unerringly to the guilt of the accused. The court found that the prosecution had conclusively established every link in the chain leaving no room for any hypothesis of innocence. The court therefore held that the circumstantial evidence conclusively proves the guilt of the appellant, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Vimla Pandey v. Renu Singh
text_content: The petitioner government teacher Vimla Pandey approached the Madras High Court in the year 2021 through a writ petition under Article 226 seeking release of withheld pension and terminal retirement benefits amounting to Rs 196000 against Renu Singh education department in Kolkata. The department had withheld pensionary dues for five years after superannuation, citing an unfinalized preliminary audit objection dating back fifteen years. The court referred to the landmark rulings in State of Jharkhand v Jitendra Kumar Srivastava holding that pension is not a bounty but a constitutional property under Article 300A which cannot be withheld without statutory authority. The court observed that an employee cannot be deprived of livelihood in old age based on stale and unadjudicated administrative inquiries. The court held that withholding pension without authority of law violates constitutional guarantees, and therefore the writ petition is allowed with nine percent interest.

title: Ramesh Malhotra v. Nitin Tripathi
text_content: The petitioner Ramesh Malhotra approached the Madras High Court in the year 2022 seeking enforcement and recovery of accumulated maintenance arrears of Rs 747000 awarded by the Family Court at Patna against Nitin Tripathi. The petitioner submitted that the husband had wilfully failed to pay monthly maintenance for over two years despite coercive recovery notices and attachment warrants issued under Industrial Disputes Act. The respondent husband pleaded business insolvency and offered to liquidate the arrears in nominal monthly instalments of negligible value. The court scrutinized the husband's company accounts, credit card statements, and recent foreign travel expenditures. The court observed that deliberate refusal to comply with maintenance orders cannot be tolerated, as it defeats the benevolent purpose of the statute. The court held that coercive measures including attachment of bank accounts and civil imprisonment must follow upon continued default, and therefore the execution petition is allowed.

title: Rekha Bhatia v. Dinesh Shah
text_content: The petitioner father Rekha Bhatia instituted guardianship and custody proceedings under the Guardians and Wards Act against the respondent mother Dinesh Shah before the Family Court at Surat in the year 2022. The petitioner sought permanent custody of the minor child aged eight years, contending that he was better equipped financially and emotionally to cater to the child's premier schooling and extracurricular development with an annual income of Rs 300000. The respondent mother opposed custody, asserting that she had been the primary caregiver since birth, that the father had remained detached due to extensive corporate travel, and that the child's tender age demanded maternal care and stability under Transfer of Property Act. The Madras High Court conducted an interactive session in chambers with the minor child and considered the detailed home evaluation report submitted by the court welfare officer. The court observed that in custody disputes, the welfare of the child is the paramount consideration, overriding financial superiority of one parent over the other. The court held that custody should remain with the mother while granting extensive weekend visitation rights to the father, and therefore the petition is disposed of.

title: Ajay Verma v. Kavita Patel
text_content: The petitioner Ajay Verma filed a habeas corpus writ petition before the Madras High Court in the year 2022 alleging that his minor child was being illegally detained by the respondent maternal grandparents Kavita Patel in Nagpur following the tragic demise of the child's mother. The petitioner asserted that as the surviving biological father, he was the natural guardian under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act and entitled to immediate custody. The grandparents resisted the petition, arguing that the father had neglected the mother during her prolonged terminal illness and pointed out that the child had resided exclusively with them since infancy. The court examined the scope of habeas corpus in custody matters and reiterated that natural guardianship must yield to the welfare of the minor. The court observed that a sudden change of custody from loving grandparents would cause severe emotional trauma to the young child. The court held that interim custody shall remain with the grandparents pending final decision by the Family Court, and therefore the writ petition is dismissed.

title: Usha Mishra v. Dinesh Malhotra
text_content: The petitioner citizen Usha Mishra approached the Madras High Court in the year 2022 invoking Article 226 of the Constitution of India to challenge a summary demolition order issued by the municipal development authority Dinesh Malhotra in Agra. The authority had arrived with bulldozers and demolished the petitioner's residential premises and commercial shop without serving any prior statutory show-cause notice, without affording an opportunity of hearing, and without allowing time to seek judicial redress, alleging that the structure was an illegal encroachment on public land. The petitioner proved registered ownership deeds, continuous property tax receipts dating back thirty years, and asserted gross violation of Article 21. The municipal authority contended that encroachments on public pathways could be removed summarily without prior notice under Indian Penal Code. The court examined the constitutional jurisprudence on shelter as an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21 and the necessity of procedural fairness. The court observed that executive bulldozing of homes without notice and hearing is completely antithetical to the rule of law and constitutional governance. The court held that the demolition was unlawful and unconstitutional, and therefore directed restitution, interim compensation of Rs 72000, and allowed the petition.

title: Anita Tripathi v. Geeta Kumar
text_content: The public interest litigation was instituted by the environmental action group Anita Tripathi before the Madras High Court in the year 2022 seeking urgent judicial intervention against the rampant discharge of untreated toxic industrial effluents into the sacred river basin traversing Delhi. The petitioners submitted certified water laboratory reports demonstrating that the chemical industrial cluster operated by Geeta Kumar was releasing carcinogenic heavy metals and untreated chemical waste directly into the river, contaminating the drinking water supply of two million residents and destroying aquatic fauna. The industrial respondents argued that they had installed effluent treatment plants and contended that stringent judicial directions would cause closure of industries employing thousands of industrial workers under Transfer of Property Act. The court appointed an independent court commissioner comprising scientists from the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute and examined the ground data. The court applied the polluter pays principle and the precautionary principle enshrined under Article 21 and international environmental jurisprudence. The court held that industrial profits cannot take precedence over the fundamental right to clean water and public health, and therefore the PIL is allowed with directions.

title: Renu Gupta v. Rekha Tripathi
text_content: The State prosecuted the accused appellant Renu Gupta for committing the offence of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code arising out of an incident that occurred at Mumbai in the year 2024. The prosecution alleged that due to longstanding animosity over partition of ancestral land, the accused assaulted the deceased with a lethal sharp-edged weapon, intentionally inflicting fatal injuries. The prosecution examined eyewitnesses including Rekha Tripathi, whose testimony was corroborated by the post-mortem report confirming that the cranial injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The defence contended that the incident occurred during a sudden fight without premeditation, argued that the witnesses were interested family members, and pleaded that the offence at most attracted Exception 4 of Section 300 punishable under Section 304 Part I of Indian Contract Act. The Madras High Court meticulously analysed the medical evidence, the nature of weapon employed, and the multiplicity of brutal blows directed at vital body parts. The court noted that the repeated infliction of forceful blows on the head ruled out any plea of sudden fight or absence of intention to kill. The court held that the prosecution has established the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore the conviction is confirmed and the appeal is dismissed.

title: Pooja Pandey v. Ramesh Patel
text_content: The petitioner Pooja Pandey preferred this petition under Section 482 of CrPC before the Madras High Court seeking to quash criminal proceedings pending in Bhopal in the year 2024. The respondent Ramesh Patel had alleged that the petitioner, acting as an independent valuer, had prepared an inflated valuation report under Arbitration and Conciliation Act facilitating credit facilities of Rs 198000. Learned counsel for the petitioner argued that the petitioner was an independent professional who acted bona fide on the basis of documents supplied by the bank and contended that no criminal mens rea could be imputed to professional opinion. The investigating agency opposed the plea, claiming that the valuation report omitted crucial encumbrances on the mortgaged property. The court carefully perused the chargesheet, witness statements, and guidelines governing professional valuation standards. The court observed that professional negligence, even if established, does not ipso facto translate into criminal conspiracy or fraud without culpable knowledge. The court held that the criminal prosecution against the professional valuer cannot be sustained, and therefore the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Kavita Agarwal v. Vikas Saxena
text_content: In this criminal appeal under the Domestic Violence Act, the appellant husband Vikas Saxena assailed the monetary relief order passed by the magistrate in Surat in the year 2024 directing him to pay Rs 54000 per month towards alternative rented accommodation for aggrieved wife Kavita Agarwal. The appellant contended that the wife was residing with her affluent parents and suffered no financial distress, arguing that the award was punitive. Learned counsel for the wife submitted that under Section 19(1)(f) of Indian Contract Act, the magistrate possesses explicit statutory power to direct the respondent to secure the same level of alternative accommodation for the aggrieved person as enjoyed in the shared household. The Madras High Court evaluated the lifestyle of the husband, the rental value of residential premises in Surat, and the legislative object of the enactment. The court found that the monetary provision for alternative accommodation was strictly in accordance with statutory guidelines and proportional to the respondent's income. The court therefore held that the order of the magistrate is unassailable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the order is confirmed.

title: Meera Agarwal v. Asha Srivastava
text_content: The complainant Meera Agarwal filed an application under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 against her husband and in-laws Asha Srivastava before the Metropolitan Magistrate at Bhopal in the year 2024. The complainant alleged that throughout her marital life, she was subjected to persistent physical assaults, verbal degradation, and economic deprivation, culminating in her being locked out of the shared household. The complainant sought statutory protection orders, a residence order under Section 19 to reside in the shared matrimonial home, and monetary relief of Rs 147000. The respondents contested the complaint, asserting that the shared household was the exclusive self-acquired property of the mother-in-law where the complainant had no legal right, and denied all allegations of domestic abuse as fabricated. The Madras High Court examined the Domestic Incident Report submitted by the Protection Officer, medical emergency room slips, and the Supreme Court ruling in Satish Chander Ahuja. The court observed that the definition of shared household encompasses any house where the aggrieved woman has lived in a domestic relationship irrespective of ownership. The court held that the complainant is entitled to reside in the shared household and receive maintenance, and therefore the domestic violence application is allowed.

title: Priya Patel v. Sunita Singh
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the State Government through Sunita Singh challenged the judgment of the High Court at Chennai in the year 2024 which struck down statutory provisions restricting the right of minority religious trusts represented by Priya Patel to appoint headmasters and teaching faculty. The State contended that setting up a state selection commission for all government-aided schools was necessary to maintain uniform pedagogical excellence under Industrial Disputes Act. Learned counsel for the minority institution submitted that the choice of headmaster is the key to administering an educational institution and preserving its ethos. The Madras High Court examined the distinction between regulatory measures promoting educational standards and administrative interference destroying institutional autonomy. The court found that divesting minority managements of the power to appoint principal faculty alters the core character of the institution. The court therefore held that the statutory restriction infringes Article 30(1) of the Constitution, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Sanjay Malhotra v. Prakash Verma
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the State authority Prakash Verma challenged the judgment of the High Court at Lucknow in the year 2024 which declared a state policy discriminating against transgender persons in public employment as violative of Articles 14 and 16 in a challenge by Sanjay Malhotra. The appellant contended that service recruitment rules under Transfer of Property Act historically recognized only binary gender categories and pleaded administrative convenience. Learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the landmark Supreme Court ruling in NALSA v Union of India and argued that denying public employment on the ground of gender identity violates fundamental equality and personal autonomy under Articles 14, 19, and 21. The Madras High Court examined the constitutional framework of substantive equality and reviewed the statutory provisions of the Transgender Persons Act. The court observed that administrative convenience can never be an acceptable justification for perpetuating institutional discrimination against marginalized citizens. The court therefore held that exclusion of transgender citizens from public employment is unconstitutional, and accordingly the State's appeal is dismissed.

title: Rohit Pandey v. Asha Tripathi
text_content: The complainant Rohit Pandey filed a consumer complaint against the manufacturer and authorized dealer Asha Tripathi before the District Consumer Commission at Kolkata in the year 2015 alleging manufacturing defect in a brand-new commercial heavy vehicle. The complainant stated that he had purchased the vehicle for Rs 47000 to earn his livelihood through self-employment, but within three weeks of delivery, the vehicle experienced repeated engine seizures, transmission failures, and structural chassis alignment defects requiring twelve visits to the authorized workshop. The manufacturer resisted liability, contending that the defects arose from rough driving conditions, overloading, and failure to observe periodic maintenance schedules under Indian Penal Code, and maintained that under the warranty terms, the customer was only entitled to free component replacement rather than vehicle replacement. The Maharashtra SCDRC referred the vehicle for forensic mechanical testing to a recognized government engineering institute under Section 13(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act. The expert report confirmed that the engine block suffered from metallurgical porosity and inherent manufacturing flaws incapable of rectification. The court held that the product suffers from an irreparable manufacturing defect, and therefore directed replacement with a new vehicle or refund with interest.

title: Sachin Rastogi v. Rajesh Sharma
text_content: In this consumer revision petition, the manufacturing company Rajesh Sharma challenged the order of the State Commission at Nagpur in the year 2017 directing recall and refund of an electronic appliance valued at Rs 2000000 sold to consumer Sachin Rastogi. The manufacturer contended that the device had functioned satisfactorily for six months before the breakdown and argued that the customer had tampered with internal circuitry through unauthorized local technicians. Learned counsel for the consumer produced job cards demonstrating that authorized technicians had visited the premises five times and had replaced the motherboard twice without successfully resolving intermittent overheating and sudden short-circuits. The Maharashtra SCDRC reviewed the warranty conditions, service logs, and statutory product liability provisions under the Consumer Protection Act. The court observed that repeated failure of primary components within the warranty period establishes that the product is inherently defective and unsafe. The court therefore held that the consumer is entitled to complete refund with compensation, and accordingly the revision petition is dismissed.

title: Priya Mishra v. Anita Tiwari
text_content: The complainant Priya Mishra instituted a consumer complaint against the respondent insurance company Anita Tiwari before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Jaipur in the year 2017 challenging the wrongful repudiation of a fire and special perils insurance claim. The complainant stated that his industrial textile warehouse situated in Jaipur was insured for Rs 152000 and suffered catastrophic destruction in an accidental electrical short-circuit fire. The independent surveyor appointed by the insurer assessed the net loss at Rs 152000, yet the insurance company repudiated the entire claim on the pretext that the insured had failed to maintain operational fire hydrants in alleged breach of policy warranty under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The complainant proved that all fire safety inspections had been conducted, fire department clearances were current, and the fire brigade had certified the accidental cause. The Maharashtra SCDRC scrutinized the survey report, the fire department findings, and the terms of the insurance contract. The court observed that insurance contracts cannot be repudiated on technical and hyper-critical interpretations of ancillary warranties where loss is genuine and accidental. The court held that the repudiation of the insurance claim is arbitrary and unlawful, and therefore directed the insurer to pay the assessed claim amount with interest.

title: Mahesh Chaturvedi v. Asha Mishra
text_content: In this consumer appeal, the appellant real estate developer Asha Mishra challenged the order of the State Commission at Mumbai in the year 2019 directing delayed possession compensation to homebuyer Mahesh Chaturvedi. The developer argued that the buyer had agreed to contractual compensation of five rupees per square foot per month under the standard allotment agreement, and contended that the consumer court had no jurisdiction to award higher statutory interest rates. Learned counsel for the homebuyer submitted that standard pre-printed builder contracts are one-sided adhesion contracts wherein the developer charges eighteen percent for payment defaults while providing nominal pennies for years of delivery delay. The Maharashtra SCDRC examined the doctrine of unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act and reviewed Supreme Court precedents on unconscionable contractual clauses. The court observed that one-sided penalty clauses in builder agreements constitute unfair trade practices and are not binding on consumer adjudicators. The court therefore held that the allottee is entitled to reasonable interest for prolonged delay, and accordingly the builder's appeal is dismissed.

title: Vimla Srivastava v. Kamla Singh

title: Sarla Saxena v. Nirmala Agarwal
text_content: In this consumer appeal, the appellant banking institution Nirmala Agarwal challenged the order of the District Consumer Commission at Pune in the year 2019 which awarded compensation to consumer Sarla Saxena for wrongful dishonour of commercial cheques. The bank contended that the cheque dishonour was occasioned by a routine technical migration to a new core banking platform and argued that no mala fide intent or actionable deficiency in service was present. Learned counsel for the consumer established that on the relevant date, the complainant had clear unencumbered liquid funds of Rs 5002000 in the account, and demonstrated that wrongful dishonour severely tarnished the commercial reputation and credit rating of the consumer in local business circles. The Maharashtra SCDRC examined the statutory duties of bankers under Hindu Marriage Act and evaluated the damages suffered by the business proprietor. The court observed that wrongful dishonour of a cheque despite sufficient balance strikes at the commercial credibility of a business and constitutes deficiency per se. The court therefore held that the compensation awarded by the forum is justified, and accordingly the bank's appeal is dismissed.

title: Mahesh Mehta v. Pooja Malhotra
text_content: The flat buyer complainant Mahesh Mehta instituted a consumer complaint against the respondent real estate developer Pooja Malhotra before the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Surat in the year 2019. The complainant averred that he had booked a residential luxury apartment in the builder's flagship township project, paying a total consideration of Rs 998000 against agreed construction-linked milestones. Under the registered builder-buyer agreement, the developer had promised handover of vacant physical possession with occupancy certificate within thirty-six months. However, seven years had elapsed, and the project remained deserted in a half-constructed shell state without basic infrastructure. The developer resisted the complaint, attributing delay to force majeure circumstances including shortage of construction raw materials, judicial bans on groundwater extraction, and municipal delays in approving revised layout plans under Hindu Marriage Act. The Maharashtra SCDRC examined the milestone certificates, photographic evidence, and the settled law laid down in Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure v Govindan Raghavan. The court observed that an allottee cannot be made to wait indefinitely for possession and is fully entitled to seek refund of entire principal with interest. The court held that the builder's failure to deliver timely possession constitutes deficiency in service, and therefore directed full refund with interest and allowed the complaint.

title: Vijay Tripathi v. Naresh Malhotra
text_content: In this consumer appeal, the appellant telecom company Naresh Malhotra challenged the order of the District Commission at Lucknow in the year 2020 awarding damages to consumer Vijay Tripathi for unauthorised activation of paid value-added services. The appellant argued that value-added caller tune services were activated via a valid interactive voice response prompt generated from the subscriber's handset and contended that billing of Rs 197000 was lawful. Learned counsel for the subscriber proved that no explicit double consent was obtained as mandated by Telecom Regulatory Authority of India guidelines, and showed that despite multiple cancellation requests sent via SMS and email, the telecom operator continued deducting daily charges for six consecutive months. The Maharashtra SCDRC scrutinized the electronic call logs, the TRAI circulars regarding consumer consent architecture, and the billing statements. The court found that the service was activated without verifiable dual confirmation and billed in direct defiance of regulatory directives. The court therefore held that activating unauthorized chargeable services constitutes unfair trade practice, and accordingly the telecom appeal is dismissed.

title: Anita Khanna v. Mahesh Tripathi
text_content: The complainant Anita Khanna instituted a consumer complaint alleging gross medical negligence against the respondent multispecialty hospital and operating surgeon Mahesh Tripathi before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Nagpur in the year 2021. The complainant claimed compensation of Rs 1503000 stating that during an elective abdominal surgery, the surgical team negligently left a surgical mop inside the peritoneal cavity, leading to severe sepsis, peritonitis, multiple corrective emergency laparotomies, and prolonged ICU hospitalization. The hospital and doctors denied negligence, contending that they had followed standard surgical protocols and argued that postoperative complications were inherent risks of major abdominal interventions under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The Maharashtra SCDRC called for an independent expert evaluation from a premier government medical college board and examined the surgical theater swab count charts. The court applied the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur and evaluated the duty of care under the classical Bolam and Bolitho standards of medical negligence. The court observed that leaving foreign surgical instruments inside a patient's body constitutes incontrovertible medical negligence that speaks for itself. The court held that the hospital and operating surgeon are jointly and severally liable, and therefore awarded substantial compensation and allowed the complaint.

title: Asha Mishra v. Amit Sharma
text_content: The complainant Asha Mishra approached the Maharashtra SCDRC in the year 2021 alleging unfair trade practice and deficiency in service against Amit Sharma bank for failing to return original title deeds of residential property mortgaged for a housing loan in Mumbai. The complainant established that he had fully repaid the entire housing loan along with interest amounting to Rs 203000 and obtained a formal no-dues certificate, yet the bank failed to return the original registered sale deeds, subsequently admitting that the documents were misplaced from the central repository. The bank offered token compensation of five thousand rupees and suggested obtaining certified copies from the sub-registrar office at bank expense. The court observed that loss of original title deeds permanently impairs the marketability and resale value of real estate and causes extreme mental agony. The court held that losing property documents is gross negligence and deficiency in service, and therefore awarded substantial compensation and allowed the complaint.

title: Nirmala Kumar v. Meera Kumar
text_content: In this consumer revision petition, the petitioner insurance company Meera Kumar assailed the order of the State Commission at Indore in the year 2022 directing payment of a health insurance mediclaim of Rs 103000 to policyholder Nirmala Kumar. The insurer contended that the policyholder had suppressed pre-existing hypertension and diabetes at the time of proposal inception, thereby violating the fundamental doctrine of uberrima fides under Income Tax Act. Learned counsel for the insured demonstrated that the hospital admission was for an emergency surgical procedure relating to acute fracture sustained in an accidental fall, which had zero causal nexus with the alleged lifestyle conditions. The Maharashtra SCDRC examined the medical discharge summary, the proposal form, and the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Manmohan Nanda v United India Assurance. The court observed that every common lifestyle condition cannot be classified as a material pre-existing disease to repudiate unrelated emergency medical claims. The court therefore held that the repudiation was unjustified and amounts to deficiency in service, and accordingly the revision petition is dismissed.

title: Usha Kapoor v. Ramesh Sharma
text_content: In this consumer appeal, the appellant nursing home Ramesh Sharma challenged the judgment of the District Consumer Commission at Agra in the year 2015 which found the hospital guilty of medical negligence in the treatment of newborn infant Usha Kapoor. The appellant argued that the newborn suffered from congenital retinopathy of prematurity and contended that the attending pediatricians had provided optimal care within the limits of medical science. Learned counsel for the complainant demonstrated that the hospital failed to arrange mandatory ophthalmological screening of the premature infant within thirty days of birth as mandated by national neonatology protocols, resulting in irreversible total blindness. The NCDRC reviewed the clinical case sheets, neonatology guidelines, and expert medical testimony. The court found that omission to conduct timely ROP screening of a high-risk premature infant was a clear breach of medical duty directly causing vision loss. The court therefore held that deficiency in medical care stands established beyond doubt, and accordingly the hospital's appeal is dismissed.

title: Renu Mishra v. Vikas Singh
text_content: The complainant business enterprise Renu Mishra filed a consumer complaint against Vikas Singh broadband and leased-line internet provider in Pune in the year 2019. The complainant had subscribed to a dedicated high-speed optical fiber leased line guaranteeing 99.9% uptime for commercial software exports. The complainant established that the leased line remained completely inoperative for eighteen consecutive days due to uncoordinated roadside cable severance, resulting in contractual penalties from foreign clients amounting to Rs 497000. The service provider pleaded force majeure, citing civic road-widening works, and relied on contractual limitation of liability clauses restricting damages to rental credits. The court examined the Service Level Agreement, the restoration logs, and the principles governing exemption clauses in consumer contracts under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The court observed that prolonged failure to restore commercial connectivity without arranging alternative routing cannot be excused under force majeure. The court held that the service provider is liable for commercial deficiency, and therefore the complaint is allowed with compensatory damages.

title: Rajesh Bhatia v. Nitin Verma
text_content: The complainant association of apartment owners Rajesh Bhatia filed a class-action consumer complaint against Nitin Verma builder in Indore in the year 2021. The allottees alleged that the builder had illegally converted designated common green areas and community clubhouse spaces into commercial retail shops valued at Rs 49000 in brazen violation of the sanctioned master plan and brochures. The developer contended that the agreement empowered the promoter to carry out modifications and revisions in building plans until final completion. The court examined the original sanctioned layout, the RERA registration disclosures, and the statutory obligations of promoters under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The court found that unilateral alterations of common amenities without two-thirds consent of allottees is completely prohibited by law. The court held that the developer must demolish commercial encroachments and restore common facilities, and therefore the complaint is allowed with punitive costs.

title: Rajesh Verma v. Nitin Mehta
text_content: The plaintiff technology company Rajesh Verma filed a commercial suit against Nitin Mehta in Chennai in the year 2015 claiming damages of Rs 5005000 for breach of a software development and master service agreement. The plaintiff established that the defendant had failed to meet core milestone deliverables and had abruptly abandoned software integration midway through the rollout phase. The defendant resisted the claim, alleging that the plaintiff had repeatedly modified project specifications and delayed approval of user acceptance testing under Consumer Protection Act. The court analyzed the sprint logs, email correspondence, and the report of an independent technical assessor. The court observed that unilateral abandonment of software commitments without following contractual cure notice procedures constitutes material breach. The court held that the plaintiff is entitled to recover advance milestone payments and consequential damages, and therefore the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

title: Lata Verma v. Prakash Joshi
text_content: In this commercial first appeal, the appellant debtor Prakash Joshi challenged the decree of recovery passed by the Commercial Division at Vadodara in the year 2016 in favour of supplier Lata Verma. The appellant contended that the trial court erred in holding that limitation was extended by an informal email correspondence and argued that an unverified electronic email does not constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt in writing under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. Learned counsel for the respondent supplier produced electronic audit certificates under Section 65B of the Evidence Act proving that the email admitting the liability of Rs 1500000 was dispatched by the authorized chief financial officer of the appellant before the expiry of the original limitation period. The NCLT Mumbai examined the statutory requirements of Section 18 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act in the context of modern electronic commercial communications. The court observed that digital communications admitting subsisting financial obligations satisfy the criteria of written acknowledgment extending limitation. The court therefore held that the recovery suit was filed well within limitation, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Rajesh Chopra v. Mahesh Saxena
text_content: The plaintiff banking corporation Rajesh Chopra instituted a summary suit under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure against borrower Mahesh Saxena before the Commercial Court at Ahmedabad in the year 2017. The plaintiff claimed recovery of a commercial term debt of Rs 255000 founded upon promissory notes, loan agreements, and continuing personal guarantee deeds. The plaintiff stated that the borrower had availed credit facilities and committed chronic payment defaults. The defendant sought unconditional leave to defend, contending that the suit was barred by limitation under Indian Contract Act, asserting that the bank had charged excessive penal interest rates, and disputing the validity of balance confirmation slips. The NCLT Mumbai examined the loan documentation, the ledger extracts certified under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, and written acknowledgments of debt. The court applied the principles in IDBI Trusteeship Services v Hubtown regarding leave to defend in summary suits. The court found that the defense raised was completely moonshine and lacked any bona fide triable issue of law or fact. The court held that the plaintiff is entitled to judgment forthwith, and therefore leave to defend is refused and the summary suit is decreed for the entire sum.

title: Ramesh Patel v. Rekha Tripathi
text_content: The plaintiff franchise operator Ramesh Patel instituted a commercial suit against the franchisor corporate brand Rekha Tripathi before the Commercial Court at Jaipur in the year 2017 seeking damages of Rs 80000 for wrongful termination of a multi-unit franchise agreement. The plaintiff stated that pursuant to the master franchise agreement, he had invested massive capital in leasing prime commercial retail properties, procuring specialized kitchen equipment, and advertising the brand across the metropolitan region of Jaipur. The plaintiff alleged that the franchisor abruptly issued a termination notice without providing the mandatory sixty-day cure period stipulated in the contract, and simultaneously opened company-owned direct retail outlets within the plaintiff's exclusive protected territorial radius under Transfer of Property Act. The defendant franchisor contended that the franchisee had committed incurable quality control breaches by sourcing local ingredients without master brand approval. The NCLT Mumbai examined the inspection reports, audit notices, and the express territorial exclusivity clauses of the agreement. The court found that the franchisor had acted mala fide to seize the established commercial clientele without affording statutory opportunity to cure. The court held that the termination is wrongful and in breach of negative covenant, and therefore the suit is decreed for substantial damages with interest.

title: Sarla Gupta v. Dinesh Joshi
text_content: In this commercial appeal, the appellant contractor Dinesh Joshi challenged the decree of damages passed in favour of project owner Sarla Gupta by the Commercial Division of the High Court at Kolkata in the year 2017. The appellant contended that the project owner had contributed to construction delays by failing to provide unencumbered site access, delayed architectural drawings, and argued that the liquidated damages clause of Rs 1498000 was a punitive penalty unenforceable under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act without proof of actual pecuniary loss. Learned counsel for the respondent project owner demonstrated that the contractual completion schedule was agreed as essential, that site access was timely provided, and pointed out that the liquidated damages represented a genuine pre-estimate of loss incurred due to delayed commercial operations. The NCLT Mumbai reviewed the landmark principles laid down in Kailash Nath Associates v DDA regarding liquidated damages under Section 74. The court found that the pre-estimated liquidated damages were reasonable and commensurate with the commercial loss suffered by the owner. The court therefore held that the contractor is liable for contractual delay damages, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Ravi Rastogi v. Vijay Kumar
text_content: The petitioner Ravi Rastogi approached the NCLT Mumbai in the year 2017 seeking to set aside a foreign arbitral award under Section 48 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act in enforcement proceedings initiated by foreign supplier Vijay Kumar in Chennai. The award had granted commercial dues of Rs 76000. The petitioner contended that the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties because the arbitral institution had appointed a sole arbitrator in violation of the contractually mandated three-arbitrator clause. The respondent submitted that institutional rules to which the parties had agreed provided for sole arbitrator appointment in expedited commercial cases. The court examined the arbitration agreement, institutional rules, and the strict grounds for refusing enforcement of New York Convention awards under Industrial Disputes Act.
