The court observed that where parties agree to institutional arbitration, the institutional procedural rules govern the composition of the arbitral tribunal. The court held that the tribunal was validly constituted in accordance with agreed rules, and therefore the objections are rejected and enforcement is allowed.

title: Anita Chopra v. Meera Dwivedi
text_content: The plaintiff banking corporation Anita Chopra instituted a summary suit under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure against borrower Meera Dwivedi before the Commercial Court at Coimbatore in the year 2017. The plaintiff claimed recovery of a commercial term debt of Rs 55000 founded upon promissory notes, loan agreements, and continuing personal guarantee deeds. The plaintiff stated that the borrower had availed credit facilities and committed chronic payment defaults. The defendant sought unconditional leave to defend, contending that the suit was barred by limitation under Income Tax Act, asserting that the bank had charged excessive penal interest rates, and disputing the validity of balance confirmation slips. The NCLT Mumbai examined the loan documentation, the ledger extracts certified under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, and written acknowledgments of debt. The court applied the principles in IDBI Trusteeship Services v Hubtown regarding leave to defend in summary suits. The court found that the defense raised was completely moonshine and lacked any bona fide triable issue of law or fact. The court held that the plaintiff is entitled to judgment forthwith, and therefore leave to defend is refused and the summary suit is decreed for the entire sum.

title: Priya Mishra v. Ramesh Sharma
text_content: The plaintiff corporate enterprise Priya Mishra instituted a commercial suit for breach of contract and recovery of liquidated damages against the defendant supplier Ramesh Sharma before the Commercial Court at Indore in the year 2018. The plaintiff stated that the parties had entered into a binding long-term commercial supply agreement for high-grade industrial alloys, whereunder the defendant was obligated to deliver scheduled monthly consignments. Upon a sudden surge in global commodity market prices, the defendant repudiated the contract and failed to supply raw materials, forcing the plaintiff to procure substitute merchandise from spot markets at exorbitant premiums to fulfill international export commitments, incurring damages of Rs 1496000. The defendant contended that the sudden price escalation rendered the contract commercially impracticable and invoked the doctrine of frustration under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act along with force majeure clauses under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The NCLT Mumbai examined the contractual terms, the price variation mechanisms, and the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Energy Watchdog v CERC. The court observed that mere abnormal rise or fall in prices is an ordinary commercial risk that does not frustrate a commercial contract. The court held that the defendant committed a deliberate breach of contract, and therefore the commercial suit is decreed for damages with contractual interest.

title: Kamla Tiwari v. Seema Saxena
text_content: In this commercial arbitration appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, the appellant public undertaking Seema Saxena challenged the judgment of the High Court at Surat in the year 2019 which upheld an arbitral award granted to private contractor Kamla Tiwari. The appellant contended that the sole arbitrator had awarded substantial unliquidated damages of Rs 47000 without any documentary proof of actual loss, and argued that the arbitrator was disqualified under the Seventh Schedule of the Act due to prior professional consultancy relationships. Learned counsel for the contractor demonstrated that the appellant had expressly waived objections under Section 12(5) by participation without protest, and established that the arbitrator had meticulously evaluated chartered accountants' loss certificates. The NCLT Mumbai analyzed the statutory framework of Section 34 and Section 37 of Consumer Protection Act and the limits of appellate interference. The court found that the arbitrator's evaluation of commercial losses was grounded upon credible evidence and within arbitral jurisdiction. The court therefore held that no ground for setting aside the arbitral award is established, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Renu Khanna v. Manju Agarwal
text_content: The plaintiff franchise operator Renu Khanna instituted a commercial suit against the franchisor corporate brand Manju Agarwal before the Commercial Court at Kanpur in the year 2019 seeking damages of Rs 53000 for wrongful termination of a multi-unit franchise agreement. The plaintiff stated that pursuant to the master franchise agreement, he had invested massive capital in leasing prime commercial retail properties, procuring specialized kitchen equipment, and advertising the brand across the metropolitan region of Kanpur. The plaintiff alleged that the franchisor abruptly issued a termination notice without providing the mandatory sixty-day cure period stipulated in the contract, and simultaneously opened company-owned direct retail outlets within the plaintiff's exclusive protected territorial radius under Indian Contract Act. The defendant franchisor contended that the franchisee had committed incurable quality control breaches by sourcing local ingredients without master brand approval. The NCLT Mumbai examined the inspection reports, audit notices, and the express territorial exclusivity clauses of the agreement. The court found that the franchisor had acted mala fide to seize the established commercial clientele without affording statutory opportunity to cure. The court held that the termination is wrongful and in breach of negative covenant, and therefore the suit is decreed for substantial damages with interest.

title: Kamla Bhatia v. Suresh Agarwal
text_content: The financial creditor financial institution Kamla Bhatia filed an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 before the National Company Law Tribunal at Chennai in the year 2020 seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the corporate debtor Suresh Agarwal. The financial creditor established that it had disbursed a consortium credit facility of Rs 301000 for constructing an industrial manufacturing plant, and demonstrated that the corporate debtor had committed continuous payment defaults exceeding the statutory threshold of one crore rupees, with default conclusively proved by the record of default certified by the Information Utility (NeSL). The corporate debtor resisted admission, contending that default was occasioned by macroeconomic factors, arguing that the loan agreement was unstamped under Negotiable Instruments Act, and asserting that ongoing debt restructuring negotiations precluded the initiation of corporate insolvency. The NCLT Mumbai examined the landmark Supreme Court judgments in Innoventive Industries and Swiss Ribbons. The court observed that under Section 7, the adjudicating authority is only required to satisfy itself whether a financial debt exists and default has occurred. The court held that debt and default stand indisputably established, and therefore the Section 7 petition is admitted and moratorium is declared.

title: Kavita Verma v. Sarla Kumar
text_content: The plaintiff non-banking finance company Kavita Verma filed a commercial recovery suit against Sarla Kumar in Kanpur in the year 2022 seeking recovery of unpaid equipment lease rentals of Rs 74000. The plaintiff established that the defendant had taken industrial machinery on hire-purchase, defaulted on instalments, and retained the equipment without paying hire charges. The defendant contended that the machinery was defective and alleged that the finance company was in breach of an oral warranty to provide maintenance under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court examined the lease agreement which clearly stipulated that the finance company was merely a financer without liability for mechanical maintenance. The court found that the defendant had signed unconditional delivery acceptance certificates acknowledging satisfactory operational condition. The court held that the borrower cannot evade repayment obligations by asserting unverified defects, and therefore the suit for recovery is decreed with interest.

title: Prakash Chopra v. Kamla Shah
text_content: In this commercial appeal, the appellant continuing partner Kamla Shah challenged the judgment of the High Court at Hyderabad in the year 2022 which directed valuation and division of firm goodwill in favour of retiring partner Prakash Chopra. The appellant contended that under the partnership deed, a retiring partner was entitled only to the book value of capital contribution without any claim to intangible brand goodwill valued at Rs 150000. Learned counsel for the retiring partner demonstrated that the restrictive clause in the deed applied only to expulsion for misconduct and argued that under Section 55 of the Indian Partnership Act, in settling accounts upon dissolution or retirement, the goodwill of the firm must be included in the assets. The NCLT Mumbai analyzed the partnership agreement, the valuation report of the certified valuer, and the statutory scheme under Indian Penal Code. The court found that the firm's prestigious brand name possessed immense commercial value in which the retiring partner had built equity over thirty years. The court therefore held that the retiring partner is entitled to his proportionate share in goodwill, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Vijay Khanna v. Priya Agarwal
text_content: The applicant Vijay Khanna approached the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2015 seeking regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in connection with an offence registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act in Chennai. The prosecution alleged that during a naka checking operation, law enforcement personnel intercepted a motor vehicle and recovered a commercial quantity of contraband substance weighing substantially above the statutory threshold. Learned counsel for the applicant argued that the mandatory provisions regarding search and seizure under Sections 42 and 50 of Negotiable Instruments Act were violated by the seizing officers and stressed that the applicant had undergone prolonged judicial custody without significant progress in trial. Opposing the plea, learned counsel for the respondent State Priya Agarwal contended that the twin statutory conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act impose an absolute bar against release unless the court forms an opinion that the accused is not guilty and is unlikely to commit any offence while on bail. The court scrutinised the chemical examiner report, seizure panchnama, and custodial records. The court held that the applicant failed to satisfy the twin conditions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act, and therefore bail is refused.

title: Kavita Chaturvedi v. Nirmala Rastogi
text_content: The plaintiff bank Kavita Chaturvedi filed a suit for foreclosure of equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds against the borrower Nirmala Rastogi in Vadodara in the year 2016. The loan amount secured by the title deeds amounted to Rs 101000 disbursed for purchasing commercial printing machinery. The defendant contended that the title deeds were deposited solely for safe custody and disputed the creation of an equitable mortgage, asserting that no memorandum of deposit was registered under the Registration Act. The Punjab & Haryana High Court examined Section 58(f) of Central Goods and Services Tax Act which recognizes mortgages by deposit of title deeds in specified commercial cities without requiring compulsory registration. The court reviewed the letter of intent, original title deeds produced from bank custody, and the borrower's contemporaneous letters acknowledging the mortgage. The court observed that delivery of title deeds with intent to create security constitutes a valid equitable mortgage under Indian law. The court therefore held that a valid mortgage exists and the bank is entitled to recover its dues, and accordingly the suit is decreed with preliminary decree.

title: Sachin Chaturvedi v. Manju Tripathi
text_content: The plaintiff financial institution Sachin Chaturvedi instituted a mortgage suit for foreclosure and sale of hypothecated immovable property against the defendant mortgagor Manju Tripathi before the civil court at Lucknow in the year 2016. The plaintiff stated that the defendant had borrowed a commercial term loan facility of Rs 4998000 and executed a registered simple mortgage deed over his prime commercial building to secure repayment with agreed interest. Upon persistent default in servicing quarterly interest instalments, the loan account was classified as non-performing and statutory recall notices were dispatched. The defendant contested the foreclosure suit, claiming that the penal interest rates charged by the mortgagee were usurious, asserting that the bank had failed to adjust insurance proceeds following a warehouse fire, and seeking extension of the equity of redemption under Code of Criminal Procedure. The Punjab & Haryana High Court examined the loan sanction letter, registered mortgage deed, audited account statements, and the provisions of Order XXXIV of the Code of Civil Procedure. The court found that the mortgage debt remained unpaid despite valid demand and noted that interest was computed in conformity with contractual terms. The court held that the mortgagee is entitled to realize its debt through foreclosure, and therefore a preliminary decree for foreclosure and sale is passed.

title: Ajay Kapoor v. Sunita Dwivedi
text_content: The land reference arose out of an acquisition of agricultural holdings in Coimbatore undertaken by the State Government through Sunita Dwivedi for an urban infrastructure corridor in the year 2016. The Land Acquisition Collector had awarded compensation at the rate of Rs 195000 per acre, which the claimant landowners Ajay Kapoor rejected under protest as grossly inadequate compared to prevailing open-market commercial values. The claimants produced registered sale deeds of adjacent parcels executed shortly prior to the Section 4 notification, valuation reports of certified experts, and demonstrated that the acquired land enjoyed immediate potential for high-density residential and industrial development. The acquiring authority opposed enhancement, submitting that the sale instances relied upon pertained to small developed plots which could not serve as comparables for large tracts of undeveloped agricultural land, and demanded a forty percent deduction for developmental expenditure. The Punjab & Haryana High Court analyzed the comparable sale exemplars, the distance from arterial highways, and the development potential under Hindu Marriage Act. The court observed that fair market value must reflect potential value while allowing reasonable deductions for internal roads and amenities. The court held that the compensation awarded by the collector is insufficient and must be enhanced, and therefore the reference petition is allowed with statutory solatium.

title: Rohit Mishra v. Vikas Singh
text_content: The complainant Rohit Mishra instituted criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against Vikas Singh before the trial court in Delhi in the year 2016. The complainant stated that in discharge of a legally enforceable debt, the accused drawer had issued an account payee cheque of Rs 1996000 drawn on a nationalised bank. Upon presentation for encashment through banking channels, the cheque was dishonoured and returned unpaid with the bank memo citing insufficiency of funds. The payee dispatched a statutory notice of demand as mandated by the Negotiable Instruments Act calling upon the drawer to pay within fifteen days. The accused admitted the signatures on the cheque but contended that the instrument had been handed over merely as security and denied the existence of any legally enforceable debt. The Punjab & Haryana High Court examined the documentary evidence including ledger accounts, the cheque return memo, and legal presumptions under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The court held that the accused failed to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and therefore the conviction of the drawer is upheld and the appeal is dismissed.

title: Rohit Chopra v. Priya Agarwal
text_content: The applicant Rohit Chopra approached the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2016 seeking anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apprehending arrest in an investigation registered at Agra. The first information report lodged by Priya Agarwal alleged offences of cheating, criminal breach of trust, and forgery under Industrial Disputes Act involving financial transactions of Rs 201000. Learned counsel for the applicant submitted that the dispute was purely commercial in character stemming from an audit disagreement between corporate partners, that all financial ledgers were already deposited with the authorities, and that the applicant had no previous criminal record. The prosecution opposed the application, submitting that custodial interrogation was essential to trace the end-use of misappropriated capital and uncover secondary bank accounts. The court weighed the constitutional mandate of personal liberty under Article 21 against the societal need for uninhibited crime detection. The court observed that in financial matters based substantially upon accounting records, pre-arrest bail should not be withheld merely for recovery purposes. The court held that the applicant has established a prima facie case for pre-arrest protection, and therefore anticipatory bail is granted with conditions.

title: Vimla Sharma v. Pooja Tiwari
text_content: The plaintiff Vimla Sharma instituted a comprehensive suit for partition and separate possession of ancestral joint family properties against the defendant coparceners Pooja Tiwari before the civil court at Coimbatore in the year 2017. The suit properties comprised agricultural holdings, residential premises, and commercial shops valued at over Rs 1005000. The plaintiff claimed a one-fourth undivided share in all properties, asserting that the joint family had continued undivided and that no formal severance of status had taken place. The defendants resisted partition, contending that a prior oral family settlement had taken place three decades ago followed by separate revenue entries, and argued that certain prime commercial shops were their self-acquired properties funded through independent business revenues rather than HUF nucleus. The Punjab & Haryana High Court scrutinized the ancestral title deeds, mutation records, income tax returns of the Hindu Undivided Family, and oral evidence. The court noted that when ancestral nucleus is established, the burden shifts heavily onto the coparcener asserting self-acquisition to prove independent funds. The court held that the defendants failed to establish prior oral partition or independent acquisition, and therefore a preliminary decree for partition is granted.

title: Rajesh Verma v. Sachin Khanna
text_content: In this regular second appeal, the appellant daughter Rajesh Verma challenged the concurrent judgments of the courts below at Nagpur in the year 2017 which had dismissed her suit for partition against her brothers Sachin Khanna. The courts below had held that the plaintiff was not entitled to coparcenary rights since her father had expired prior to the enactment of the Hindu Succession Amendment Act, 2005. The appellant contended that the landmark Constitution Bench ruling in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma conclusively settled that the amended Section 6 confers coparcenary rights on daughters by birth irrespective of whether the father was alive on the date of amendment. The Punjab & Haryana High Court examined the statutory interpretation of amended Section 6 of Indian Contract Act and reviewed the status of the ancestral properties as of December 2004. The court found that no registered partition deed or final decree of court had been executed prior to the statutory cut-off date. The court therefore held that the daughter is an equal coparcener entitled to an equal share, and accordingly the appeal is allowed and preliminary decree is passed.

title: Sachin Gupta v. Sushma Sharma
text_content: The plaintiff Sachin Gupta filed a civil suit for partition against Sushma Sharma seeking metes and bounds division of an ancestral residential building in Vadodara in the year 2019. Following the preliminary decree determining one-half share each, disputes arose during final decree proceedings regarding the feasibility of physical division of the single compact residential structure. The court commissioner submitted a report stating that dividing the small structure into two separate residential units would render both portions uninhabitable and destroy their economic value. The plaintiff moved an application under the Partition Act seeking public auction of the property and division of sale proceeds, which the defendant opposed. The Punjab & Haryana High Court examined Sections 2 and 3 of Indian Contract Act governing sale in lieu of partition where physical division cannot reasonably be made. The court observed that where metes and bounds partition destroys utility, court-directed sale amongst co-owners or public auction is the sole practical remedy. The court held that the property shall be put to sale with first option to co-sharers, and therefore the final decree application is allowed with directions.

title: Manju Kapoor v. Kamla Gupta
text_content: The petitioner landowners Manju Kapoor approached the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2019 challenging the land acquisition proceedings initiated by the development authority Kamla Gupta in Hyderabad. The petitioners contended that the acquisition notification under Section 192 had lapsed by operation of statutory sunset clauses because the authority failed to pronounce the final award within two years of the declaration under Indian Contract Act. The development authority pleaded that the delay was occasioned by interim status quo orders passed in collateral writ petitions and sought exclusion of time. The court examined the record of earlier litigation, the computation of statutory limitation periods, and the mandatory nature of statutory limitation. The court observed that when the statute prescribes that proceedings shall lapse upon expiry of the stipulated period, courts cannot rewrite the legislative mandate. The court held that the acquisition proceedings have legally lapsed due to non-declaration of award in time, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and acquisition is quashed.

title: Renu Rastogi v. Pooja Chaturvedi
text_content: The plaintiff Renu Rastogi filed a commercial suit for permanent injunction against Pooja Chaturvedi before the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2019 seeking to restrain the defendant from infringing registered trademarks and passing off goods using deceptively similar brand packaging in Ahmedabad. The plaintiff proved long-standing commercial use and substantial advertising expenditure of Rs 75000 establishing immense consumer goodwill in the market. The defendant contended that the disputed mark was generic and descriptive, claiming prior user in a localized rural market prior to the plaintiff's registration. The court evaluated the phonetic, visual, and conceptual similarity between the rival trademarks under Negotiable Instruments Act and assessed the likelihood of public confusion. The court observed that registration confers an exclusive statutory monopoly and noted that the defendant's packaging was a deceptive imitation designed to mislead consumers. The court held that the defendant is guilty of trademark infringement and passing off, and therefore a permanent injunction is granted with compensatory damages.

title: Rajesh Srivastava v. Dinesh Chaturvedi
text_content: This anticipatory bail application under Section 438 of CrPC was moved by Rajesh Srivastava before the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2019 in relation to an FIR registered at Kanpur alleging economic offences under Sections 420 and 409 involving misappropriation of public funds amounting to Rs 205000. The State represented by Dinesh Chaturvedi contended that the applicant was the principal custodian of the government welfare treasury and had orchestrated fictitious payments to non-existent beneficiaries. The applicant asserted that he was merely a subordinate officer who signed disbursement vouchers on instructions of superior administrative authorities and volunteered to surrender his passport and join the probe daily. The court examined the special audit reports, the transaction logs, and the statements of treasury officials implicating the applicant directly. The court observed that economic offences involving large-scale siphoning of public money require thorough custodial examination and unhindered investigation. The court therefore held that the grant of anticipatory bail in such grave economic offences would prejudice investigation, and accordingly the application is dismissed.

title: Kavita Malhotra v. Pushpa Malhotra
text_content: The petitioner Kavita Malhotra approached the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2019 seeking upward revision and enhancement of maintenance under Section 125 CrPC originally awarded by the magistrate in Surat. The petitioner contended that seven years had elapsed since the initial order, educational expenses of the children had quadrupled, and the respondent husband Pushpa Malhotra had received substantial salary increments resulting in an income of Rs 73000. The respondent resisted the enhancement, submitting that his personal living costs had increased and contending that the original order was final and conclusive. The court examined Section 127 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which explicitly empowers courts to alter monthly allowances upon proof of changed circumstances. The court found that the documented increase in the cost of living index together with the respondent's career advancement constituted a decisive change in circumstances. The court therefore held that the wife and children are entitled to enhanced financial support, and accordingly the petition is allowed and maintenance is enhanced.

title: Kamla Yadav v. Meera Joshi
text_content: The petitioner landowners Kamla Yadav approached the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2020 challenging the land acquisition proceedings initiated by the development authority Meera Joshi in Hyderabad. The petitioners contended that the acquisition notification under Section 304 had lapsed by operation of statutory sunset clauses because the authority failed to pronounce the final award within two years of the declaration under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The development authority pleaded that the delay was occasioned by interim status quo orders passed in collateral writ petitions and sought exclusion of time. The court examined the record of earlier litigation, the computation of statutory limitation periods, and the mandatory nature of statutory limitation. The court observed that when the statute prescribes that proceedings shall lapse upon expiry of the stipulated period, courts cannot rewrite the legislative mandate. The court held that the acquisition proceedings have legally lapsed due to non-declaration of award in time, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and acquisition is quashed.

title: Vikas Verma v. Sunita Khanna
text_content: The petitioner Vikas Verma preferred this petition under Section 482 of CrPC before the Punjab & Haryana High Court seeking to quash criminal proceedings pending in Mumbai in the year 2020. The respondent Sunita Khanna had alleged that the petitioner, acting as an independent valuer, had prepared an inflated valuation report under Arbitration and Conciliation Act facilitating credit facilities of Rs 196000. Learned counsel for the petitioner argued that the petitioner was an independent professional who acted bona fide on the basis of documents supplied by the bank and contended that no criminal mens rea could be imputed to professional opinion. The investigating agency opposed the plea, claiming that the valuation report omitted crucial encumbrances on the mortgaged property. The court carefully perused the chargesheet, witness statements, and guidelines governing professional valuation standards. The court observed that professional negligence, even if established, does not ipso facto translate into criminal conspiracy or fraud without culpable knowledge. The court held that the criminal prosecution against the professional valuer cannot be sustained, and therefore the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Deepak Joshi v. Sanjay Rastogi
text_content: In this criminal appeal arising out of proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the appellant Deepak Joshi assailed the concurrent findings of guilt recorded by the appellate court at Vadodara in the year 2020. The respondent payee Sanjay Rastogi had supplied commercial inventory and received an account payee cheque for Rs 76000 towards discharge of the outstanding commercial invoices. Upon presentation to the drawee bank, the instrument was dishonoured with the remark stop payment instructions. A formal statutory notice was served upon the drawer within the prescribed period of limitation, yet the drawer failed to make payment. The appellant drawer claimed that the goods delivered were defective and argued that the statutory presumption had been successfully rebutted. The Punjab & Haryana High Court reviewed the trial court record and noted that the drawer had neither returned the supplied merchandise nor sent any contemporaneous protest communication prior to the dishonour of the negotiable instrument. The court observed that mere oral assertions unsupported by documentary proof cannot displace the statutory presumption operating in favour of the payee. The court therefore held that the complainant has established the existence of a legally enforceable debt, and accordingly the conviction is confirmed.

title: Prakash Khanna v. Anita Dwivedi
text_content: The accused Prakash Khanna faced trial before the Sessions Court at Coimbatore in the year 2021 for committing murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that the accused along with co-accused persons attacked the deceased with iron rods outside a commercial premise. The sole eyewitness Anita Dwivedi identified the accused in court during trial, but admitted in cross-examination that visibility was poor due to night conditions and acknowledged that no test identification parade had been conducted during police investigation. The defence produced independent witnesses establishing that the accused was present at his workplace forty kilometres away at the time of the alleged incident. The Punjab & Haryana High Court scrutinized the dock identification, the absence of prior test identification, and the credible documentary evidence supporting the plea of alibi. The court observed that dock identification made for the first time in court without corroborative test identification is inherently fragile and unsafe to convict. The court held that the accused is entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the accused is acquitted of the charge.

title: Meera Patel v. Anita Kapoor
text_content: In this first appeal, the appellant vendor Anita Kapoor assailed the decree of specific performance granted to purchaser Meera Patel by the civil court in Delhi in the year 2022. The agreement to sell pertained to agricultural land situated in the outskirts of Delhi with consideration amounting to Rs 753000. The appellant argued that the contract had become frustrated and unenforceable due to subsequent notification of the land for industrial development and contended that escalating market valuations rendered the grant of specific performance inequitable under Section 20 of Hindu Marriage Act. Learned counsel for the respondent purchaser submitted that the purchaser had deposited the entire balance consideration in court and insisted that subsequent price inflation cannot be a ground to deny specific relief. The Punjab & Haryana High Court balanced equitable principles with contractual sanctity and reviewed the conduct of the vendor who delayed obtaining requisite revenue clearances. The court observed that a defaulting vendor cannot be permitted to take advantage of his own default and market appreciation during litigation. The court therefore held that the trial court rightly exercised judicial discretion, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Suresh Gupta v. Nitin Mishra
text_content: In this regular civil appeal, the appellant tenant Nitin Mishra challenged the decree of eviction passed in favour of landlord Suresh Gupta by the appellate rent tribunal in Nagpur in the year 2022. The eviction proceedings were grounded upon unauthorised subletting of the demised premises and material impairment of property value under the Rent Control Act. The landlord established that the tenant had parted with exclusive possession of a substantial portion of the premises to a third party without obtaining prior written consent as mandated by Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The tenant argued that the third party was merely an employee and business associate assisting in daily operations and not an unauthorised subtenant. The Punjab & Haryana High Court examined the report of the local commissioner appointed to inspect the premises, the electricity bills, and the partnership agreement. The court found that exclusive commercial control over the subdivided portion was transferred to a stranger without landlord approval. The court therefore held that unlawful subletting stands conclusively established, and accordingly the tenant's appeal is dismissed.

title: Vikas Malhotra v. Manju Joshi
text_content: The revisionist Vikas Malhotra approached the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2023 assailing the conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act recorded by the appellate court in Vadodara. The complainant payee Manju Joshi alleged that the accused had borrowed a friendly financial accommodation of Rs 4995000 and issued a cheque towards the discharge of the said legally enforceable debt. The cheque on presentation was dishonoured and returned by the banker due to account closed by drawer. The statutory notice of demand was dispatched by registered post with acknowledgement due and was returned with postal endorsement of refusal. The drawer contended that he had lost the signed blank cheque and claimed that the statutory notice was never tendered to him. The court referred to settled judicial precedents holding that endorsement of refusal constitutes valid tender and deemed service under the General Clauses Act. The court observed that no police complaint was ever lodged regarding the alleged loss of the negotiable instrument. The court held that the accused drawer is guilty of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and therefore the petition is dismissed.

title: Dinesh Singh v. Sachin Agarwal
text_content: This anticipatory bail application under Section 438 of CrPC was moved by Dinesh Singh before the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the year 2023 in relation to an FIR registered at Bhopal alleging economic offences under Sections 420 and 409 involving misappropriation of public funds amounting to Rs 78000. The State represented by Sachin Agarwal contended that the applicant was the principal custodian of the government welfare treasury and had orchestrated fictitious payments to non-existent beneficiaries. The applicant asserted that he was merely a subordinate officer who signed disbursement vouchers on instructions of superior administrative authorities and volunteered to surrender his passport and join the probe daily. The court examined the special audit reports, the transaction logs, and the statements of treasury officials implicating the applicant directly. The court observed that economic offences involving large-scale siphoning of public money require thorough custodial examination and unhindered investigation. The court therefore held that the grant of anticipatory bail in such grave economic offences would prejudice investigation, and accordingly the application is dismissed.

title: Ramesh Rastogi v. Vimla Singh
text_content: The plaintiff Ramesh Rastogi filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable residential property in Bhopal executed in the year 2017 against Vimla Singh. In the alternative, the plaintiff claimed refund of earnest money with twenty-four percent interest and substantial damages. During trial, it emerged that the defendant vendor did not possess sole transferable title to the suit property, which was co-owned by his estranged siblings who were not signatories to the agreement to sell. The Rajasthan High Court examined Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act governing specific performance of a part of contract and evaluated whether the purchaser was willing to accept the vendor's undivided fractional share without claiming abatement of price. The court found that the contract could not be specifically enforced in its entirety without infringing third-party rights of non-signatory co-owners. The court held that decreeing specific performance would be inequitable, and therefore the alternative relief of refund of earnest money with interest is granted.

title: Vikas Agarwal v. Mukesh Shah
text_content: The plaintiff Vikas Agarwal instituted a civil suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell against the defendant vendor Mukesh Shah before the civil court at Patna in the year 2019. The plaintiff stated that the parties had entered into a registered agreement to sell an immovable commercial property for a total sale consideration of Rs 78000, whereof a substantial earnest money deposit was duly paid upon execution. The plaintiff averred that he was always ready and willing to perform his part of the contract by paying the balance consideration and obtaining the sale deed. The defendant resisted the suit, contending that time was of the essence of the contract and claiming that the plaintiff had defaulted in paying the balance amount within the agreed ninety days, thereby forfeiting the earnest money deposit under Income Tax Act. The Rajasthan High Court examined the correspondence between parties, the bank solvency certificates produced by the plaintiff, and the terms of the agreement. The court reiterated the settled legal principle that in agreements for sale of immovable property, time is ordinarily not the essence of the contract unless explicitly so stipulated. The court held that the plaintiff has established continuous readiness and willingness throughout, and therefore the suit for specific performance is decreed.

title: Pushpa Mehta v. Geeta Bhatia
text_content: The revisionist tenant Pushpa Mehta approached the Rajasthan High Court in the year 2022 assailing an order of eviction passed under summary eviction provisions of the Rent Control Act in Agra. The respondent landlord Geeta Bhatia had sought recovery of immediate possession of the residential property on the ground of personal requirement as a retired senior citizen needing ground-floor accommodation due to medical infirmities. The tenant sought leave to defend under Section 147, contending that the landlord owned multiple alternative residential flats in Agra and argued that the eviction petition was a stratagem to coerce enhanced rent. The court examined whether the affidavit filed by the tenant disclosed any triable issue of law or fact warranting a full-fledged trial. The court noted that vague assertions regarding alternative accommodation without specific property identification do not constitute triable issues. The court held that the landlord's need is genuine and pressing, and therefore the revision petition is dismissed and the tenant is directed to vacate.

title: Nirmala Rastogi v. Pankaj Rastogi
text_content: The plaintiff bank Nirmala Rastogi filed a suit for foreclosure of equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds against the borrower Pankaj Rastogi in Chennai in the year 2022. The loan amount secured by the title deeds amounted to Rs 299000 disbursed for purchasing commercial printing machinery. The defendant contended that the title deeds were deposited solely for safe custody and disputed the creation of an equitable mortgage, asserting that no memorandum of deposit was registered under the Registration Act. The Rajasthan High Court examined Section 58(f) of Negotiable Instruments Act which recognizes mortgages by deposit of title deeds in specified commercial cities without requiring compulsory registration. The court reviewed the letter of intent, original title deeds produced from bank custody, and the borrower's contemporaneous letters acknowledging the mortgage. The court observed that delivery of title deeds with intent to create security constitutes a valid equitable mortgage under Indian law. The court therefore held that a valid mortgage exists and the bank is entitled to recover its dues, and accordingly the suit is decreed with preliminary decree.

title: Ajay Dwivedi v. Prakash Mishra
text_content: The plaintiff financial institution Ajay Dwivedi instituted a mortgage suit for foreclosure and sale of hypothecated immovable property against the defendant mortgagor Prakash Mishra before the civil court at Agra in the year 2022. The plaintiff stated that the defendant had borrowed a commercial term loan facility of Rs 1505000 and executed a registered simple mortgage deed over his prime commercial building to secure repayment with agreed interest. Upon persistent default in servicing quarterly interest instalments, the loan account was classified as non-performing and statutory recall notices were dispatched. The defendant contested the foreclosure suit, claiming that the penal interest rates charged by the mortgagee were usurious, asserting that the bank had failed to adjust insurance proceeds following a warehouse fire, and seeking extension of the equity of redemption under Hindu Marriage Act. The Rajasthan High Court examined the loan sanction letter, registered mortgage deed, audited account statements, and the provisions of Order XXXIV of the Code of Civil Procedure. The court found that the mortgage debt remained unpaid despite valid demand and noted that interest was computed in conformity with contractual terms. The court held that the mortgagee is entitled to realize its debt through foreclosure, and therefore a preliminary decree for foreclosure and sale is passed.

title: Rohit Yadav v. Sanjay Tiwari
text_content: In this commercial first appeal, the appellant debtor Sanjay Tiwari challenged the decree of recovery passed by the Commercial Division at Nagpur in the year 2015 in favour of supplier Rohit Yadav. The appellant contended that the trial court erred in holding that limitation was extended by an informal email correspondence and argued that an unverified electronic email does not constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt in writing under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. Learned counsel for the respondent supplier produced electronic audit certificates under Section 65B of the Evidence Act proving that the email admitting the liability of Rs 4997000 was dispatched by the authorized chief financial officer of the appellant before the expiry of the original limitation period. The Supreme Court of India examined the statutory requirements of Section 18 of Code of Criminal Procedure in the context of modern electronic commercial communications. The court observed that digital communications admitting subsisting financial obligations satisfy the criteria of written acknowledgment extending limitation. The court therefore held that the recovery suit was filed well within limitation, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the decree is confirmed.

title: Kamla Dwivedi v. Sushma Patel
text_content: The petitioner civil servant Kamla Dwivedi filed a service writ petition before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2015 challenging the proceedings of the Departmental Promotion Committee convened by the respondent department Sushma Patel in Bhopal. The petitioner contended that he was senior in the feeder cadre of Executive Engineers and possessed outstanding annual performance appraisal reports, yet his junior colleagues were promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer while his candidature was superseded without any communicating reason. The respondent department defended the promotion orders, contending that promotions were governed by the principle of merit-cum-seniority under Consumer Protection Act and stated that the DPC had evaluated the relative merit of all officers within the zone of consideration based on benchmark gradings. The court called for the original DPC minutes, the appraisal dossiers, and examined the criteria applied during selection. The court found that uncommunicated below-benchmark remarks in the petitioner's appraisal reports had been taken into consideration by the DPC in violation of the law laid down in Dev Dutt v Union of India. The court held that consideration of uncommunicated adverse remarks vitiates the promotion process, and therefore the petition is allowed directing a review DPC.

title: Naresh Kapoor v. Ravi Saxena
text_content: In this tax appeal, the revenue department Ravi Saxena challenged the decision of the ITAT at Ahmedabad in the year 2015 deleting a TDS default demand raised against employer corporation Naresh Kapoor. The department had demanded tax and interest of Rs 73000 for alleged failure to deduct TDS under Section 192 on perquisites provided to executive employees by way of interest-free housing loans and stock options. Learned counsel for the assessee corporation demonstrated that the recipient employees had already declared the full value of the benefits in their individual income tax returns and had paid due income taxes thereon. The Supreme Court of India examined the first proviso to Section 201(1) of Code of Criminal Procedure which incorporates the principle laid down in Hindustan Coca-Cola. The court noted that where the payee has furnished return of income, accounted for the payment, and discharged taxes, the payer cannot be treated as an assessee-in-default. The court therefore held that the revenue cannot recover the tax a second time from the deductor, and accordingly the revenue appeal is dismissed.

title: Ramesh Kumar v. Kamla Mehta
text_content: The petitioner journalist Ramesh Kumar filed a writ petition under Article 226 before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2015 challenging an order of preventive detention passed against him by the district magistrate Kamla Mehta in Bengaluru under the National Security Act. The detention order was grounded upon investigative articles published by the petitioner reporting on municipal corruption in medical supplies during a public health emergency. The State argued that the publications incited public disorder and justified detention under Transfer of Property Act to maintain public order. The court examined the grounds of detention, the constitutional safeguards under Article 22(5), and the fundamental right to free expression under Article 19(1)(a). The court observed that legitimate criticism of public administration cannot be conflated with a threat to public order or national security. The court held that the detention order is an impermissible muzzling of free press, and therefore the petition is allowed and the detenu is directed to be released.

title: Sanjay Chaturvedi v. Nitin Gupta
text_content: The petitioner candidate Sanjay Chaturvedi filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2015 challenging an order passed by the Returning Officer Nitin Gupta in Jaipur rejecting his nomination papers for the legislative assembly constituency under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Returning Officer had rejected the nomination paper on the hyper-technical ground of a minor clerical omission in the accompanying electoral affidavit, despite the petitioner submitting a rectification affidavit before the deadline for scrutiny. The Election Commission raised a preliminary objection, arguing that under Article 329(b) of the Constitution, all electoral disputes must await completion of the election and can only be adjudicated through an election petition under Consumer Protection Act. The court examined the narrow exceptions where writ intervention is permissible to facilitate rather than stall the democratic election process. The court observed that where rejection of nomination is patently arbitrary and perverse, leaving a candidate remediless until post-election defeats democracy. The court held that the rejection of nomination was wholly arbitrary, and therefore the writ petition is allowed directing acceptance of nomination.

title: Ramesh Singh v. Sanjay Shah
text_content: The petitioner infrastructure company Ramesh Singh filed a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2016 challenging an arbitral award passed in Mumbai in a dispute involving Sanjay Shah. The arbitral tribunal had awarded claims of Rs 252000 in favour of the respondent, rejecting the petitioner's counterclaims for liquidated damages. The petitioner contended that the award suffered from patent illegality, argued that the tribunal had rewritten contractual price escalation formulas, and asserted conflict with the public policy of India. The respondent defended the award, submitting that judicial review under Section 34 is strictly circumscribed and does not permit re-appreciation of evidence under Transfer of Property Act. The court examined the principles formulated by the Supreme Court in Associate Builders and Ssangyong Engineering. The court observed that an arbitral tribunal is the ultimate master of factual evidence and contractual interpretation unless its construction is totally perverse. The court held that the arbitral award does not suffer from any patent illegality or public policy violation, and therefore the Section 34 petition is dismissed.

title: Renu Chaturvedi v. Pankaj Srivastava
text_content: In this company appeal under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the suspended director Pankaj Srivastava challenged the order of the NCLT at Coimbatore in the year 2016 which admitted a Section 9 application filed by operational creditor Renu Chaturvedi. The appellant contended that the operational creditor's claim of Rs 748000 was subject to a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods raised in email correspondence long prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice under Section 8 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. Learned counsel for the operational creditor submitted that the alleged dispute was a spurious defense raised after demand notice to evade insolvency proceedings. The Supreme Court of India examined the email exchanges, the rejection notes, and the seminal ruling in Mobilox Innovations v Kirusa Software. The court found that contemporaneous communications revealed that the corporate debtor had rejected the consignments and raised debit notes prior to notice. The court therefore held that a genuine pre-existing dispute exists barring Section 9 insolvency, and accordingly the appeal is allowed and CIRP is quashed.

title: Geeta Mehta v. Sunita Kapoor
text_content: This application under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act was filed by Geeta Mehta through counsel before the Supreme Court of India in 2016. The applicant had been arrested at Coimbatore following an alleged seizure of narcotic contraband valued at Rs 1003000 in the illicit market. The respondent State represented by Sunita Kapoor opposed the grant of regular bail, highlighting that the quantity recovered fell within the commercial bracket. The applicant contended that no contraband was recovered from his conscious possession and submitted that his name surfaced solely on the basis of an inadmissible confessional disclosure made by a co-accused while in police custody. The court examined the constitutional guarantee of speedy trial under Article 21 vis-a-vis the legislative restrictions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act. The court noted that the prosecution had not produced any independent corroborative evidence connecting the applicant with the alleged drug syndicate. The court therefore held that reasonable grounds exist for believing that the accused is not guilty, and consequently bail is granted subject to stringent conditions.

title: Amit Khanna v. Amit Bhatia
text_content: The appellant assessee Amit Khanna approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2016 challenging the order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal at Patna which upheld the disallowance of business expenditure amounting to Rs 300000 made by the Assessing Officer Amit Bhatia. The Assessing Officer had treated the expenditure incurred on software development, digital system migration, and cloud infrastructure as capital expenditure, disallowing the deduction claimed as revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act. The assessee contended that software licenses and digital upgrades do not create an enduring capital asset in modern computing environments but merely facilitate efficient operation of existing business processes, thereby qualifying fully as revenue expenditure under Code of Criminal Procedure. The Supreme Court of India examined the commercial nature of software licensing agreements and reviewed the leading precedents distinguishing capital from revenue expenditure. The court observed that in the fast-evolving technology sector, expenditures incurred to update and maintain digital systems are essential running operational costs. The court held that the expenditure on software upgrades is deductible as revenue expenditure, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the disallowance is set aside.

title: Lata Malhotra v. Ramesh Kapoor
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the Commissioner of Income Tax Ramesh Kapoor challenged the order of the Tribunal at Hyderabad in the year 2016 which allowed deduction under Section 80-IA of the Income Tax Act to infrastructure corporation Lata Malhotra. The revenue argued that the assessee was merely a works contractor executing government road development tenders and not an infrastructure enterprise developing, maintaining, and operating an infrastructure facility within the statutory scheme. Learned counsel for the assessee demonstrated that the enterprise had assumed complete financial, technical, and operational risks under a Public-Private Partnership concession agreement, having invested Rs 147000 in constructing arterial bridges. The Supreme Court of India analyzed the concession terms, the statutory language of Section 80-IA, and the explanation inserted by Finance Act. The court found that the assessee was an infrastructure developer assuming entrepreneurial risk rather than a simple supply contractor. The court therefore held that the assessee is entitled to the ten-year tax holiday deduction, and accordingly the revenue's appeal is dismissed.

title: Anita Singh v. Rekha Yadav
text_content: The petitioner environmentalist Anita Singh filed a PIL before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2016 challenging the commercial felling of thousands of heritage trees in Patna for constructing an elevated highway project by the infrastructure corporation Rekha Yadav. The petitioner showed that the environmental impact assessment was flawed and demonstrated that viable alternative civil engineering alignments could save the tree canopy. The infrastructure agency contended that the road was essential to decongest vehicular traffic and promised compensatory afforestation of saplings. The court reviewed international protocols on urban forestry, the right to clean air under Article 21, and the recommendations of the Tree Authority. The court observed that planting distant saplings cannot instantly replace century-old oxygen-generating heritage trees that combat severe urban air pollution. The court held that the infrastructure authority must redesign the project alignment to preserve the heritage trees, and therefore the PIL is allowed.

title: Pushpa Khanna v. Usha Agarwal
text_content: The petitioner Pushpa Khanna challenged the revised promotion policy notified by Usha Agarwal public financial institution in Indore in the year 2017. The petitioner alleged that the new policy introduced subjective interview marks of forty percent for promotion to senior management cadre, which drastically altered the rules of the game midway through the recruitment cycle and facilitated nepotistic selections. The financial institution justified the policy, submitting that leadership positions in modern banking require high interpersonal and analytical skills best tested in interviews. The court examined the service regulations under Industrial Disputes Act and reviewed precedents concerning excessive allocation of interview marks in public employment promotions. The court found that allocating disproportionate weight to viva voce in promotion from within an existing workforce creates room for arbitrary favoritism. The court held that the excessive interview weighting is arbitrary and violative of Article 14, and therefore the petition is allowed and promotion criteria are modified.

title: Kavita Dwivedi v. Kamla Chaturvedi
text_content: The revisionist tenant Kavita Dwivedi approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2018 assailing an order of eviction passed under summary eviction provisions of the Rent Control Act in Kanpur. The respondent landlord Kamla Chaturvedi had sought recovery of immediate possession of the residential property on the ground of personal requirement as a retired senior citizen needing ground-floor accommodation due to medical infirmities. The tenant sought leave to defend under Section 138, contending that the landlord owned multiple alternative residential flats in Kanpur and argued that the eviction petition was a stratagem to coerce enhanced rent. The court examined whether the affidavit filed by the tenant disclosed any triable issue of law or fact warranting a full-fledged trial. The court noted that vague assertions regarding alternative accommodation without specific property identification do not constitute triable issues. The court held that the landlord's need is genuine and pressing, and therefore the revision petition is dismissed and the tenant is directed to vacate.

title: Rekha Saxena v. Sushma Yadav
text_content: The petitioner Rekha Saxena filed this bail application in connection with a case registered under Section 125 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act at Hyderabad in the year 2018. The prosecution case against the petitioner, presented by Sushma Yadav, was that intermediate quantity of psychotropic substance was recovered from a business premise occupied by the applicant. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the recovered quantity did not attract the rigorous threshold of commercial quantity and pointed out that the search was carried out after sunset without obtaining any search authorization or recording grounds of belief under Section 42 of Consumer Protection Act. The State argued that the applicant was a repeat offender involved in distribution of prohibited chemical drugs. The court examined the case diary, the seizure memo, and the chemical analysis certificate. The court observed that where recovery falls below commercial quantity, the statutory bar of Section 37 is not attracted and regular bail principles apply. The court held that continued judicial custody is unnecessary for the completion of trial, and therefore bail is granted upon furnishing adequate security.

title: Nitin Kumar v. Lata Pandey
text_content: The applicant Nitin Kumar approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2018 seeking anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apprehending arrest in an investigation registered at Pune. The first information report lodged by Lata Pandey alleged offences of cheating, criminal breach of trust, and forgery under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code involving financial transactions of Rs 1999000. Learned counsel for the applicant submitted that the dispute was purely commercial in character stemming from an audit disagreement between corporate partners, that all financial ledgers were already deposited with the authorities, and that the applicant had no previous criminal record. The prosecution opposed the application, submitting that custodial interrogation was essential to trace the end-use of misappropriated capital and uncover secondary bank accounts. The court weighed the constitutional mandate of personal liberty under Article 21 against the societal need for uninhibited crime detection. The court observed that in financial matters based substantially upon accounting records, pre-arrest bail should not be withheld merely for recovery purposes. The court held that the applicant has established a prima facie case for pre-arrest protection, and therefore anticipatory bail is granted with conditions.

title: Vikas Yadav v. Amit Sharma
text_content: In this criminal appeal, the appellant Vikas Yadav challenged the judgment of conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code recorded by the Sessions Court at Bhopal in the year 2018. The prosecution case against the appellant rested entirely on circumstantial evidence as deposed by witness Amit Sharma. The circumstantial links relied upon were the last seen theory, motive relating to disputed business accounts of Rs 48000, and recovery of the weapon of offence pursuant to a disclosure statement recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. The appellant contended that the chain of circumstantial evidence was fragmented, pointing out that an interval of over twelve hours elapsed between the last seen encounter and the estimated time of death, and alleged that the weapon recovery was planted by investigating officials. The Supreme Court of India examined the golden principles governing circumstantial evidence and evaluated whether every link pointed unerringly to the guilt of the accused. The court found that the prosecution had conclusively established every link in the chain leaving no room for any hypothesis of innocence. The court therefore held that the circumstantial evidence conclusively proves the guilt of the appellant, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Sanjay Chaturvedi v. Renu Verma
text_content: The appellant assessee Sanjay Chaturvedi filed a tax appeal before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2018 challenging the levy of mandatory interest under Section 234B and Section 234C of the Income Tax Act confirmed by the Tribunal at Pune in proceedings initiated by the revenue Renu Verma. The assessing officer had charged interest of Rs 1005000 for shortfall in payment of advance tax instalments, which arose entirely because the assessee had received substantial unexpected capital gains from compulsory land acquisition on the final week of the financial year. The assessee argued that under the proviso to Section 234C of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, no interest can be charged for shortfall in advance tax where the shortfall arises on account of unforeseen capital gains and the assessee discharges the remaining tax liability in subsequent instalments. The court examined the dates of compensation disbursement, the advance tax challans, and the statutory relief provided in the proviso to Section 234C. The court observed that the law does not compel an assessee to perform the impossible task of anticipating unexpected capital gains before they arise. The court held that the assessee is entitled to statutory relief from interest, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the interest levy is cancelled.

title: Deepak Chopra v. Nirmala Tiwari
text_content: In this land acquisition appeal, the acquiring authority Nirmala Tiwari challenged the judgment of the Reference Court at Nagpur in the year 2019 which enhanced the market valuation of acquired lands from Rs 1005000 to double the amount in favour of claimant Deepak Chopra. The appellant contended that the Reference Court committed patent illegality by relying on post-notification sale exemplars and failed to make necessary deductions for developmental charges in a large-scale acquisition of over two hundred acres. Learned counsel for the landowners supported the enhancement, submitting that the acquired lands were surrounded by established educational institutions and commercial complexes possessing exceptional infrastructural advantages. The Supreme Court of India examined the topographical maps, the timeline of notifications under Indian Contract Act, and the settled principles governing developmental deductions. The court found that the Reference Court had applied correct deduction percentages commensurate with the large tract of land acquired. The court therefore held that the enhanced compensation determined by the Reference Court is just and reasonable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Naresh Gupta v. Pooja Saxena
text_content: In this regular second appeal, the appellant daughter Naresh Gupta challenged the concurrent judgments of the courts below at Indore in the year 2019 which had dismissed her suit for partition against her brothers Pooja Saxena. The courts below had held that the plaintiff was not entitled to coparcenary rights since her father had expired prior to the enactment of the Hindu Succession Amendment Act, 2005. The appellant contended that the landmark Constitution Bench ruling in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma conclusively settled that the amended Section 6 confers coparcenary rights on daughters by birth irrespective of whether the father was alive on the date of amendment. The Supreme Court of India examined the statutory interpretation of amended Section 6 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and reviewed the status of the ancestral properties as of December 2004. The court found that no registered partition deed or final decree of court had been executed prior to the statutory cut-off date. The court therefore held that the daughter is an equal coparcener entitled to an equal share, and accordingly the appeal is allowed and preliminary decree is passed.

title: Manju Tiwari v. Kamla Singh
text_content: In this regular second appeal, the appellant daughter Manju Tiwari challenged the concurrent judgments of the courts below at Bhopal in the year 2019 which had dismissed her suit for partition against her brothers Kamla Singh. The courts below had held that the plaintiff was not entitled to coparcenary rights since her father had expired prior to the enactment of the Hindu Succession Amendment Act, 2005. The appellant contended that the landmark Constitution Bench ruling in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma conclusively settled that the amended Section 6 confers coparcenary rights on daughters by birth irrespective of whether the father was alive on the date of amendment. The Supreme Court of India examined the statutory interpretation of amended Section 6 of Indian Contract Act and reviewed the status of the ancestral properties as of December 2004. The court found that no registered partition deed or final decree of court had been executed prior to the statutory cut-off date. The court therefore held that the daughter is an equal coparcener entitled to an equal share, and accordingly the appeal is allowed and preliminary decree is passed.

title: Anita Verma v. Sanjay Tiwari
text_content: The financial creditor financial institution Anita Verma filed an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 before the National Company Law Tribunal at Delhi in the year 2019 seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the corporate debtor Sanjay Tiwari. The financial creditor established that it had disbursed a consortium credit facility of Rs 4998000 for constructing an industrial manufacturing plant, and demonstrated that the corporate debtor had committed continuous payment defaults exceeding the statutory threshold of one crore rupees, with default conclusively proved by the record of default certified by the Information Utility (NeSL). The corporate debtor resisted admission, contending that default was occasioned by macroeconomic factors, arguing that the loan agreement was unstamped under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and asserting that ongoing debt restructuring negotiations precluded the initiation of corporate insolvency. The Supreme Court of India examined the landmark Supreme Court judgments in Innoventive Industries and Swiss Ribbons. The court observed that under Section 7, the adjudicating authority is only required to satisfy itself whether a financial debt exists and default has occurred. The court held that debt and default stand indisputably established, and therefore the Section 7 petition is admitted and moratorium is declared.

title: Sarla Khanna v. Vimla Shah
text_content: The applicant Sarla Khanna approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2019 seeking regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in connection with an offence registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act in Pune. The prosecution alleged that during a naka checking operation, law enforcement personnel intercepted a motor vehicle and recovered a commercial quantity of contraband substance weighing substantially above the statutory threshold. Learned counsel for the applicant argued that the mandatory provisions regarding search and seizure under Sections 42 and 50 of Income Tax Act were violated by the seizing officers and stressed that the applicant had undergone prolonged judicial custody without significant progress in trial. Opposing the plea, learned counsel for the respondent State Vimla Shah contended that the twin statutory conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act impose an absolute bar against release unless the court forms an opinion that the accused is not guilty and is unlikely to commit any offence while on bail. The court scrutinised the chemical examiner report, seizure panchnama, and custodial records. The court held that the applicant failed to satisfy the twin conditions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act, and therefore bail is refused.

title: Kavita Chopra v. Rohit Agarwal
text_content: In this income tax appeal, the Commissioner of Income Tax Rohit Agarwal challenged the order of the Tribunal at Nagpur in the year 2019 which allowed deduction under Section 80-IA of the Income Tax Act to infrastructure corporation Kavita Chopra. The revenue argued that the assessee was merely a works contractor executing government road development tenders and not an infrastructure enterprise developing, maintaining, and operating an infrastructure facility within the statutory scheme. Learned counsel for the assessee demonstrated that the enterprise had assumed complete financial, technical, and operational risks under a Public-Private Partnership concession agreement, having invested Rs 96000 in constructing arterial bridges. The Supreme Court of India analyzed the concession terms, the statutory language of Section 80-IA, and the explanation inserted by Finance Act. The court found that the assessee was an infrastructure developer assuming entrepreneurial risk rather than a simple supply contractor. The court therefore held that the assessee is entitled to the ten-year tax holiday deduction, and accordingly the revenue's appeal is dismissed.

title: Mahesh Agarwal v. Amit Mehta
text_content: The petitioner registered taxpayer Mahesh Agarwal filed a writ petition before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2019 challenging an order passed by the respondent GST revenue authority Amit Mehta in Vadodara disallowing Input Tax Credit amounting to Rs 200000. The department had blocked the petitioner's electronic credit ledger and issued a demand notice with interest and penalties on the ground that the input tax credit availed by the petitioner in return Form GSTR-3B did not match the auto-populated details reflected in Form GSTR-2A, alleging that the selling suppliers had failed to remit the collected tax to the government exchequer. The petitioner demonstrated that he had purchased goods under genuine tax invoices, paid the entire value along with applicable GST through banking channels, and possessed valid e-way bills establishing actual receipt of physical goods. The court examined Section 16(2) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act and reviewed precedents including Bharti Airtel and Arise India. The court observed that a bona fide purchasing dealer who has satisfied all conditions cannot be penalized for subsequent tax remittance defaults of registered suppliers. The court held that the denial of Input Tax Credit is legally unsustainable, and therefore the writ petition is allowed and the demand order is quashed.

title: Pushpa Dwivedi v. Sarla Yadav
text_content: The appellant assessee Pushpa Dwivedi filed an income tax appeal before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2019 challenging an order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal at Jaipur which confirmed a penalty of Rs 2001000 levied under Section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act by the assessing authority Sarla Yadav. The penalty was imposed following the disallowance of a depreciation claim on commercial wind energy equipment in regular assessment proceedings. The appellant contended that full and accurate details of the capital expenditure, equipment installation certificates, and depreciation rates were openly disclosed in the return of income, and argued that a bona fide legal claim rejected by the revenue cannot be equated with concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars. The court reviewed the statutory provisions of Section 271(1)(c) of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and the seminal Supreme Court ruling in CIT v Reliance Petroproducts. The court observed that mere making of a claim that is not accepted by the Assessing Officer does not attract penalty when all facts are fully disclosed. The court held that the levy of penalty is wholly unjustified and untenable, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the penalty order is deleted.

title: Sunita Agarwal v. Pooja Srivastava
text_content: In this regular civil appeal, the appellant tenant Pooja Srivastava challenged the decree of eviction passed in favour of landlord Sunita Agarwal by the appellate rent tribunal in Patna in the year 2020. The eviction proceedings were grounded upon unauthorised subletting of the demised premises and material impairment of property value under the Rent Control Act. The landlord established that the tenant had parted with exclusive possession of a substantial portion of the premises to a third party without obtaining prior written consent as mandated by Industrial Disputes Act. The tenant argued that the third party was merely an employee and business associate assisting in daily operations and not an unauthorised subtenant. The Supreme Court of India examined the report of the local commissioner appointed to inspect the premises, the electricity bills, and the partnership agreement. The court found that exclusive commercial control over the subdivided portion was transferred to a stranger without landlord approval. The court therefore held that unlawful subletting stands conclusively established, and accordingly the tenant's appeal is dismissed.

title: Anita Khanna v. Amit Saxena
text_content: The plaintiff Anita Khanna instituted a civil suit for permanent injunction against the defendant Amit Saxena before the civil court at Indore in the year 2020. The plaintiff averred that he was the absolute owner and in lawful settled possession of the suit parcel of land by virtue of a registered conveyance deed executed under Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant, who was an adjoining landholder possessing no lawful title or interest, had attempted to forcibly trespass into the property, damage the boundary wall, and dispossess the plaintiff without due process of law. The defendant filed a written statement asserting competing ownership over a common pathway and claimed customary easement rights over the disputed boundary strip. The Supreme Court of India examined the chain of title deeds, revenue khasra entries, electricity meter connections, and the report of the local commissioner. The court applied the classical tests under the Specific Relief Act governing grant of perpetual injunction to protect settled peaceful possession against unlawful interference. The court observed that a person in peaceful settled possession is entitled to protect his holding even against lawful owners except through due process. The court held that the plaintiff has established lawful possession and threatened invasion, and therefore the suit for permanent injunction is decreed.

title: Rajesh Agarwal v. Pooja Khanna
text_content: In this commercial arbitration appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, the appellant public undertaking Pooja Khanna challenged the judgment of the High Court at Ahmedabad in the year 2020 which upheld an arbitral award granted to private contractor Rajesh Agarwal. The appellant contended that the sole arbitrator had awarded substantial unliquidated damages of Rs 499000 without any documentary proof of actual loss, and argued that the arbitrator was disqualified under the Seventh Schedule of the Act due to prior professional consultancy relationships. Learned counsel for the contractor demonstrated that the appellant had expressly waived objections under Section 12(5) by participation without protest, and established that the arbitrator had meticulously evaluated chartered accountants' loss certificates. The Supreme Court of India analyzed the statutory framework of Section 34 and Section 37 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act and the limits of appellate interference. The court found that the arbitrator's evaluation of commercial losses was grounded upon credible evidence and within arbitral jurisdiction. The court therefore held that no ground for setting aside the arbitral award is established, and accordingly the commercial appeal is dismissed.

title: Sarla Mishra v. Rohit Tripathi
text_content: In this criminal appeal arising out of proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the appellant Sarla Mishra assailed the concurrent findings of guilt recorded by the appellate court at Kolkata in the year 2020.
