The respondent payee Rohit Tripathi had supplied commercial inventory and received an account payee cheque for Rs 498000 towards discharge of the outstanding commercial invoices. Upon presentation to the drawee bank, the instrument was dishonoured with the remark stop payment instructions. A formal statutory notice was served upon the drawer within the prescribed period of limitation, yet the drawer failed to make payment. The appellant drawer claimed that the goods delivered were defective and argued that the statutory presumption had been successfully rebutted. The Supreme Court of India reviewed the trial court record and noted that the drawer had neither returned the supplied merchandise nor sent any contemporaneous protest communication prior to the dishonour of the negotiable instrument. The court observed that mere oral assertions unsupported by documentary proof cannot displace the statutory presumption operating in favour of the payee. The court therefore held that the complainant has established the existence of a legally enforceable debt, and accordingly the conviction is confirmed.

title: Sunita Tripathi v. Naresh Bhatia
text_content: The petitioner Sunita Tripathi invoked the inherent powers of the Supreme Court of India under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the year 2020 seeking quashing of the First Information Report registered at Coimbatore for alleged offences of cheating, forgery, and criminal conspiracy. The private respondent Naresh Bhatia had lodged the complaint alleging that the petitioner had defaulted on a commercial supply agreement valued at Rs 203000 and had misappropriated advances. The petitioner contended that the dispute was essentially of a civil nature arising out of contractual differences and that the criminal prosecution was initiated maliciously to exert illegitimate pressure for recovery of money. The respondent State asserted that the allegations disclosed prima facie ingredients of criminal breach of trust and cheating from the inception of the contract. The court examined the principles enunciated in Bhajan Lal and analysed the contractual documents executed between the parties under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The court observed that a mere failure to perform a contractual promise does not give rise to criminal liability in the absence of fraudulent intent at the threshold. The court held that the criminal proceedings constitute a manifest abuse of process of the court, and therefore the petition is allowed and the FIR is quashed.

title: Sanjay Bhatia v. Deepak Srivastava
text_content: The petitioner Sanjay Bhatia approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2020 challenging the summary blockage of its electronic credit ledger by the GST Commissioner Deepak Srivastava in Chennai under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The petitioner argued that the authorities had blocked credit amounting to Rs 103000 without assigning reasons in writing, without providing any pre-decisional hearing, and without establishing reasonable grounds to believe that credit was fraudulently availed. The revenue authority submitted that intelligence inputs suggested circular trading within a shell company network. The court examined the scope of Rule 86A and emphasized that power to block credit is a drastic emergency measure that requires objective satisfaction on record. The court observed that Rule 86A cannot be exercised mechanically as an arm-twisting recovery measure during ordinary audit inquiries. The court held that the blockage order violates principles of natural justice and statutory conditions, and therefore the petition is allowed directing unblocking.

title: Pankaj Singh v. Anita Chopra
text_content: The petitioner hospital Pankaj Singh approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2020 challenging a TDS demand notice issued by Anita Chopra Income Tax Officer in Pune. The department contended that retainer consultancy payments made to visiting specialist medical doctors should have been subjected to salary TDS under Section 192 rather than professional fee TDS under Section 194J, raising a differential demand of Rs 4997000. The hospital produced consultancy contracts demonstrating that the doctors were independent practitioners who received fixed retainers plus revenue shares, did not receive provident fund or leave benefits, and were not bound by master-servant employment rules. The court evaluated the tests distinguishing contract of service from contract for services under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The court found that the professional arrangements established independent consultancy rather than employer-employee relationship. The court held that TDS was correctly deducted under Section 194J, and therefore the demand treating the hospital as in default is quashed.

title: Nitin Tiwari v. Pankaj Bhatia
text_content: The citizen welfare forum Nitin Tiwari instituted a public interest litigation before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2020 highlighting the catastrophic dilapidation of municipal roads, open sewer trenches, and ubiquitous potholes across the metropolitan area of Jaipur. The petitioners placed on record photographic documentation and hospital statistics showing that over two hundred commuters had suffered fatal accidents or permanent spinal disabilities during the monsoon season due to unpaved roads and uncovered drainage manholes maintained by the Municipal Corporation Pankaj Bhatia. The municipal body pleaded financial constraints, shortage of bituminous asphalt, and delays in processing maintenance tenders under Indian Contract Act. The court examined the statutory duties imposed upon municipal authorities under the Municipal Corporation Act and the constitutional dimensions of Article 21. The court observed that citizens who pay municipal taxes possess an inalienable fundamental right to safe, motorable, and dignified public roads. The court held that the municipal corporation has failed miserably in discharging its statutory obligations, and therefore the PIL is allowed with time-bound repair directions.

title: Vikas Sharma v. Rohit Verma
text_content: In this constitutional appeal, the elected legislator Rohit Verma challenged the judgment of the High Court at Coimbatore in the year 2020 which declared his election to Parliament void under Section 100 of the Representation of the People Act upon an election petition filed by rival candidate Vikas Sharma. The High Court had found that the elected member had failed to disclose multiple pending criminal charges and substantial commercial assets of Rs 5002000 in his affidavit. The appellant contended that the omissions were unintentional inadvertent oversights that did not materially affect the result of the election under Indian Contract Act. The Supreme Court of India examined the landmark ruling in Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms regarding voters' fundamental right to know under Article 19(1)(a). The court observed that non-disclosure of criminal antecedents and assets taints the purity of the electoral process and constitutes a corrupt practice. The court therefore held that the election was rightly set aside, and accordingly the appeal of the disqualified member is dismissed.

title: Anita Kumar v. Prakash Pandey
text_content: The petitioner journalist Anita Kumar filed a writ petition under Article 226 before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2020 challenging an order of preventive detention passed against him by the district magistrate Prakash Pandey in Hyderabad under the National Security Act. The detention order was grounded upon investigative articles published by the petitioner reporting on municipal corruption in medical supplies during a public health emergency. The State argued that the publications incited public disorder and justified detention under Arbitration and Conciliation Act to maintain public order. The court examined the grounds of detention, the constitutional safeguards under Article 22(5), and the fundamental right to free expression under Article 19(1)(a). The court observed that legitimate criticism of public administration cannot be conflated with a threat to public order or national security. The court held that the detention order is an impermissible muzzling of free press, and therefore the petition is allowed and the detenu is directed to be released.

title: Rekha Chopra v. Manju Mishra
text_content: The citizen welfare forum Rekha Chopra instituted a public interest litigation before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2020 highlighting the catastrophic dilapidation of municipal roads, open sewer trenches, and ubiquitous potholes across the metropolitan area of Agra. The petitioners placed on record photographic documentation and hospital statistics showing that over two hundred commuters had suffered fatal accidents or permanent spinal disabilities during the monsoon season due to unpaved roads and uncovered drainage manholes maintained by the Municipal Corporation Manju Mishra. The municipal body pleaded financial constraints, shortage of bituminous asphalt, and delays in processing maintenance tenders under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court examined the statutory duties imposed upon municipal authorities under the Municipal Corporation Act and the constitutional dimensions of Article 21. The court observed that citizens who pay municipal taxes possess an inalienable fundamental right to safe, motorable, and dignified public roads. The court held that the municipal corporation has failed miserably in discharging its statutory obligations, and therefore the PIL is allowed with time-bound repair directions.

title: Seema Saxena v. Nitin Verma
text_content: The plaintiff Seema Saxena filed a commercial suit for permanent injunction against Nitin Verma before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2021 seeking to restrain the defendant from infringing registered trademarks and passing off goods using deceptively similar brand packaging in Nagpur. The plaintiff proved long-standing commercial use and substantial advertising expenditure of Rs 149000 establishing immense consumer goodwill in the market. The defendant contended that the disputed mark was generic and descriptive, claiming prior user in a localized rural market prior to the plaintiff's registration. The court evaluated the phonetic, visual, and conceptual similarity between the rival trademarks under Transfer of Property Act and assessed the likelihood of public confusion. The court observed that registration confers an exclusive statutory monopoly and noted that the defendant's packaging was a deceptive imitation designed to mislead consumers. The court held that the defendant is guilty of trademark infringement and passing off, and therefore a permanent injunction is granted with compensatory damages.

title: Dinesh Malhotra v. Sanjay Rastogi
text_content: In this first appeal, the appellant mortgagor Sanjay Rastogi challenged the final decree for foreclosure and sale passed in favour of mortgagee Dinesh Malhotra by the civil court in Chennai in the year 2021. The appellant contended that under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, the equity of redemption remained alive until the confirmation of court auction sale and tendered a partial payment of Rs 195000 in court while praying for rescheduling of dues. Learned counsel for the respondent mortgagee submitted that the mortgagor had failed to deposit the full redemption amount within the six months granted under the preliminary decree and argued that the right to redeem stood legally extinguished upon final decree. The Supreme Court of India examined the statutory scheme of Order XXXIV Rules 4 and 5 of CPC and the judicial precedents governing mortgagor's right to redeem prior to sale confirmation. The court noted that equity of redemption is an inviolable statutory right which can be exercised upon depositing the entire outstanding debt with costs prior to auction. The court held that upon failure to tender the complete mortgage debt, foreclosure must proceed, and therefore the appeal is dismissed.

title: Pankaj Kapoor v. Vijay Singh
text_content: The petitioner Pankaj Kapoor approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2021 seeking to set aside a foreign arbitral award under Section 48 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act in enforcement proceedings initiated by foreign supplier Vijay Singh in Kanpur. The award had granted commercial dues of Rs 98000. The petitioner contended that the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties because the arbitral institution had appointed a sole arbitrator in violation of the contractually mandated three-arbitrator clause. The respondent submitted that institutional rules to which the parties had agreed provided for sole arbitrator appointment in expedited commercial cases. The court examined the arbitration agreement, institutional rules, and the strict grounds for refusing enforcement of New York Convention awards under Consumer Protection Act. The court observed that where parties agree to institutional arbitration, the institutional procedural rules govern the composition of the arbitral tribunal. The court held that the tribunal was validly constituted in accordance with agreed rules, and therefore the objections are rejected and enforcement is allowed.

title: Rajesh Rastogi v. Pushpa Malhotra
text_content: The applicant Rajesh Rastogi approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2021 seeking anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apprehending arrest in an investigation registered at Lucknow. The first information report lodged by Pushpa Malhotra alleged offences of cheating, criminal breach of trust, and forgery under Code of Criminal Procedure involving financial transactions of Rs 53000. Learned counsel for the applicant submitted that the dispute was purely commercial in character stemming from an audit disagreement between corporate partners, that all financial ledgers were already deposited with the authorities, and that the applicant had no previous criminal record. The prosecution opposed the application, submitting that custodial interrogation was essential to trace the end-use of misappropriated capital and uncover secondary bank accounts. The court weighed the constitutional mandate of personal liberty under Article 21 against the societal need for uninhibited crime detection. The court observed that in financial matters based substantially upon accounting records, pre-arrest bail should not be withheld merely for recovery purposes. The court held that the applicant has established a prima facie case for pre-arrest protection, and therefore anticipatory bail is granted with conditions.

title: Kavita Sharma v. Kavita Patel
text_content: In this writ appeal, the management Kavita Patel challenged the judgment of the Single Judge at Kanpur in the year 2021 which upheld the award of the Industrial Tribunal ordering full reinstatement with back wages for employee Kavita Sharma. The management argued that the employee had lost the confidence of the employer due to financial irregularities involving company inventory worth Rs 98000 and contended that monetary compensation was the only proper remedy. Learned counsel for the workman demonstrated that the criminal court had completely acquitted the workman on the identical set of allegations, and established that the management had initiated disciplinary action solely as an act of anti-union victimization. The Supreme Court of India examined the scope of judicial review under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act and reviewed the findings of the tribunal. The court observed that where an enquiry is found to be mala fide and punitive, reinstatement with back wages is the standard statutory remedy. The court therefore held that the order of reinstatement is just and lawful, and accordingly the management appeal is dismissed.

title: Deepak Malhotra v. Renu Patel
text_content: In this civil appeal, the employer company Renu Patel assailed the judgment of the High Court at Pune in the year 2021 which quashed the retrenchment of seventy workmen represented by union representative Deepak Malhotra. The appellant contended that economic distress caused by cancellation of export licenses necessitated workforce downsizing and asserted that full retrenchment compensation of Rs 5002000 had been deposited in the workmen's bank accounts. Learned counsel for the union argued that the company had flagrantly violated the mandatory rule of last come, first go enshrined in Section 25-G of the Industrial Disputes Act by retaining junior contract workers while retrenching senior permanent employees without publishing any seniority list. The Supreme Court of India examined the seniority rosters, the deployment of subcontracted personnel, and the statutory requirements under Negotiable Instruments Act. The court observed that compliance with Section 25-G is mandatory and deviation therefrom renders the entire retrenchment exercise void. The court therefore held that the retrenchment violates the statutory last come first go rule, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

title: Priya Pandey v. Kavita Chopra
text_content: The petitioner retired employee Priya Pandey instituted proceedings under Section 7 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 against the employer Kavita Chopra before the Controlling Authority at Pune in the year 2021. The petitioner claimed statutory gratuity of Rs 98000 based on thirty-two years of continuous service, which the employer had withheld following his superannuation. The employer contended that gratuity was lawfully forfeited under Section 4(6) of the Act because the employee was subjected to disciplinary proceedings on the eve of retirement for alleged administrative negligence resulting in operational financial loss to the enterprise. The employee argued that under Section 4(6) of Negotiable Instruments Act, gratuity can be forfeited only where services are terminated for riotous or disorderly conduct or an offence involving moral turpitude, and pointed out that no termination order was ever passed prior to superannuation. The Supreme Court of India examined the statutory provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act and the judicial precedents governing forfeiture of accrued terminal benefits. The court observed that gratuity is a hard-earned statutory entitlement and cannot be withheld or forfeited in the absence of a lawful dismissal order on specified grounds. The court held that the withholding of gratuity is wholly illegal, and therefore directed payment of full gratuity with ten percent compound interest.

title: Rekha Kumar v. Rekha Saxena
text_content: The petitioner citizen Rekha Kumar approached the Supreme Court of India in the year 2021 invoking Article 226 of the Constitution of India to challenge a summary demolition order issued by the municipal development authority Rekha Saxena in Nagpur. The authority had arrived with bulldozers and demolished the petitioner's residential premises and commercial shop without serving any prior statutory show-cause notice, without affording an opportunity of hearing, and without allowing time to seek judicial redress, alleging that the structure was an illegal encroachment on public land. The petitioner proved registered ownership deeds, continuous property tax receipts dating back thirty years, and asserted gross violation of Article 21. The municipal authority contended that encroachments on public pathways could be removed summarily without prior notice under Consumer Protection Act. The court examined the constitutional jurisprudence on shelter as an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21 and the necessity of procedural fairness. The court observed that executive bulldozing of homes without notice and hearing is completely antithetical to the rule of law and constitutional governance. The court held that the demolition was unlawful and unconstitutional, and therefore directed restitution, interim compensation of Rs 300000, and allowed the petition.

title: Seema Kapoor v. Sanjay Verma
text_content: The public interest litigation was instituted by the environmental action group Seema Kapoor before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2021 seeking urgent judicial intervention against the rampant discharge of untreated toxic industrial effluents into the sacred river basin traversing Hyderabad. The petitioners submitted certified water laboratory reports demonstrating that the chemical industrial cluster operated by Sanjay Verma was releasing carcinogenic heavy metals and untreated chemical waste directly into the river, contaminating the drinking water supply of two million residents and destroying aquatic fauna. The industrial respondents argued that they had installed effluent treatment plants and contended that stringent judicial directions would cause closure of industries employing thousands of industrial workers under Hindu Marriage Act. The court appointed an independent court commissioner comprising scientists from the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute and examined the ground data. The court applied the polluter pays principle and the precautionary principle enshrined under Article 21 and international environmental jurisprudence. The court held that industrial profits cannot take precedence over the fundamental right to clean water and public health, and therefore the PIL is allowed with directions.

title: Pushpa Malhotra v. Ramesh Bhatia
text_content: In this civil appeal, the appellant Ramesh Bhatia challenged the decree of permanent injunction granted by the trial court in Chennai in the year 2022 restraining the appellant from constructing on a disputed vacant plot measuring five hundred square yards. The respondent plaintiff Pushpa Malhotra had established continuous possession and produced municipal sanction plans for development. The appellant contended that the trial court erred in granting permanent injunction without requiring the plaintiff to seek a declaration of title, pointing out that a genuine cloud was cast over the plaintiff's ownership by an rival agreement to sell. The Supreme Court of India examined the law laid down in Anathula Sudhakar v P. Buchi Reddy regarding suits for injunction simpliciter versus suits requiring declaratory relief. The court found that the defendant had merely raised bare denials without producing any registered document of title capable of casting a real cloud. The court therefore held that the suit for permanent injunction simpliciter is fully maintainable, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed and the injunction is upheld.

title: Sanjay Yadav v. Mukesh Singh
text_content: The plaintiff corporate enterprise Sanjay Yadav instituted a commercial suit for breach of contract and recovery of liquidated damages against the defendant supplier Mukesh Singh before the Commercial Court at Hyderabad in the year 2022. The plaintiff stated that the parties had entered into a binding long-term commercial supply agreement for high-grade industrial alloys, whereunder the defendant was obligated to deliver scheduled monthly consignments. Upon a sudden surge in global commodity market prices, the defendant repudiated the contract and failed to supply raw materials, forcing the plaintiff to procure substitute merchandise from spot markets at exorbitant premiums to fulfill international export commitments, incurring damages of Rs 51000. The defendant contended that the sudden price escalation rendered the contract commercially impracticable and invoked the doctrine of frustration under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act along with force majeure clauses under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The Supreme Court of India examined the contractual terms, the price variation mechanisms, and the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Energy Watchdog v CERC. The court observed that mere abnormal rise or fall in prices is an ordinary commercial risk that does not frustrate a commercial contract. The court held that the defendant committed a deliberate breach of contract, and therefore the commercial suit is decreed for damages with contractual interest.

title: Asha Agarwal v. Prakash Pandey
text_content: The accused Asha Agarwal faced trial before the Sessions Court at Coimbatore in the year 2022 for committing murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that the accused along with co-accused persons attacked the deceased with iron rods outside a commercial premise. The sole eyewitness Prakash Pandey identified the accused in court during trial, but admitted in cross-examination that visibility was poor due to night conditions and acknowledged that no test identification parade had been conducted during police investigation. The defence produced independent witnesses establishing that the accused was present at his workplace forty kilometres away at the time of the alleged incident. The Supreme Court of India scrutinized the dock identification, the absence of prior test identification, and the credible documentary evidence supporting the plea of alibi. The court observed that dock identification made for the first time in court without corroborative test identification is inherently fragile and unsafe to convict. The court held that the accused is entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt, and therefore the appeal is allowed and the accused is acquitted of the charge.

title: Rajesh Gupta v. Seema Gupta
text_content: The petitioner Rajesh Gupta preferred this petition under Section 482 of CrPC before the Supreme Court of India seeking to quash criminal proceedings pending in Kolkata in the year 2023. The respondent Seema Gupta had alleged that the petitioner, acting as an independent valuer, had prepared an inflated valuation report under Code of Criminal Procedure facilitating credit facilities of Rs 1498000. Learned counsel for the petitioner argued that the petitioner was an independent professional who acted bona fide on the basis of documents supplied by the bank and contended that no criminal mens rea could be imputed to professional opinion. The investigating agency opposed the plea, claiming that the valuation report omitted crucial encumbrances on the mortgaged property. The court carefully perused the chargesheet, witness statements, and guidelines governing professional valuation standards. The court observed that professional negligence, even if established, does not ipso facto translate into criminal conspiracy or fraud without culpable knowledge. The court held that the criminal prosecution against the professional valuer cannot be sustained, and therefore the petition is allowed and proceedings are quashed.

title: Ramesh Dwivedi v. Sanjay Malhotra
text_content: The petitioner assessee Ramesh Dwivedi filed a writ petition before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2023 challenging the validity of a notice issued under Section 148 and the reassessment order passed under Section 147 of the Income Tax Act by the respondent Assessing Officer Sanjay Malhotra in Varanasi. The assessing officer had reopened the concluded regular assessment after four years, alleging that taxable income amounting to Rs 248000 had escaped assessment on account of unexplained accommodation entries and share capital received at substantial premium. The petitioner demonstrated that during the original scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3), full disclosures regarding share capital, bank statements, and investor confirmations had been furnished and examined, rendering the reopening a mere impermissible change of opinion without new tangible material. The court scrutinized the reasons recorded for reopening, the audit objections, and the statutory requirements under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The court reiterated the settled legal position in Kelvinator of India that reassessment cannot be initiated on the basis of a mere change of opinion. The court held that the reopening is devoid of new tangible material and lacks jurisdiction, and therefore the petition is allowed and reassessment is quashed.

title: Ramesh Shah v. Renu Yadav
text_content: The petitioner resident association Ramesh Shah filed a PIL before the Supreme Court of India in the year 2023 seeking an urgent independent structural safety audit of high-rise residential complexes constructed by the urban development authority Renu Yadav in Indore. The petitioners showed that multiple newly delivered residential towers exhibited extensive structural beam cracks, spalling concrete, and foundation settlement, threatening the lives of thousands of occupant families. The development authority downplayed the cracks as superficial cosmetic shrinkage. The court constituted an expert committee of senior civil engineering professors from the Indian Institute of Technology to conduct non-destructive testing. The expert report confirmed severe structural integrity compromises and substandard cement quality in load-bearing columns. The court held that the state authority cannot endanger human lives through shoddy construction, and therefore the PIL is allowed directing immediate structural retrofitting.

title: Vikas Tiwari v. Vikas Sharma
text_content: The complainant Vikas Tiwari instituted criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against Vikas Sharma before the trial court in Agra in the year 2024. The complainant stated that in discharge of a legally enforceable debt, the accused drawer had issued an account payee cheque of Rs 80000 drawn on a nationalised bank. Upon presentation for encashment through banking channels, the cheque was dishonoured and returned unpaid with the bank memo citing insufficiency of funds. The payee dispatched a statutory notice of demand as mandated by the Negotiable Instruments Act calling upon the drawer to pay within fifteen days. The accused admitted the signatures on the cheque but contended that the instrument had been handed over merely as security and denied the existence of any legally enforceable debt. The Supreme Court of India examined the documentary evidence including ledger accounts, the cheque return memo, and legal presumptions under Hindu Marriage Act. The court held that the accused failed to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and therefore the conviction of the drawer is upheld and the appeal is dismissed.

title: Vimla Joshi v. Usha Rastogi
text_content: In this consumer appeal, the appellant nursing home Usha Rastogi challenged the judgment of the District Consumer Commission at Jaipur in the year 2018 which found the hospital guilty of medical negligence in the treatment of newborn infant Vimla Joshi. The appellant argued that the newborn suffered from congenital retinopathy of prematurity and contended that the attending pediatricians had provided optimal care within the limits of medical science. Learned counsel for the complainant demonstrated that the hospital failed to arrange mandatory ophthalmological screening of the premature infant within thirty days of birth as mandated by national neonatology protocols, resulting in irreversible total blindness. The Tamil Nadu SCDRC reviewed the clinical case sheets, neonatology guidelines, and expert medical testimony. The court found that omission to conduct timely ROP screening of a high-risk premature infant was a clear breach of medical duty directly causing vision loss. The court therefore held that deficiency in medical care stands established beyond doubt, and accordingly the hospital's appeal is dismissed.

title: Anil Shah v. Mahesh Malhotra
text_content: The complainant Anil Shah instituted a consumer complaint against the cellular telecom service provider Mahesh Malhotra before the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Patna in the year 2018. The complainant alleged that without any prior notification, verification, or statutory consent, the telecom operator abruptly disconnected his postpaid corporate mobile connection which he had utilized for eighteen years. The abrupt disconnection occurred while the complainant was traveling abroad, rendering his banking accounts and international travel bookings inaccessible, and resulting in direct commercial losses of Rs 246000. The telecom service provider defended the disconnection, alleging that the mobile number was flagged for suspicious international roaming activity and claimed immunity under the Indian Telegraph Act and general subscription conditions under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The Tamil Nadu SCDRC examined the TRAI regulations governing disconnection of telecommunication services and verified that the subscriber's billing was current without arrears. The court observed that telecommunication has become an essential lifeline and arbitrary disconnection without notice constitutes gross deficiency in service. The court held that the telecom company acted with highhanded negligence, and therefore directed immediate reconnection with compensation and allowed the complaint.

title: Pankaj Sharma v. Anil Yadav
text_content: The complainant business enterprise Pankaj Sharma filed a consumer complaint against Anil Yadav broadband and leased-line internet provider in Ahmedabad in the year 2018. The complainant had subscribed to a dedicated high-speed optical fiber leased line guaranteeing 99.9% uptime for commercial software exports. The complainant established that the leased line remained completely inoperative for eighteen consecutive days due to uncoordinated roadside cable severance, resulting in contractual penalties from foreign clients amounting to Rs 1996000. The service provider pleaded force majeure, citing civic road-widening works, and relied on contractual limitation of liability clauses restricting damages to rental credits. The court examined the Service Level Agreement, the restoration logs, and the principles governing exemption clauses in consumer contracts under Industrial Disputes Act. The court observed that prolonged failure to restore commercial connectivity without arranging alternative routing cannot be excused under force majeure. The court held that the service provider is liable for commercial deficiency, and therefore the complaint is allowed with compensatory damages.

title: Vijay Pandey v. Manju Bhatia
text_content: The complainant Vijay Pandey filed a consumer complaint against the manufacturer and authorized dealer Manju Bhatia before the District Consumer Commission at Patna in the year 2019 alleging manufacturing defect in a brand-new commercial heavy vehicle. The complainant stated that he had purchased the vehicle for Rs 105000 to earn his livelihood through self-employment, but within three weeks of delivery, the vehicle experienced repeated engine seizures, transmission failures, and structural chassis alignment defects requiring twelve visits to the authorized workshop. The manufacturer resisted liability, contending that the defects arose from rough driving conditions, overloading, and failure to observe periodic maintenance schedules under Consumer Protection Act, and maintained that under the warranty terms, the customer was only entitled to free component replacement rather than vehicle replacement. The Tamil Nadu SCDRC referred the vehicle for forensic mechanical testing to a recognized government engineering institute under Section 13(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act. The expert report confirmed that the engine block suffered from metallurgical porosity and inherent manufacturing flaws incapable of rectification. The court held that the product suffers from an irreparable manufacturing defect, and therefore directed replacement with a new vehicle or refund with interest.

title: Meera Pandey v. Rohit Patel
text_content: The complainant Meera Pandey filed a consumer complaint against Rohit Patel general insurance company for repudiation of a commercial vehicle total loss claim amounting to Rs 79000 in Indore in the year 2020. The vehicle was stolen from a secured transport yard, and an FIR was immediately registered with police authorities. The insurer rejected the theft claim citing a thirty-day delay in formally intimating the insurance company, invoking strict notification policy clauses. The court referred to the circular issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority and the Supreme Court judgment in Gurshinder Singh v Shriram General Insurance. The court observed that where theft is immediately reported to the police and verified as genuine by the final untraced report, mere delay in intimating the insurer cannot defeat a legitimate claim. The court held that the repudiation based solely on delayed intimation is illegal, and therefore directed the insurance company to settle the claim in full.

title: Nitin Verma v. Nitin Rastogi
text_content: The complainant Nitin Verma instituted a consumer complaint alleging gross medical negligence against the respondent multispecialty hospital and operating surgeon Nitin Rastogi before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Bengaluru in the year 2020. The complainant claimed compensation of Rs 75000 stating that during an elective abdominal surgery, the surgical team negligently left a surgical mop inside the peritoneal cavity, leading to severe sepsis, peritonitis, multiple corrective emergency laparotomies, and prolonged ICU hospitalization. The hospital and doctors denied negligence, contending that they had followed standard surgical protocols and argued that postoperative complications were inherent risks of major abdominal interventions under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The Tamil Nadu SCDRC called for an independent expert evaluation from a premier government medical college board and examined the surgical theater swab count charts. The court applied the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur and evaluated the duty of care under the classical Bolam and Bolitho standards of medical negligence. The court observed that leaving foreign surgical instruments inside a patient's body constitutes incontrovertible medical negligence that speaks for itself. The court held that the hospital and operating surgeon are jointly and severally liable, and therefore awarded substantial compensation and allowed the complaint.

title: Ramesh Joshi v. Anita Mishra
text_content: The complainant Ramesh Joshi instituted a consumer complaint against the cellular telecom service provider Anita Mishra before the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Lucknow in the year 2020. The complainant alleged that without any prior notification, verification, or statutory consent, the telecom operator abruptly disconnected his postpaid corporate mobile connection which he had utilized for eighteen years. The abrupt disconnection occurred while the complainant was traveling abroad, rendering his banking accounts and international travel bookings inaccessible, and resulting in direct commercial losses of Rs 499000. The telecom service provider defended the disconnection, alleging that the mobile number was flagged for suspicious international roaming activity and claimed immunity under the Indian Telegraph Act and general subscription conditions under Transfer of Property Act. The Tamil Nadu SCDRC examined the TRAI regulations governing disconnection of telecommunication services and verified that the subscriber's billing was current without arrears. The court observed that telecommunication has become an essential lifeline and arbitrary disconnection without notice constitutes gross deficiency in service. The court held that the telecom company acted with highhanded negligence, and therefore directed immediate reconnection with compensation and allowed the complaint.

title: Vimla Tripathi v. Anil Chopra
text_content: The complainant Vimla Tripathi filed a consumer complaint under the Consumer Protection Act against the respondent commercial bank Anil Chopra before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Indore in the year 2023. The complainant alleged that due to gross deficiency in banking service and systemic security vulnerabilities in the bank's electronic gateway, unauthorized cyber transactions amounting to Rs 155000 were fraudulently debited from his savings account in multiple tranches within twenty minutes without any one-time password being delivered to his registered mobile number. The complainant immediately notified the bank branch within three hours and lodged a police cyber complaint, but the bank refused reimbursement, alleging that the customer had compromised his confidential credentials through negligence under Code of Criminal Procedure. The Tamil Nadu SCDRC examined the Reserve Bank of India circular governing customer protection in unauthorized electronic banking transactions and reviewed the server audit logs. The court observed that where the consumer notifies the financial institution within three working days, the customer liability is zero under binding RBI directions. The court held that the bank is guilty of deficiency in service, and therefore directed full refund of the debited amount with nine percent interest and costs.

title: Sushma Verma v. Nitin Kapoor
text_content: The complainant Sushma Verma filed a consumer complaint against Nitin Kapoor general insurance company for repudiation of a commercial vehicle total loss claim amounting to Rs 97000 in Kolkata in the year 2015. The vehicle was stolen from a secured transport yard, and an FIR was immediately registered with police authorities. The insurer rejected the theft claim citing a thirty-day delay in formally intimating the insurance company, invoking strict notification policy clauses. The court referred to the circular issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority and the Supreme Court judgment in Gurshinder Singh v Shriram General Insurance. The court observed that where theft is immediately reported to the police and verified as genuine by the final untraced report, mere delay in intimating the insurer cannot defeat a legitimate claim. The court held that the repudiation based solely on delayed intimation is illegal, and therefore directed the insurance company to settle the claim in full.

title: Suresh Malhotra v. Sunita Kapoor
text_content: In this consumer appeal, the appellant banking institution Sunita Kapoor challenged the order of the District Consumer Commission at Jaipur in the year 2016 which awarded compensation to consumer Suresh Malhotra for wrongful dishonour of commercial cheques. The bank contended that the cheque dishonour was occasioned by a routine technical migration to a new core banking platform and argued that no mala fide intent or actionable deficiency in service was present. Learned counsel for the consumer established that on the relevant date, the complainant had clear unencumbered liquid funds of Rs 101000 in the account, and demonstrated that wrongful dishonour severely tarnished the commercial reputation and credit rating of the consumer in local business circles. The UP SCDRC examined the statutory duties of bankers under Hindu Marriage Act and evaluated the damages suffered by the business proprietor. The court observed that wrongful dishonour of a cheque despite sufficient balance strikes at the commercial credibility of a business and constitutes deficiency per se. The court therefore held that the compensation awarded by the forum is justified, and accordingly the bank's appeal is dismissed.

title: Prakash Patel v. Sanjay Tiwari
text_content: In this consumer revision petition, the manufacturing company Sanjay Tiwari challenged the order of the State Commission at Surat in the year 2017 directing recall and refund of an electronic appliance valued at Rs 154000 sold to consumer Prakash Patel. The manufacturer contended that the device had functioned satisfactorily for six months before the breakdown and argued that the customer had tampered with internal circuitry through unauthorized local technicians. Learned counsel for the consumer produced job cards demonstrating that authorized technicians had visited the premises five times and had replaced the motherboard twice without successfully resolving intermittent overheating and sudden short-circuits. The UP SCDRC reviewed the warranty conditions, service logs, and statutory product liability provisions under the Consumer Protection Act. The court observed that repeated failure of primary components within the warranty period establishes that the product is inherently defective and unsafe. The court therefore held that the consumer is entitled to complete refund with compensation, and accordingly the revision petition is dismissed.

title: Rajesh Malhotra v. Vimla Shah
text_content: The complainant Rajesh Malhotra instituted a consumer complaint against the respondent insurance company Vimla Shah before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission at Ahmedabad in the year 2021 challenging the wrongful repudiation of a fire and special perils insurance claim. The complainant stated that his industrial textile warehouse situated in Ahmedabad was insured for Rs 750000 and suffered catastrophic destruction in an accidental electrical short-circuit fire. The independent surveyor appointed by the insurer assessed the net loss at Rs 750000, yet the insurance company repudiated the entire claim on the pretext that the insured had failed to maintain operational fire hydrants in alleged breach of policy warranty under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. The complainant proved that all fire safety inspections had been conducted, fire department clearances were current, and the fire brigade had certified the accidental cause. The UP SCDRC scrutinized the survey report, the fire department findings, and the terms of the insurance contract. The court observed that insurance contracts cannot be repudiated on technical and hyper-critical interpretations of ancillary warranties where loss is genuine and accidental. The court held that the repudiation of the insurance claim is arbitrary and unlawful, and therefore directed the insurer to pay the assessed claim amount with interest.

title: Anita Mishra v. Deepak Malhotra
text_content: The complainant Anita Mishra filed a complaint against Deepak Malhotra diagnostic pathology center in Agra in the year 2021 claiming damages of Rs 247000 for issuing an erroneous and false negative biopsy report regarding a malignant tumor. The complainant alleged that the inaccurate diagnostic report delayed vital oncological chemotherapy by fourteen months, allowing the cancer to metastasize into advanced Stage IV. The diagnostic center pleaded human error in slide preparation and claimed limitation of liability under the disclaimer printed on the report. The court examined the revised histopathology findings from two independent oncology institutes confirming obvious presence of malignant cells in the original slides. The court observed that diagnostic laboratories hold patients' lives in their hands and cannot escape liability for gross diagnostic blunders through preprinted disclaimers. The court held that the diagnostic center is guilty of egregious medical negligence, and therefore the complaint is allowed with compensatory damages.

title: Deepak Joshi v. Usha Patel
text_content: In this consumer revision petition, the petitioner insurance company Usha Patel assailed the order of the State Commission at Jaipur in the year 2022 directing payment of a health insurance mediclaim of Rs 149000 to policyholder Deepak Joshi. The insurer contended that the policyholder had suppressed pre-existing hypertension and diabetes at the time of proposal inception, thereby violating the fundamental doctrine of uberrima fides under Central Goods and Services Tax Act. Learned counsel for the insured demonstrated that the hospital admission was for an emergency surgical procedure relating to acute fracture sustained in an accidental fall, which had zero causal nexus with the alleged lifestyle conditions. The UP SCDRC examined the medical discharge summary, the proposal form, and the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Manmohan Nanda v United India Assurance. The court observed that every common lifestyle condition cannot be classified as a material pre-existing disease to repudiate unrelated emergency medical claims. The court therefore held that the repudiation was unjustified and amounts to deficiency in service, and accordingly the revision petition is dismissed.

title: Vijay Rastogi v. Ravi Srivastava
text_content: The complainant Vijay Rastogi approached the UP SCDRC in the year 2024 alleging unfair trade practice and deficiency in service against Ravi Srivastava bank for failing to return original title deeds of residential property mortgaged for a housing loan in Indore. The complainant established that he had fully repaid the entire housing loan along with interest amounting to Rs 153000 and obtained a formal no-dues certificate, yet the bank failed to return the original registered sale deeds, subsequently admitting that the documents were misplaced from the central repository. The bank offered token compensation of five thousand rupees and suggested obtaining certified copies from the sub-registrar office at bank expense. The court observed that loss of original title deeds permanently impairs the marketability and resale value of real estate and causes extreme mental agony. The court held that losing property documents is gross negligence and deficiency in service, and therefore awarded substantial compensation and allowed the complaint.
